#3621. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3620. Nintendo Wanted Ocarina Of Time To Feel Better In The Remake, Not Just Different

Remaking a game like The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time required Nintendo to nail a fine balance between staying faithful to the original and updating it where it mattered. The Ocarina of Time remake largely sticks to the original's foundations while adding features like a dedicated jump button and updated controls. That was one of several changes, as Nintendo's core design philosophy was to modernize execution and comfort while preserving the original emotional and narrative intent.

As Legend of Zelda producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained in an interview with GameSpot, early pre-production focused on setting clear boundaries for what would and wouldn't change in the remake. "One of the first discussions we had leading up to the full-blown development of the title was really clearly establishing what it is we were going to change and what it is that we weren't going to change," Fujibayashi said via a translator. "Starting with the kind of stuff that we wanted to change, was really focused on leveraging the capabilities of the Nintendo Switch 2 hardware because it was going to be developed for that hardware. Leveraging all that capability so that we can remove any stress from the gameplay experience so that people can enjoy the game, fully."

In addition to the changes in the game's controls, Fujibayashi added that the updated graphics also allowed the team to "provide a lot more information" to players, and the sound design also got a big upgrade: 5.1-channel surround sound for the background music.

To reduce friction, the team concluded that a dedicated jump action would give players more agency to explore the world without changing the core experience. "There was a lot of heavy discussion, as you mentioned, about the jump button," Fujibayashi said. "Ultimately, we ended up in the conclusion that being able to allow players to jump anywhere will make the gameplay experience a lot smoother and allow players to be really able to fully enjoy the experience that this game is trying to provide."

The Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time launches for Switch 2 on November 5, and it's already one of the year's best-reviewed games.

"The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a reverent remake with stellar presentation, letting the original greatness shine through," Steve Watts wrote in GameSpot's Ocarina of Time remake review.

#3619. Inside LA’s Election Night Parties as DSA-Backed Nithya Raman Threatens to Unseat Karen Bass

Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”

But I can report that there were a lot of ecstatic and tipsy socialists in oversized vintage jackets at the DSA election party on the edge of Skid Row in Los Angeles Tuesday night. And, boy, did these socialists have a lot to celebrate.

Democrats were trouncing Republicans nationally. Democratic socialists were projected to take at least seven seats in the House, up from two. And in Los Angeles, the DSA’s preferred mayoral candidate, Nithya Raman, appeared poised to unseat Karen Bass. The incumbent Democratic mayor held a less than 1% lead in early returns, but ballots are expected to skew toward the more progressive candidate, Raman.

“Karen Bass said that she would need to be up 10 points on election night to be comfortable,” one DSA-LA leader told the crowd. He gestured at a graphic showing Bass’s narrow lead and said, “I’m not good at math because I’m gay. Is that 10 points? I don’t think so.” (Bass didn’t actually say that, but a pundit on KTLA did say something to that effect.)

Karen Bass during an election night event in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

At the DSA party, people cheered victories elsewhere in the country by socialists and establishment Democrats alike, but they booed when Bass appeared on television, and laughed when a Fox News commentator suggested the economy was doing well. At one point, organizers put on Hasan Piker’s livestream, and at another they played an AI-generated video showing Raman dancing while wearing a traditional Russian fur hat with ear flaps and a red star. When local TV station KTLA suggested Raman would likely win and Mayor Bass’s face appeared onscreen, someone shouted, “Whoa, get fucked, Karen.” It kind of encapsulated the strongest force animating the DSA members I talked to in this mayoral race: their dislike for Mayor Bass. They even called her the C-word onstage: “conservative.”

The DSA and Raman have had something of an on-again, off-again relationship. The organization helped propel her to an upset City Council victory in 2020, only to reprimand her over disagreements about Israel, housing policy, and the city’s mansion tax. The local DSA chapter endorsed her candidacy late in the campaign, but the national organization almost stripped it from her at the eleventh hour. The national DSA voted last week to preserve its Los Angeles chapter’s endorsement of Raman by a single vote, after a dispute over her refusal to embrace the movement to boycott Israel.

“I think people here have varying levels of begrudgingness about supporting Raman, but I think everyone here voted for her,” said one DSA-LA member at the party who worked on the chapter’s video team and declined to give her name.

Still, the DSA members at the party seemed to think this mayoral race offered another encouraging sign for their organization, even if Raman isn’t quite New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. She was attacked consistently by her opponents—mainly Spencer Pratt—as a dangerous extremist, but with the help of the DSA (it said members knocked on more than 110,000 doors this election cycle) she might be the first LA mayoral candidate to defeat an incumbent in over 20 years.

Meanwhile, at the Raman campaign’s official election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Feliz, there weren’t any signs calling to “Tax the Rich” or to implement “Medicare for All,” as there were at the DSA party, but comedian Guy Branum from Apple TV’s Platonic sounded pretty similar to those socialists. He argued that Raman’s coalition reflected a class divide within Hollywood.

“Nithya has way more of entertainment’s middle class,” Branum said, describing workers worried about their next job. And Raman’s husband, television writer Vali Chandrasekaran, understands the industry’s problems firsthand, he argued.

Branum, who hangs with the couple socially, also wanted voters to appreciate one of her lessdiscussed qualifications. “They lead with the master’s in urban planning, and the Harvard, and the MIT,” he said. “But what you really need to see is that [she can dance]. You really need to see that hair let loose.” (Vanity Fair did not stick around at the party long enough to verify Raman’s dancing skills.)

Raman held her election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

Raman’s campaign manager, Ian Manheimer, was pretty psyched when he took the stage outside the Greek. “Holy shit! What is good, Los Angeles?” he shouted. Nearly three quarters of his campaign staff had never worked on a political campaign before, he told the crowd. Regardless, they managed to knock on over 100,000 doors, according to Manheimer.

The campaign’s grassroots operation had apparently become a bit of a competition. Volunteer Leo Blain, 25, told VF he’d knocked on more than 300 doors, putting him near the top of the campaign leaderboard. But the person to beat was Raman’s father, whom volunteers said had knocked on more than 1,000. All of that knocking was crucial, especially since Raman didn’t have a lot of institutional support or name recognition. Many of California’s most prominent Democrats stayed on the sidelines, because most of them would do anything to avoid the choice between an establishment incumbent and a rising DSA-endorsed challenger. But their neutrality didn’t necessarily mean indifference. A high-ranking official in Sacramento told me that plenty of state legislators were privately rooting for Bass, who had served as Speaker of the California Assembly before heading to Congress.

John, a DSA member who volunteered for Raman after having worked on Tom Steyer’s gubernatorial campaign, expected strong support for Raman among the local socialists, arguing that her independent thinking was a positive.

Raman’s party also included some unlikely converts. Kathleen Jensen, a Toluca Lake resident who previously supported Republican Rick Caruso, told me she considered Raman brilliant and wanted a “doer” in City Hall. Although she said some of her Democrat friends remained uneasy about Raman’s DSA association.

By 10:30 p.m., Bass’s election night party at the Loews Hotel in Hollywood had grown considerably quiet as her supporters began to digest the initial results. But the people who remained were still getting down to Snoop Dogg. The demographic differences between the parties were striking. Raman’s crowd skewed whiter, and more Asian, and the music was more alternative and disco. Bass’s crowd was notably more Black, reflecting the mayor’s decades of relationships in the city’s African American community.

Vaval Victor, 28, a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, the historically Black fraternity with which Bass has worked, remained confident that she would pull through. “She started the LA Black Dems Club in her kitchen,” he said, invoking her long history of organizing. “People are thirsty for hope.”

Bass had spent the campaign defending her record on homelessness, city finances, and last year’s catastrophic fires. Caruso, whom she defeated four years earlier, had swooped in at the end to say that he was voting for her, giving some of the city’s more conservative voters permission to support the incumbent. But early election-night returns were not the decisive advantage her campaign hoped for.

For all the divisions this mayoral race exposed, the three parties shared something that had been in short supply among Democrats lately: liberal joy.

#3618. PS5 Is Closing In On 100 Million Sales, Despite Getting More Expensive

During a briefing on its latest financial results, Sony revealed it sold 2.6 million PS5 consoles in its last quarter, which ended on September 30. This brings lifetime PS5 sales to 97.9 million, just months before the console enters its sixth year on the market. By comparison, the PS4 had shipped 103.0 million units at the same point in its lifecycle, but Sony's gaming ecosystem is performing much better thanks to higher digital revenue and a massive active user base.

This comes at a time when the PS5 has only gotten more expensive since launch, thanks to the global components shortage that has seen memory prices surge. Sony says it has been in discussions with manufacturers to secure enough memory for the next fiscal year and expects its hardware sales to remain profitable into the next year. The company has raised its forecast, as it expects sales of first- and third-party games--like GTA 6--to increase.

GTA 6 is projected to have sold almost 8 million copies ahead of its November 19 launch, and PS5 sales are said to be dominating by a wide margin compared with Xbox Series X|S. Sony also keeps 30% of the revenue from the game through platform fees, so GTA 6's early success will only improve PlayStation's fortunes.

With manufacturing adjustments that make the PS5 cheaper to produce and monetization of its monthly active users--which peaked at 127 million in September--business looks solid for Sony's game division.

Sony also touched on plans for its next PlayStation console, saying it's making "solid progress" on development and will announce it at an "appropriate time" in the future.

#3617. Met Gala Announces Unconventional 2027 Theme After John Galliano Controversy

The 2027 Met Gala is embracing a brand-new, unconventional theme following controversy surrounding its original plan to honor designer John Galliano.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art revealed on Thursday, November 5, that “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” will be curated by Andrew Bolton alongside Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben.

The theme asks individuals “to see the everyday anew” and focuses on elevating simple garments including T-shirts and jeans, while also exploring how “disposable” materials can become wearable art.

“I didn’t have a plan B,” Bolton, 60, told Vogue. “It was really important to come up with an exhibition that wasn’t just a masterwork show or something that we could do a little bit more easily. I wanted it to be as challenging and as provocative and as beautiful as a John show would have been.”

He continued, “That was really important to me: to come up with an idea that wasn’t a substitute. And it had to have some sort of contemporary resonance.”

After the Met Gala on May 3, the exhibit will open to the public from May 9 to January 9, 2028. The new theme comes two months after Galliano, 65, stepped back from the 2027 Met Gala exhibition, which was originally themed “John Galliano: Horizons.”

“I am profoundly grateful to The Metropolitan Museum of Art, and particularly to Max Hollein, Andrew Bolton and Anna Wintour, for the extraordinary honour of proposing an exhibition devoted to my work,” his official statement read in August. “To have my creative journey considered by an institution that I have admired throughout my life moved me more deeply than I can express. I will remain forever grateful for the confidence, care and scholarship that Max, Andrew, Anna and the entire Met team brought to this project.”

He continued, “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time.”

The announcement of Galliano’s involvement in the 2027 Met Gala received backlash due to his previous antisemitic and racist comments.

“I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry,” he wrote in his statement. “I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture. It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one’s conduct over time.”

Galliano went on to note that he did “not want the debate surrounding him” to put the Metropolitan Museum of Art “in a difficult position” or take away from the Costume Institute. Wintour supported the decision.

“John’s decision to ask the Museum to postpone the exhibition devoted to his work is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” she said in a statement at the time. “I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support.”

#3616. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3615. This Handheld Gaming Hub Has A Lot More Going On Than You’d Expect

There's no shortage of dedicated video capture devices on the market, but if you're looking for something that cuts down on cable clutter and adds some cyberpunk vibes to your setup, you'll want to check out the Chizha Mount Ling 2 Pro. GameSpot recently went hands-on with it, and while it's a great capture device for PC handhelds like the Steam Deck and the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X, it's hard to recommend if you're planning to grab Switch 2 footage specifically.

See on Kickstarter

According to Chizha, the Mount Ling Pro 2can be used as a dock; it has a built-in capture card that can record gameplay at up to 4K 60fps, and you can install an NVMe solid-state drive (up to 4TB) in the bottom slot for your recording purposes. This essentially condenses multiple devices into one portable hub, and if that sounds good to you, you can check out the Kickstarter for it right now. If you pledge now, you can get the device for $150 for the version with a capture card, after which it will cost $250 at retail.

One of the cool things about it is that it has a front display that will tell you what resolution your system is currently outputting as well as how much power you're drawing from it--useful information for content creators. In our testing, we found that it works very nicely with PC gaming handhelds, but there's still work to be done on the Switch 2 front.

"I noticed that the color being displayed was a lot more washed out than when using an official Switch 2 dock," senior video producer Jean-Luc Seipke explained. "This happened when testing on our Samsung TV. When we tested it again using a portable monitor, however, everything looked consistent. I did speak this concern to the creators, and they told me it might be a firmware issue, and they're currently trying to sort out and fix it. The other issue I noticed is with upscaling. When running games that are clearly not 4K and are upscaled, I noticed that the quality of the image looked significantly worse than on the official Switch 2 dock. When docked, the Switch 2 triggers an upscale method that kind of like smooths out the image and makes everything look nicer. For whatever reason, that is just not triggering correctly when plugged into this dock."

#3614. Tim Burton Partners With Loewe for a ‘Nightmare Before Christmas’ Capsule Collection

“Things in life are the best as surprises,” says Tim Burton, the iconoclast filmmaker, calling from London. More than 40 years after making his directorial debut with Pee-wee’s Big Adventure (1985), and penning the poem that would eventually inspire The Nightmare Before Christmas, Burton is expanding his artistic remit once more. The director has partnered with Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, the designers of Loewe, for a new capsule collection featuring memorable vignettes and characters from the latter film. “When they came to me and were talking about it,” Burton tells Vanity Fair, “I just got very excited, because I’m a frustrated designer myself.”

The capsule, available starting November 12, includes a range of handbags with whimsical recreations of the film’s most beloved characters. Zero, Jack Skellington’s dog, floats on the side of a handbag; the Harlequin Demon is rendered with feathers and leather scales; and Skellington himself is painted as a peekaboo surprise inside a carryall.

“They took something that means a lot to me and they put their own spin on it,” he says of working with Loewe. “The way they make things, the textures and the elements involved are just beautiful,” he continues. “It’s exciting for me to see it happen.”

Jack Skellington peekaboos from the inside of a handbag.

Snakes pop out of a woven leather bucket bag.

In the more than three decades since the film was released, Jack Skellington and The Nightmare Before Christmas have become synonymous with a certain brand of Halloween-like spookiness, a soft spot for Christmas and the holidays, and a wondrous gothic style and sensibility. The film originated from a poem Burton wrote in 1982 while working as an animator at Walt Disney Productions. “It was something that came not so much from a thought, but was just more slightly from the subconscious,” Burton says in a documentary short accompanying the Loewe collection.

But just as film and animation have changed over the years, the meaning of the film and its legacy have too. The Nightmare Before Christmas has become arguably one of the most renowned stop-motion-animation films. The painstaking process of making the film required the creation of 227 puppets and the shooting of 109,440 frames to bring the story to life. “I love [stop motion] because it’s all handmade,” Burton says. “When you see the puppets and the sets, you wish everybody could experience the tactile nature of what goes into making a stop-motion film, or any film.”

In the age of artificial intelligence, the movie has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton says of the proliferation of AI, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.”

A still from a documentary short featuring Burton that accompanies the collection.

Rather than be overly protective about some of his most famous intellectual property, Burton wanted to let the legacy leather-goods house and its designers follow their own instincts. “They consulted me, and we talked about this and that, but I respect them and I respect what they do,” he says. “It’s more fun for me to see things beautifully done.” Fashion, after all, he says, is a medium different from film. “I mean, I’ve seen Nightmare merchandise, and some of it’s good and some of it’s really bad,” he says with a laugh. “And even the bad ones are kind of good sometimes.” One example? A “big fat Jack Skellington.” “Well, no, he’s not a big fat Jack Skellington, but as a stuffed little toy, he’s kind of cute,” Burton adds with a laugh. “Things change and mutate, and you just [need to] keep the spirit of something, but then do something [with] your own interpretation of it.”

Many members of The Nightmare Before Christmas’s original 1993 audience are now adults atop creative industries. Burton’s work, in a way, is part of their own imagination. “The things that inspired you from the very beginning, they just stay with you,” Burton says. “Whether it’s conscious or not, it’s just part of your DNA.”

Revisiting past work, Burton says, “can be a beautiful experience, but not always.” Though he says he “had no real desire” to make a sequel to Nightmare, Burton did direct 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, a sequel to the 1988 film Beetlejuice, starring Winona Ryder and Catherine O’Hara. Returning to the film 35 years later “made sense” for him “emotionally.” “It was like, nobody’s getting any younger and blah, blah, blah,” Burton says. “I really did that movie not to make a sequel, but it was something that I enjoyed, and we tried to do it in the style of the first movie, shot it quickly, did live effects. So it was an experience that meant a lot to me. And I think for me, it’s always important to make something that I really, really feel.”

Burton illustrating some of his characters.

There’s plenty of interest in Burton revisiting other parts of his oeuvre too. Since the release of Corpse Bride in 2005, fans have been clamoring for a live-action remake of the film. Burton laughs when asked if he’d ever honor the request, and while he doesn’t deliver a straight answer, he doesn’t exactly say no. “I’ve got thoughts swirling around and all sorts of things going on, but I’ve been through too much to go, Okay,” he says, noting that he’s had projects mutate and change over the years. “I keep it open, and I’m just finishing something, so I’m in an open spot now, and I’m really excited to look for what the next thing is.”

Away from the big screen, Burton has experienced somewhat of a resurgence with the success of Netflix’s Wednesday, and he’s enjoyed ventures outside of the film industry. This capsule with Loewe is one of those projects, and the director also collaborated with A$AP Rocky, whom he describes as “a real artist,” for the visual rollout of his album released earlier this year, Don’t Be Dumb, creating characters for its cover and a music video. “I love this stuff because film has [become] such a business. It’s gotten so big,” he says. “That’s why I enjoyed doing stuff with Rocky. It’s what I love doing, and it’s just a different form of doing it.”

Burton hasn’t been on the lookout for new opportunities, but he likes being surprised by them. “It’s always just this nice, beautiful, strange surprise when somebody asks to do something or collaborate,” he says. “I mean, that’s what film’s all about. You’re working with different artists and you’re working with different people with one [goal] in mind. So it’s not that much different. I like those kinds of surprises.”

#3613. Woman Recruits Children to Break Into Neighbor's Home to Steal Furniture

A Florida woman was arrested after she allegedly recruited her kids to break into her neighbor’s apartment and steal furniture, which they left outside.

Nicole Bottiglieri-Vega has been charged with grand theft, contributing to the delinquency of a child, criminal mischief and resisting arrest.

Authorities learned of the incident when Miami police responded to an apartment complex on October 29 after a man and his wife returned home from work and found that several of their belongings were left in a common area outside of their unit, according to a probable cause arrest affidavit obtained by Us.

The property manager then reviewed surveillance camera footage, which allegedly showed Bottiglieri-Vega, 42, and two children entering the apartment after they forced a back door open.

Police said that Bottiglieri-Vega and the children started to remove furniture and other items from the apartment before they placed them outside.

The property manager confirmed that Bottiglieri-Vega and her children moved into the apartment complex just two weeks prior to the incident.

Officers tried to speak to Bottiglieri-Vega, but she refused to open the door when they knocked. The officers eventually forced their way into her unit and found her in a bedroom.

Bottiglieri-Vega allegedly resisted her arrest, but the officers managed to get her into custody.

Following the incident, Bottiglieri-Vega’s neighbors said they were worried about her children’s welfare because she allegedly smokes crack cocaine. Discarded glass pipes and small baggies were also seen near her home.

Bottiglieri-Vega was taken to the Miami police headquarters and placed in her holding cell. Authorities said she slipped out of her handcuffs and tried to escape, but the officers quickly stopped her and got her handcuffs back on.

Following her arrest, Bottiglieri-Vega has reportedly refused to answer questions when detectives have tried to interview her about the incident.

Bottiglieri-Vega is currently in custody at Miami-Dade County Jail and is being held on a $1,300 bond, according to online records viewed by Us. She has pleaded not guilty, but it’s not currently clear whether she has retained legal counsel.

The City of Miami Police Department had no additional information to share when contacted by Us about updates in the case. The investigation remains ongoing, and the Department of Children and Families is also looking into the allegations.

It’s not currently clear who has custody of Bottiglieri-Vega’s children in light of her arrest.

#3612. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time’s 2026 Remake Looks Stunning Next To The Original N64 Game

Since its launch last year, the Switch 2 has proven itself to be a portable powerhouse, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake may just be the best game to show off its capabilities. The upgraded version of the timeless adventure looks even better when compared to the original N64 game that first debuted in 1998, as Nintendo has leveraged the Switch 2 hardware to create the definitive version of the game, blending atmospheric design with imaginatively designed character models.

And if you want to see just how gorgeous that glow-up is, click the video below for a guided tour of Hyrule across two eras of Nintendo hardware. No commentary, just comparisons.

For this video, we captured footage using an original NTSC 1.0 N64 cartridge running on an Analogue 3D with de-blur enabled. While there are a couple of Nintendo 64 emulators on the market, the Analogue 3D is generally considered to be the best of the lot. It's designed to capture the essence of a CRT TV display through various effects and filters.

Ocarina of Time on the N64 was a game that had to work creatively around the limitations of the console and its cartridge system, at a time when the gaming industry was embracing CD-ROMs. Limitations do breed creativity, and the game is still fondly remembered for being a visual tour de force from an era when 3D games were making impressive strides. As for the Switch 2 version, the footage speaks for itself. It's crisp, the text is sharp, the extra effects are nice little touches, and the art direction has a Studio Ghibli feel to it.

For more on the technical wizardry behind it, you can read our big The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake interview with producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, as they spoke to GameSpot about what it took to modernize a classic game and keep its soul intact. "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a reverent remake with stellar presentation, letting the original greatness shine through," Steve Watts wrote in GameSpot's Ocarina of Time remake review.

As Meghan Markle and Prince Harry try to find their forever home, there are still a lot of questions lingering about their professional lives, and specifically their work with Netflix. While Markle has yet to make a full return to acting, she and the Duke of Sussex have been working behind the scenes on a number of Netflix projects. However, their deal with the streamer has been a bit rocky. They still have two projects in the works, though, so what’s really going on?

In 2020, just two years after tying the knot, Markle and Prince Harry stepped down from their royal duties and moved to Southern California. That same year, they signed an overall deal with Netflix and have since released several shows, including Markle’s lifestyle series With Love, Meghan. Despite Archewell Productions renewing its partnership with Netflix in 2025 under a multi-year first-look deal, it seems like things have stalled for two projects that are in development.

In March, Netflix had backed out of its partnership with Markle’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, reportedly due to performance. Even though the Harry & Meghan docuseries was a success, their follow-up projects haven’t generated the same type of viewership. Plus, With Love, Meghan had a controversial launch, and it's been reported that Netflix may have lost money with the partnership.

That being said, the couple, who recently moved back to the UK, still have two Netflix films in the works, Meet Me at the Lake and The Wedding Date. A source tells Page Six that they are “in development,” but there hasn’t been any progress since March. Another source shared that that's simply standard practice in the industry:

It’s Hollywood. People know how this town works, and things are not made in a day. This is all part of the process. There are a lot of steps.

Both films are adaptations of beloved books. Meet Me at the Lake is based on Carley Fortune’s 2023 novel and has been in development since August 2023. The Wedding Date, meanwhile, has been in development since 2025 and is based on Jasmine Guillory’s 2018 contemporary romance. In addition, Markle and Prince Harry were also working on an untitled scripted polo drama, but nothing more has been revealed on that front.

Whether any of those projects will move forward remains to be seen. However, we do know that there is progress being made on at least one of them.

Even though both Meet Me at the Lake and The Wedding Date haven’t made much progress, fans shouldn’t get too worried yet, especially when it comes to the first title I mentioned.

Carley Fortune, who is also the author of Every Summer After, which was recently adapted by Prime, spoke out about Meet Me at the Lake’s future at Netflix. In July, she shared that the film, which comes from Archewell and Netflix, is “still in development.” They have a director attached, and the script is being revised, which is great news.

Considering the film has been in development for three years now, one would think that it might simply be too late for anything to come of it. However, that doesn’t seem to be the case. Fortune opened up about working with Archewell and Markle on the project, and they all really care about the adaptation, which is why it’s taking so long:

When we were optioning the film, I had a really good long call with Meghan and Tracy Ryerson, who is with Archewell, and I felt like they really understood the story and what mattered about the story. And we spoke a lot about the story Meet Me at the Lake is, you know, it’s romance, but it’s very much about a mother and daughter, too. And we talked a lot about parenthood and also about how these love stories are about so much more. Like, it’s a story about grief; it’s a story about mental health. And so I felt like it was in good hands with them.

On top of Meet Me at the Lake, Netflix is working on another Fortune adaptation, This Summer Will Be Different, so the streamer is certainly interested in telling those stories. Additionally, Season 2 of Every Summer After is in the works following a successful Season 1 launch. Based on the end of ESA's first season, Season 2 will adapt Fortune’s novel One Golden Summer, which is set in the same universe as Every Summer After.

Not much else has been shared, but Fortune’s update should make fans feel better about her project with Markle. Hopefully, we'll get a solid update about the royals' other projects soon. For now, people will just have to continue waiting.

#3610. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3608. Elon Musk Spent $474 Million on the 2026 Midterm Elections. On Election Day, He Fell Silent.

Elon Musk, the Tesla CEO and former intimate of President Donald Trump’s, may have ever so slightly eroded his 14 (that we know of) children’s inheritances during the 2026 midterm elections, spending $474 million (of his estimated $901.7 billion bankroll) on Republican campaigns across the US. But as Election Day continued across the country, the prolific user of his own social media platform, X, remained relatively restrained.

“Vote red today,” was an early tweet, interspersed between abundant promotions of his company’s AI agent, Grok Bot. A shared tweet featuring Michigan Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was simply captioned with the raised eyebrow emoji.

And that was the most Musk had to say about the midterms on Tuesday, despite what The New York Times reports is the most that “any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle,” barring former New York City mayor Michael R. Bloomberg’s spend on his own 2020 presidential campaign, which cost him more than $1 billion.

And as the blue wave continued, Musk started removing tweets instead of adding them. Early Wednesday morning, around the time James Talarico took the stage to celebrate his win in Texas, Musk removed the missive he had pinned to the top of his account, an October 29 post in which he said his “biggest concern…if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028,” is that they will open the borders, create a larger Supreme Court, and grant statehood to DC and Puerto Rico. “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election,” he concluded. "Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.”

Per the Times, Musk’s spend is likely to exceed the $474 million currently reported, as any donations made after October 14 have yet to be counted. Of that current figure, $216 million went to his own super PAC (America PAC), with $212 of that going to support US Senate hopeful Ken Paxton. An additional $168 million went to the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund, and $30 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the primary super PAC for House Republicans. An additional $16 million went to state-focused political efforts in Michigan, Texas, and Wisconsin, while $44 million went to federal Republican groups or candidates.

That’s a lot of money to most of us, but by early Wednesday morning, Musk appeared to be taking the expenditure in stride. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted at 1:12 a.m. ET, followed almost immediately by “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” punctuated by the shrug emoji.

#3607. Prime Video Reveals 'Off Campus' Season 2 Premiere Date After Major Changes

Off Campus has found success on Prime Video while going through some major changes including cast exits and other onscreen shakeups.

Based on Elle Kennedy‘s book series, Off Campus follows an elite ice hockey team — and the women in their lives — as they “grapple with love, heartbreak, and self-discovery — forging deep friendships and enduring bonds while navigating the complexities that come with transitioning into adulthood,” per the show’s official synopsis.

Season 1, which premiered in May 2026, was centered on Hannah (Ella Bright) and Garrett’s (Belmont Cameli) love story.

Going by Kennedy’s book order, Logan’s (Antonio Cipriano) story was expected to be next, followed by Dean’s (Stephen Kalyn) and Tucker’s (Jalen Thomas Brooks). News broke, however, that Dean and Allie (Mika Abdalla) would be leading season 2 in a surprising shakeup, with the show set to return April 28, 2027.

The changes didn’t stop there. Keep scrolling for a breakdown of the show’s biggest BTS shakeups:

After Josh Heuston had a scene-stealing role as Justin in season 1, news broke that he wouldn’t return — for now.

“[He is] not [in] next season, but I love Josh and I would not write him off if I can find a way to bring Justin back at some point,” creator Louisa Levy told TV Guide at the time. “We never got a chance to meet Stella, who is the person he ends up with in the book. So maybe we’ll find a way to fold him into a future season.”

Levy noted that it wasn’t always the plan for Justin to be absent. “We don’t have him [available] next season, but never say never,” she added.

With Justin gone, Levy hinted that season 2 is going to look a little different.

“There’s going to be less live songs. Because we don’t have all of Hannah’s songwriting journey to play into,” she said during Obsessed Fest in June 2026. “We don’t have Josh and After Hours this season so we don’t have those bands. But we still have a lot of music in other ways. We will still have some light music in the show.”

Levy concluded: “I still think the heart of the show lives in those needle drops and those songs that underscore a moment — as well as the actual score.”

Abdalla previously teased how season 2 will differ from Kennedy’s The Score.

“[It’s the] same as season 1 [where] season 1 didn’t exactly follow the books,” Abdalla shared on a June 2026 episode of the “Hey Jonas!” podcast. “There’s some new fun stuff and some fun new little things that we’re adding in.”

With Dean taking over instead of Logan, all bets are off when it comes to future orders — and even possible character changes as new cast members are brought on.

#3606. GTA 6 Boss Talks The Game’s Budget And Calls Out A “High-Profile” Game For Releasing In A Rough State

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game that Rockstar Games has ever made, and it was no doubt very expensive to produce. But just how much did it cost? We know it's not $1.5 billion, but Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has now reacted to the discussion around the game's development costs.

He told The Wall Street Journal, "It was expensive and it took a long time."

The game has been in development for years, and was delayed multiple times. Zelnick said Take-Two's mission is to "make the best entertainment on Earth," and this takes time.

"Our strategy is to be the most creative, the most innovative, and the most efficient. Our cultural tenets are seek excellence in everything we do, work together as a team, and be kind. That approach sometimes is, in fact, really expensive," the executive said. "The good news is that we have a P&L and a balance sheet that supports that. And if we get it right--we don't always--but if we get it right, it actually pays for itself and then some."

Everyone expects GTA 6 to be a huge commercial success, but Zelnick said in the interview that he will not claim success before it occurs. "Arrogance is the enemy of continued success," he said.

Rockstar's ambition is to make the "most amazing entertainment experience of all time," Zelnick added. "They've done that before, and I'm hopeful that we will do that again. Like everyone else, I'm going to wait and see how it's received. I feel really good about it, but I'll wait and see," he said.

Also in the interview, Zelnick addressed GTA 6's latest delay to November 2026, saying it was "expensive and inconvenient" but was the right call for the game.

"There are a lot of companies who have a great mission statement, a stated strategy, and a culture, but then when push comes to shove, they do something that's at odds with that," he said. "My view is that culture, like character, is tested in the breach. It's a testing moment."

At the same time, Zelnick said he got a similar call from an executive asking for more time on a Take-Two project--and Zelnick said no. "I got a similar call and said, 'Actually, we're shipping,'" he said. "Thankfully, I was right, but imagine if I had been wrong?"

A dig at Cyberpunk 2077?

Also in the interview, Zelnick said other game companies can be too devoted to hitting deadlines, instead of taking more time, and spending more money, to get a game out in a better state. He didn't single any companies out, but he said a recent "high-profile" game that launched in such a rough state that it had to be pulled was an example of this--this could be a reference to CD Projekt Red and Cyberpunk 2077.

"That's the other piece that was left out of this discussion," he added. "What happens when people take the other approach? The other approach being, we're slavishly devoted to a schedule, and we're just going to ship despite what is going on. I am not going to throw any competitors under the bus, but if you know anything about the video game business, in the past few years, there was a very high-profile release that fell into this category. They shipped, and they had to pull the title after shipping, because it didn't work."

Cyberpunk 2077 had such a rough launch that it was pulled from the PlayStation Store; thousands of people separately sought refunds.

Despite releasing in such a rough state, Cyberpunk 2077 sold nearly 14 million copies in its first three weeks to become one of the most commercially successful RPG releases of all time. Executives at CD Projekt Red got gigantic bonuses, too.

CD Projekt joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski said it “was for sure wrong” to launch the game in that state, but he pushed back against the theory that the studio did so to appease investors who wanted to see financial returns.

Following Cyberpunk 2077’s rough launch, CD Projekt Red steadily supported the game with numerous updates and improvements over the years, culminating with a massive, game-changing 2.0 update in 2023 alongside the Phantom Liberty expansion. Today, the game has sold more than 40 million copies.

According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 could reach 25 million pre-purchases by launch, and that would work out to around $2 billion in revenue. That would be enough to cover the game's development cost and most of the marketing spend.

GTA 6 releases on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

#3603. Marvel’s Wolverine Has Lost Its Momentum, And Sony’s Numbers Show It

Marvel's Wolverine got off to a strong start when it launched in September, but since then, it looks like things have cooled off massively for the game. In its new earnings report, Sony finally dropped a sales number for Insomniac's new Marvel game, revealing that it has sold 2.4 million units so far.

Marvel's Wolverine, as it initially debuted as September's best-selling game, delivering the highest launch-month dollar sales for a Sony-published game since Helldivers 2 back in February 2024. While 2.4 million sales on its own sounds pretty impressive, compared to other Sony first-party titles, the numbers do not look good. In its report, Sony listed several more games that drastically outperformed Marvel's Wolverine, including Insomniac's previous release, Marvel's Spider-Man 2.

That game sold through 2.5 million units on its first day of release, while other titles like Ghost of Yotei outperformed Marvel's Wolverine in just a few days. The game also arrived during a busy time on the gaming calendar, as the last two months have seen multiple games launch ahead of GTA 6 on November 19.

Between Control Resonant, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, and live-service games jockeying for both attention and money, Marvel's Wolverine was facing an uphill battle--and that hill probably felt very steep amidst lukewarm reviews and negative online chatter.

Sony hasn't revealed how much it cost to develop Marvel's Wolverine either, but it probably wasn't cheap. The holiday season should see sales increase, and a Black Friday discount will always help shift more units, but for now, Marvel's Wolverine looks like a black mark on an otherwise-solid quarter for Sony. PS5 sales are closing in on 100 million units sold, development on the PlayStation 6 is picking up speed, and the company made a cool $3.95 billion in the last quarter across all of its divisions.

#3602. Of Mics and Men: After MAGA Meltdown, the Manosphere Winds Down

Two years ago, on the night of the 2024 presidential election, Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White took to the podium at Donald Trump’s Palm Beach victory party and rattled off a list of thank-yous to some rowdy podcasters and YouTube pranksters: the NELK Boys, Adin Ross, Theo Von, Bussin’ With the Boys, and “last but not least, the mighty and powerful Joe Rogan.” Just months before, these names were seldom mentioned in the mainstream press, but now they were recognized on a national stage as having powered Trump’s return to office by hosting him on their platforms and revealing his more personable side. The victory that night seemed to go well beyond the electoral conquest; one of the defining cultural legacies of the 2024 election cycle is the imprecise but vivid concept of the manosphere.

By 2026, the novelty of Trump and Von joking about the potency of cocaine, as they did in one of the signature moments of the 2024 campaign, has worn off. The president’s approval rankings tanked despite his enduring presence as a pop culture figure. Rogan endorsed Trump in the final days of that 2024 race, but he recently described Trump’s “really crazy” 1,300-word Truth Social tirade against Bill Maher as having the ring of a “girl who got dumped.” He has roundly criticized Trump’s handling of the Epstein Files, a signature issue for the podcast class, and described the Iran war as a “betrayal.” If the end of MAGA is in sight amid Tuesday’s blue tsunami, so is the notion that Republicans had captured the coveted, low-propensity demographic of young men: The New York Times estimated that Democrats won 18-to-29-year-old men by 24 points on Tuesday, a 38-point swing from Trump’s 2024 victory among them. Democrats are content creators too now, and the most notable political appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience over the past couple of years was James Talarico’s. “You need to run for president,” Rogan told Texas’s new senator-elect.

And so when C-SPAN made the somewhat mind-boggling announcement that the staid public-affairs network would simulcast election night coverage hosted by Patrick Bet-David, a Florida-based podcaster known for his interviews with Andrew Tate and Nick Fuentes, it was less of a capitulation to the so-called manosphere than an emblem of the modern media free-for-all. Of the online personalities loosely associated with Rogan’s milieu, Bet-David’s backstory is the most colorful. A refugee from Iran, he joined the Army upon arriving in the United States; he has said he worked for a time as a bodyguard to a high-level Los Angeles cocaine dealer. Bet-David now operates a media company called Valuetainment, formed after he made his riches with an insurance company that has been widely described as a multi-level marketing operation. After interviewing the leading looksmaxxing personality, Clavicular, last week, he was now responsible for providing C-SPAN’s conservative perspective. A spokesperson for the network described the programming to me as an effort to achieve “a marriage of traditional media and new media.”

“In the 2024 election, we invited Pete Buttigieg, God knows how many times, never showed up,” Bet-David told me in the lead-up to the evening. “Pete Buttigieg was here last week. We did a two-hour podcast together right before the midterms. And so the market is realizing that’s the direction you got to go.”

As he entertained a characteristically ragtag group of political-for-the-night personalities, Bet-David sat at his decision desk in a pinstripe suit with cartoonishly wide peak lapels. There were the young conservative provocateurs CJ Pearson and Nick Shirley, and the Groyper-adjacent, recent Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, who described the night as a “really tough election for my party.”

Bet-David joked to Michael Franzese that he knows about gas prices—before refashioning himself as a political commentator, the former Colombo crime family capo ran a multi-million-dollar gasoline tax bootlegging scheme in the 1980s. In voicing his opposition to the war in Iran, Franzese said, “We had a saying on the street, the best way to defeat your enemies is to make them your friends.” He bemoaned how Trump “makes everything all about him.”

Other guests included Ann Coulter, Piers Morgan, Roger Stone, Bill O’Reilly, and Cenk Uygur, whose Young Turks show was simulcasting on another C-SPAN channel. For some reason, Jackass’s Steve-O appeared toward the end of the night. He pointed out to Bet-David that Marco Rubio is “stronger for you guys” than JD Vance.

Two years ago, I watched a similar scene unfold in an airplane hangar in Fort Lauderdale. It was, as Bet-David and I agreed on Tuesday, a wild night: He was hosting an election night party at Valuetainment’s headquarters at the peak of the manosphere chatter and at the onset of what seemed to so many to be the era of MAGA cultural domination. Men in tightly tapered polyester pants hopped out of Ferraris and Teslas to watch a crowd of UFC fighters, rappers, former mobsters, and Candace Owens wax poetic about how the age of Jennifer Lopez and Beyoncé, who had appeared alongside Kamala Harris in previous weeks, was over. In this new era of masculinity, there was no time anymore for liberal Hollywood political pieties: Mark Zuckerberg had just started wearing a gold chain and describing Trump’s fist pump after the attempted assassination as “one of the most badass things I’ve ever seen in my life.”

And the vibe shift, as it could only be called, was shocking for a period. There was a moment, for instance, in the heady aftermath of the 2024 election when Von attended an Oscars week poker night hosted by Timothée Chalamet at the Chateau Marmont. (The actor had recently appeared on his show.) Just weeks later, Von was at a UFC fight where White warmly embraced the Tate brothers. The entire category of celebrity appeared to be flattening in real time.

But to those on the inside of the podcaster-comedian boom, another swing of the pendulum already seemed to be coming. Andrew Schulz, a frequent Rogan guest, conducted one of Trump’s trademark podcast interviews in the summer of 2024. “After the Trump thing, I wasn’t like, ‘We got it now,’” he told me the following year. “After the Trump thing, I was like, ‘We just interviewed the president of the United States, what the fuck?’” He thought that the deafening manosphere discourse might indicate the presence of a cultural bubble. “I just think that we are what people are listening to now,” he said, “but that could change tomorrow.”

Alex Bruesewitz, a 29-year-old Trump adviser, was largely credited with orchestrating the candidate’s podcast tour in 2024. A social media operative who had built connections with big-name celebrities, influencers, and podcasters in the lead-up to the presidential election—he had brokered Trump’s alliance with Nicki Minaj and recently flew on Air Force One with Mike Tyson—Bruesewitz told me on Wednesday morning that he had soured on the Republican party.

“I consider myself more of a Trump voter than a Republican voter,” he said. “If the party moves in the direction of people like Ted Cruz, for example, in 2028, there's going to be a lot of people like myself…who will not participate in the Republican elections moving forward.”

In the midterms cycle, Bruesewitz said, the podcasting world “wasn’t there for us to engage.” The likes of Von and Schulz have echoed Rogan’s criticisms of the Iran war and how the Trump administration managed the release of the Epstein files.

“I don’t think that any of them were ever team Trump,” he said. “We simply just had conversations with them in 2024. The post-election reaction, saying that they’re part of this right-wing manosphere, I think that actually had an effect on how they covered us during our first two years. I think that they didn’t want to be labeled right-wing, and so they evened out a bit.”

Another reason, Bruesewitz supposed, for the end of Republican podcasting dominance and the blue tsunami: “Republican candidates were really lame and they weren’t interesting people…there was a little bit of an expectation that these candidates could go communicate with low-propensity voters with podcasting again, but I pushed back on their teams. I was like, Look, there’s zero percent chance that any of these podcasters are going to want to have on your boring candidates.”

By the end of the night on Tuesday, Bet-David and Steve-O were making plans to hang out before the stuntman left town. All of the guests on the C-SPAN–Bet-David collaboration seemed likely to keep talking about politics online, but it would be difficult to assign any of them a specific party agenda. In the airplane hangar two years prior, Bet-David had ended the night with what felt like a seismic exhortation, telling a raucous crowd, “For the rest of our lives we will share this night together.” On Tuesday, he was more practical as he signed off for the evening.

#3600. Arkane Union Accuses Microsoft Of “Sabotaging” Development Of Marvel’s Blade

As the fate of Arkane Lyon hangs in the balance, a union representing workers from the French studio offered strong words toward Arkane's parent company, Microsoft. In short, the union blames Microsoft for "sabotaging" the production of its Blade game.

French trade union STJV (per VGC) claimed that development on Marvel's Blade is "going fine," but said that workers face the "harsh reality" that Microsoft may close the studio for financial reasons. But the union said that the onus for Arkane's tough financial situation is on Microsoft itself, claiming that a hiring freeze that lasted 19 months "artificially caused delay and additional cost."

STJV asserts that closing Arkane would be more costly than finishing Marvel's Blade, adding that a studio closure would be the result of Microsoft's "never-ending search for maximum profit optimization." The union argues that Arkane is profitable, but "not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The union's statement lists demands that include protections for employees and giving workers a say in a potential buyer for Arkane. In accordance with French labor laws, the studio has been in a "consultation period" since Xbox began its reset earlier this year, and it was recently granted an extra month to find a buyer before facing closure. A recent report suggests that three companies, including Ubisoft, submitted bids to acquire Arkane.

Arkane is perhaps best known for developing the Dishonored games. Its Arkane Lyon team is primarily responsible for Dishonored 2 and Deathloop, while its sister team in Austin developed Prey and Redfall before Microsoft closed Arkane Austin in 2024.

Bethesda and Arkane Lyon announced Marvel's Blade at The Game Awards 2023, but besides the release of official concept art showcasing the game's setting of Paris, practically nothing of the game has been shown since then. The title's future remains as unclear as the fate of its developer.

#3596. Laura Loomer, Elon Musk, George Santos, and More React to Election Night: “I Hope Everyone Is Learning Arabic”

The midterm elections marked a night of historic firsts: Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator elected in Kansas in nearly 100 years; Chris Pappas is now the first openly gay man to be voted into the Senate; Keisha Lance Bottoms is the first Black woman to be elected as a US governor; Bentley Hudgins is the first transgender and nonbinary lawmaker to be voted into the Georgia General Assembly—the list goes on.

How better to chronicle a generational evening in US history than on social media? Our founding fathers recounted watershed moments via post riders and printed broadsides; in the mid-19th century, dispatches were sent via the Pony Express. President Lincoln’s shooting was rushed to the public via Morse code tapped over the wires, and during World War I, we utilized undersea telegraph cables. Yet in our long history spanning radio broadcasts, satellite television, and smoke signals, nothing has quite captured the zeitgeist like an X post.

“CNN is now saying the national anthem has been changed to a reggaeton cover of Pink Pony Club,” tweeted one user last night, right as the media joined a chorus of policy analysts and pundits to announce a new dawn as Democrats took control of Congress—a blue wave. Or rather, a blue tsunami.

Social media users across the country then took to X to mourn, deny, or celebrate the victory. Yet amid the cacophony of social media’s tweets, posts, replies, comments, and reels, the most notorious influencer grew shockingly quiet: President Donald Trump himself. Despite posting a half-hearted image of a MAGA-red hat reading “VETO,” Trump has not said much online in the hours following the victory.

In the months leading up to the midterms, social media did more than simply sway victories. In fact, it propelled candidates like Jon Ossoff to the forefront through short-form vertical videos, made contenders such as Abdul El-Sayed go viral through clips set to songs like Eminem’s 2010 hit “Not Afraid,” and directed Gen Z focus to key races through memes (“TEXAS JUST WENT BLUE. PUT PRONOUNS BACK IN YOUR BIO NOW,” New York City Council member Chi Ossé posted in his Instagram Stories last night).

More than three quarters of young adults relied on social media or platforms like YouTube as a source for their midterm election news this year. An astounding 67% of millennials also got the lowdown from content creators. Call it absurd, call it brain rot, or call it sensational: There’s no doubt that social media has become a phenomenon, and the Twitterverse is still alive and well in 2026.
