#3537. Magic’s Most Broken New Mechanic Perfectly Captures the Essence of Star Trek

I wasn’t sold on Magic’s Star Trek crossover, but then the Federation showed me the strength of a diverse crew

Of all the Magic: The Gathering sets released this year, I had the least amount of interest in Star Trek, but after playing a few hours as part of a Magic Arena preview this week, I’ve completely changed my tune. I bear no ill will toward the United Federation of Planets, and I recognize the profound impact Trek has had on pop culture over the last 60 years. I’ve just never become a fan. More importantly, most of my skepticism towards it as a Magic set stems from its incongruous nature as hard sci-fi crossing over with a high-fantasy trading card game that I adore.

If there’s one thing I do know about Star Trek, however, it’s that its vision of the future is brimming with optimism and curiosity. In tandem with that is an emphasis on the importance of diversity. I remember my dad watching Star Trek: The Next Generation when I was very young, and the “Wookiee guy” kind of scared me. These days, Worf (who is actually a Klingon) would probably be my favorite character. So it makes sense that what finally won me over about Magic's Trek connects directly to the franchise's idealistic core message.

I had a predictably frustrating experience playing Draft and Sealed on Arena while trying out a few different color combos. Nothing seemed to click. (I tried and failed a mostly green ramp and counters strategy.) Then I got Sarek, Federation Ambassador (even I know that’s Spock’s dad!) in a new pool of cards and immediately recognized that he has strong Commander vibes thanks to a new Magic mechanic designed specifically for the Star Trek set.

Sarek’s "Federation" ability lets you draw one card for every five creature types among non-Borg creatures you control at the start of combat on your turn. If you draw three or more (you have 15+ creature types), he puts two +1/+1 counters on all of your creatures as well. He feels like one of those Commanders with a powerful ability that’s challenging to execute fully on, but if you like a convoluted deck-building challenge, he’s probably one of the more immensely satisfying Commanders from the set.

Since Sarek is Bant (white-blue-green), that gave me access to a large number of cards in my pool, and I quickly realized I had a few more Federation abilities there. Captain Jonathan Archer immediately reminded me of cards like Rinoa Heartilly or Rufus Shinra that generate their own animal companion. For Captain Archer, that’s his trusty beagle Porthos. With two copies of the captain in my deck, his Federation ability became the glue that held it all together: For a cost of one green mana, he taps to give one target creature +X/+X where X is the number of creature types among non-Borg creatures you control.

It’s not game-breaking by any means, but that kind of scalable buff means that you can reliably ensure that one of your creatures gets consistently big enough to punch through your opponents defenses, or at least whittle away at their board.

Archer is a Human Officer, while the Porthos creature token he creates is a Dog, so together they already bring that buff up to +3/+3. But Star Trek at large is chock-full of aliens with jobs, so all I really needed to do was look for useful creatures to help pad out the deck. Xenobotanist is a Vulcan Scientist (score two points for the Federation!) mana dork that can tap to add one mana of any color. David and Carol Marcus, Creators (Human Scientist) also help with ramp by creating a New Planet land token upon entering.

Perhaps the most clutch addition for this Archer strategy was Shuttle Ace, a Kelpian Pilot that has flying during your turn and gains you two life whenever it becomes tapped. Because of all the Spacecrafts in this set, Star Trek has plenty of flyers, but that didn’t stop Shuttle Ace from becoming a solid late-game finisher for me. (You can also tap him to charge up your own Spacecraft for some easy lifegain.)

I also had Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist, which has a Federation ability when she enters that lets you look at the top X cards of your library based on your non-Borgs, then you put one card into your hand and the rest on the bottom of your library. That grants some pretty huge card advantage, letting me sneak Shuttle Ace in when I needed him most.

The other really important card in this deck is Saavik, Stoic Student. She has Flash and her Federation ability deals X damage to target attacking or blocking creature based on your non-Borg count when she enters. In one late-game match, I tricked my opponent into blocking an underpowered Porthos and then dropped Saavik in during combat to obliterate a strong blocker. My opponent actually rage-quit, which is always a good sign that your deck is doing something right.

The general strategy here is to go wide with a variety of creature types. Since size doesn’t matter as much as diversity, I also dipped into some +1/+1 counter production to beef up my army. Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign, is an interesting card for that since every time he taps, for the rest of your turn, he adds an extra counter every time you distribute a counter. In a set full of Spacecraft that require you to Station, you can tap him very easily without putting him in combat where he might die. Perhaps my best combat trick happened when I did exactly that and then played Test of Conviction, a dilemma card that can put a +1/+1 counter on each creature you control. Thanks to Boimler, that became +2/+2 to the seven creatures I had on the board.

The few times I drew Sarek, he proved himself worth the inclusion. Since he’s a Vulcan Advisor, all I needed was one of the many Human Officers available to me and one other creature type to trigger his card draw. Having it come at the start of combat feels a bit awkward, but with enough instants and Flash creatures, it’s still totally worth it. None of my Limited matches dragged on long enough for me to reach the 15 creature types needed to trigger his counter distribution, but I got close enough that it certainly feels possible. If I’m lucky enough to pull a physical copy, I’ll surely build him as a Commander.

According to Wizards of the Coast’s official description of the Federation mechanic, it has everything to do with the fundamental ethos of the Federation itself: “The Federation draws strength from its many species contributing their knowledge and resources toward a better future.” That’s kind of a beautiful sentiment in itself, and the way it translates into the mechanic makes for a compelling gameplay strategy that also serves as a flavorful adaptation of Trek’s central theme.

It’s easy to pull off in a sci-fi set featuring a bunch of different aliens, but I’m curious to see how it might function outside Limited formats. One of the other Federation cards is Jean-Luc, Mon Capitaine from the Enterprise-Q scene box. Captain Picard sports some spectral faerie wings here, and all of your faeries enter with an additional +1/+1 counter on them for each non-Borg you have out. That strikes me as a really interesting and hilarious Commander deck to try building. There are about 308 legal creature types in Magic, so what might that look like if you make a deck with just enough powerful faeries supplemented by a wide variety of creature types?

To make a deck like this work, you don’t need to hyper-focus on a singular strategy or synergistic mechanics. You can get away with a few core pieces and include a bunch of cards that provide you with value as long as you pay attention to creature type variety. Because each species brings its own strengths to the table, those strengths contribute to a better future — and a better Magic deck.

#3536. Project Hail Mary's Andy Weir Has Tried To Write Screenplays, But Feels 'Constrained' By This Obstacle [Exclusive]

"Project Hail Mary" was based on Andy Weir's 2021 novel of the same name, and by this point it seems as though the author has a knack for stories that play well on the big screen. "Project Hail Mary" dominated the box office upon its March 2026 release, and the 2015 adaptation of his book "The Martian" saw similar commercial success. Both were also met with critical acclaim. As such, it wouldn't seem all that silly for Weir to consider going straight to the screenplay with his future projects and skipping the novel stage altogether. But it seems the writer feels constrained by the idea of working in a visual medium.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai spoke with Weir, who referenced an audiobook called "Exoplanet" that he executive produced. This particular audiobook is an Audible Original sci-fi thriller that plays more like a movie than a book, using sound effects to convey action rather than a narrator providing a play-by-play of events. This, it seems, was a challenge for Weir, who likened it to his difficulties with writing screenplays.

"If you're writing a book, which is what I do, I can just throw in a paragraph of exposition and explain things directly to the reader and that's done," he explained. "You can't do that in an audiobook unless you have a narrator." According to Weir, "Exoplanet" writer Benjamin Percy immediately shut down the idea of having a narrator for the audiobook. "Everything is sounds that are happening in the setting," continued Weir. "I'm like, 'Okay, that makes it harder. It's your funeral.' But [Percy] pulled it off. He did a great job." Interestingly, it's this same challenge that has held Weir back from writing a movie script, despite his efforts to give it a try.

Andy Weir is currently working on his next book which looks set to tackle a hot button topic by focusing on artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, many fans are surely hoping for a sequel to "Project Hail Mary." But it seems the author isn't quite ready for that yet — thought that could very well change in the near future. What he almost certainly won't be doing, however, is writing a screenplay.

As Weir told /Film, "I've tried my hand at writing scripts and screenplays in the past, and I've always felt really constrained and claustrophobic by that because you have very little space to do things." The "That" to which Weir refers is the lack of being able to insert a paragraph of exposition to explain things to readers as straightforwardly as possible. Weir continued:

"Exposition now has to be done through dialogue or visuals. Usually visuals. Visuals do a great job of exposition because you can see the whole everything that's going on, and you don't need to describe actions, you can show them. But in an audiobook, you can't have paragraphs of the exposition and you can't have visuals showing you everything that's going on. So it's very constrained."

Based on his comments about visuals being a great way to convey exposition, It sounds as though Weir would at least be more open to writing a film than a narrative audiobook along the lines of "Exoplanet." For now, however, it seems as though he's happy sticking to novels, which is no doubt fine with both his fans and studios, who, as evidenced by "Project Hail Mary" becoming one of the best movies of 2026, will continue to benefit from great films based on his ideas regardless.

Sony Pictures Classics has acquired all rights in the United States, Latin America, and Asia to “Violette,” marking the indie studio’s fourth collaboration with director Jean-Pierre Jeunet. The company also released Jeunet’s previous hits “Amelie,” “The City of Lost Children,” and “Micmacs.”

“Violette” stars Leïla Bekhti (“Once Upon My Mother”), Matthias Schoenaerts (“Rust and Bone”), and Melvil Poupaud (“One Fine Morning”). #3534. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3533. Why Godzilla Minus Zero Is Rated R

This article contains light spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

For about as long as the Motion Picture Association (formerly "of America") has existed, the conventional wisdom has been that blockbuster genre movies should receive the most inviting rating possible. This concept has existed at least since Steven Spielberg's "Jaws" took the movie industry and pop culture by storm, as its PG rating allowed a wide audience to experience it. Certainly there have been exceptions, most famously at the hands of Spielberg himself, whose 1984 output revealed the necessity for a rating in between PG and R: the PG-13.

This middle ground rating then became the go-to standard for films that are edgy and adult without crossing a line into becoming too much for young teens. Its popularity has resulted in many filmmakers pushing its limits, especially as it came to be known as essentially the default movie rating. So far, every "Godzilla" film has received a rating of PG-13 or lower, as most of the movies involve giant monster-on-giant monster violence (thus meaning it's impossible to emulate in real life, as per the MPA's general view on violence).

However, that has now changed with the release of "Godzilla Minus Zero," which has been given an R rating by the MPA. At first blush, it might seem that this is the "Godzilla" franchise's move to appeal to an edgier audience, in the same way the Marvel Cinematic Universe was only too happy to make "Deadpool and Wolverine" a hard-R. Yet "Minus Zero" isn't R-rated merely for surface-level indulgences like harsh language, extreme violence, or even sex. Instead, "Godzilla Minus Zero" earns the R for two very specific reasons, both of which make the higher rating more understandable.

Ever since the very first "Godzilla" in 1954, the giant monster has been intentionally positioned as an allegory for the ravages of war — specifically, war with atomic weapons, whose devastation Japan had recently experienced. Though Ishirõ Honda's film is a much more thoughtful and somber affair than modern audiences would expect, it's still got enough B-movie flavor to explain why the franchise went on to become increasingly focused on spectacle and even more kid-friendly. While the darkness inherent in "Godzilla" has cropped up in several movies since, the allegorical nature of the character is usually kept to subtext.

Writer/director Takashi Yamazaki takes the franchise further in "Godzilla Minus Zero" by depicting real-life war violence: the immediate aftermath of the US bombing of Hiroshima. In the film, the fictional character Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) is one of the few survivors of the attack, and we're shown a flashback in which he finds the charred remains of his family.

The upsetting reality of this moment not only fuels the themes of the film, but directly informs Murakami's character, as we learn that his plan is to lure Godzilla to New York City and have the beast attack America. In this brief but powerful fantasy sequence, we see Godzilla shoot his heat rays at the city, causing people's faces to melt off before they incinerate. It's a sequence which does something rare, especially for blockbuster genre films: it depicts an intentional act of genocide on Americans. It's a moment reminiscent of something like "Terminator 2" (which Yamazaki was inspired by), yet even more pointed given the emotion behind it. As such, it makes sense that the MPA would consider it rougher material than previous "Godzilla" movies.

As many have pointed out during the MPA's 60-odd year existence, the organization's rationale for a film's rating is often frustratingly vague. Many filmmakers are annoyed by the process of submitting and resubmitting their movie to get their desired rating, with many decisions coming down to the tiniest omission of a handful of frames, as opposed to large swathes of material. While the MPA's rulings are made on a literal case-by-case basis, the general idea seems to be that they're usually judging a film by its overall tone and effect on an audience, rather than ticking checkboxes. While some elements like nudity and more than one F-bomb in the dialogue are near-guaranteed criteria for an R, some movies earn the rating through what the MPA likes to call "thematic elements."

As such, the R rating for "Godzilla Minus Zero" is more of a cumulative one than anything else. Even if the Hiroshima flashback and NYC dream sequence were edited out, the film might edge close to an R solely for its grisly fight sequences between Godzilla and King Ghidorah. Both kaiju are particularly vicious in the way they take advantage of their respective regenerative powers, with the monsters ripping off each other's heads and limbs, and we see sinewy tendons stretching before they snap. Although it's still fantasy monster violence, when the film as a whole is taken into account, it does feel like giving it a PG-13 would be inappropriate, too. Ultimately, the rating is a reflection of how strong Takashi Yamazaki's filmmaking is. It makes "Godzilla Minus Zero" the latest in a proud lineage of light R-rated films, meaning it's likely to become a gateway genre movie for generations to come.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

While there are obvious frontrunners on the season of Dancing with the Stars airing on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve always thought Connor Wood could make a deep run on the show. It turns out I’m not the only one who thinks this, as both Derek Hough and a DWTS champion have predicted that the man who goes by Fibula online will make it all the way to the end.

I feel like it's a big deal when a judge makes a prediction about Dancing with the Stars, so I’m not taking Derek Hough’s words lightly. During an interview with TV Insider, he boldly claimed that he really thinks Connor Wood and his partner Rylee Arnold will be in the finale, stating:

Well, there you have it, Derek Hough really thinks Connor Wood will make it to the end, but he's not the only one.

While Derek Hough saying Wood could make the final is huge, there’s another big name who thinks the comedian has what it takes. That person is Joey Graziadei, Season 33’s winner. Speaking to TV Insider about the podcast host, the man who won with Jenna Johnson said:

I will almost guarantee that he makes the finale. I think he can. I think that he’s the perfect blend of his dancing has gotten better, and I would be shocked if he doesn’t have the votes. He seems online to have a really big army behind him and Rylee. He’s just doing it so well.

Joey went on to say that he thinks people can see how committed Wood is to this process, as well as his improvement. In short, “he is what this show is about.” And you know what? Graziadei would know. He won his season of Dancing with the Stars, and he also came in with very little experience. The Bachelor star brought that up too, explaining:

That’s kind of the route I fell under. No one expected me to be good, and I got better throughout, and I think that’s part of the things people look for on that show.

I think Graziadei makes such a good point here, plus he knows from experience. He wasn’t the person on his season with the most dance experience. However, he was so solid all season; he improved big time, and he won. That’s exactly why Connor Wood could make it to the finale too.

The co-host of Brooke and Connor Make a Podcast has shown massive improvement over the weeks, and the joy he and his partner are getting out of this process is infectious. I mean, I wanted to scream with excitement just like they did when they got their first tens (and an eight from Shirley Ballas, which is high praise from her considering how low she scored other contestants) on Halloween Night.

Also, you can’t look past the passionate fans Wood and Arnold have. He has 1.4 million followers on TikTok, and she has 2.1 million. Their videos consistently get millions and millions of views, and we cannot forget the ultra-viral situation that was launched by him saying he had a crush on Jennifer Lawrence and her replying that she saw him on 8th Avenue drinking a smoothie and he paid her no mind.

All I’m saying here is it’s obvious people ride for Papa (which is a nickname Wood has had to try and explain many times), and that mixed with his commitment and improvement on the show is a recipe made for a finalist.

Now, to see if he can go the distance, you can watch Dancing with the Stars every Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3531. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

Buyer: Sumerian PicturesSection: Directors’ FortnightDirector: Eivind LandsvikBuzz: Sumerian Pictures before it was a film distributor is a long time record label, and the still upstart film side has finally picked up a feature that has some music ties. “Low Expectations” is a Norwegian film that stars Marie Ulven, better known as the Norwegian indie bedroom singer girl in red. She stars in the film alongside “The Worst Person in the World” actor Anders Danielsen Lie as arguably a version of herself, a rising pop star whose growing success becomes harder to reconcile with her inner life, leading her to take a part-time job at a high school from her hometown. “Low Expectations” is Landsvik’s feature directorial debut after directing two shorts, one that was accepted into Cannes in 2023 called “Tits,” and another that won a Norwegian Film Critics prize, “Sofia, Last Summer” from 2021. The film actually opens this week, September 11 in Norway, but Sumerian will release it in North America in 2027.

Buyer: Independent Film Company and Sapan StudioSection: Out of CompetitionDirector: Leah NelsonBuzz: This hand-drawn animated black and white film has a stacked voice cast featuring Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Beanie Feldstein, Seth Rogen, and Samira Wiley, as well as Pamela Adlon, Sarah Silverman, Bowen Yang, Wanda Sykes, Phil Rosenthal, Adam Shapiro, Pat Finn, and Sugar Lyn Beard. It’s adapted from a memoir/graphic novel and is a story about a mother and daughter struggling with an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. The film will first play in the Centrepiece section at TIFF, then the distributors will plan an awards season rollout late this year before opening wider in early 2027.

Buyer: KimStimSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Katharina RivillisBuzz: Wim Wenders produced this debut film about a German exchange student living in New Mexico shortly after the 9/11 attacks on the U.S. and how the teenager begins to feel homesickness while abroad in the desert heat. KimStim is an upstart indie distributor, and it is planning a North American theatrical release in 2027.

Buyer: Zeitgeist Films in association with Kino LorberSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Judith GodrècheBuzz: Based on a memoir by a Nobel Prize-winning author Annie Ernaux, “A Girl’s Story” follows Ernaux in 2020 on a book tour and then all the way back to her teen years in the summer of 1958 and is a reflection on the “cruelty of other girls and the bitterness of sexual initiation,” per the film’s synopsis. Our positive review called it a very faithful and loyal adaptation of the Nobel Laureate’s work and a strong entry among other recent Ernaux adaptations like “Happening” and “Simple Passion.” Godrèche, who was a figurehead in the French #MeToo movement, also directs her own daughter Tess Barthélemy in the lead role as the young Ernaux. Zeitgeist is planning a release at New York’s Film Forum in April 2027 followed by a national rollout.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: CompetitionDirector: Rodrigo SorogoyenBuzz: Per IndieWire’s review by Ryan Lattanzio — Javier Bardem plays a hotheaded filmmaker, one of those “brilliant assholes” mostly incapable of making great art without wringing it out of tyrannical behavior, in Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s Spanish industry drama “The Beloved.” The director of a memorable 2019 movie called “Madre,” a warped tale of motherhood in which a woman strikes up an affair with a dead ringer of her long-lost son, now turns his camera (or cameras, as Sorogoyen experiments with many visual formats to bewildering effect here) on fatherhood and its sins. Bardem stars as Esteban Martinez, who is casting the leading female role in his new film “Desierto,” a role he has written for his estranged daughter Emilia (Victoria Luengo).

Kino Lorber plans a qualifying run in 2026 with an awards push for Bardem, then a broader North American release in 2027. Deadline first reported the news.

Buyer: Watermelon PicturesSection: Special ScreeningsDirector: Diego LunaBuzz: The “Andor” star directed this immigrant drama film about a young woman who relocates from Mexico to Spain in order to reconnect with her mother. Star Anna Díaz earned praise for her performance, and she holds her own alongside her mother played by Adriana Paz. The film next plays TIFF, and no release plans have been set. Read more here.

Buyer: Greenwich EntertainmentSection: CompetitionDirector: Kōji FukadaBuzz: This Japanese drama follows an artist and an architect each grappling with the remnants of past relationships who connect in the rural Nagi region of Japan. Greenwich is planning a theatrical release in the U.S. and Canada in early 2027.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Out of CompetitionDirector: Andy GarciaBuzz: A true labor of love, star Andy Garcia also wrote, directed, and produced this throwback detective noir (he also designed all the music and co-wrote the original score with his longtime collaborator Arturo Sandoval), which he’s been working on for nearly 20 years.

In the film, Garcia stars as Joe Diamond, billed by SPC as “a man out of time, an urban legend with an emotional traumatic past. He has the uncanny ability to solve crimes that even the LAPD cannot — armed only with the savvy and dry humor reminiscent of the gumshoe detectives of that genre. It is a love letter to Los Angeles and an homage to the great noir films of the past.”

The film also stars Vicky Krieps, Brendan Fraser, Bill Murray, Dustin Hoffman, Rosemarie DeWitt, and more. Sony Pictures Classics acquired worldwide rights (ex. France, Germany, Italy, CIS) to the film and will announce release plans at a later date.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: Director’s FortnightDirector: Reed Van DykBuzz: The directorial debut of Reed Van Dyk was a stunner out of Director’s Fortnight, with our critic writing that it is an “intimate and psychologically astute” war film based on a 2012 New Yorker article about the aftermath of the Iraq War and the impact of U.S. influence in the region. The film follows a U.S. Marine who returns to Iraq to visit with an Iraqi woman and her family whom were caught up in a firefight when he was deployed. The film stars Boyd Holbrook, Kenneth Branagh, and Hiam Abbass. Kino Lorber is planning a fall release with some awards ambitions in mind, and it will play some other fall festivals before then.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: CompetitionDirector: Emmanuel MarreBuzz: 1-2 Special’s third acquisition out of Cannes is writer/director Emmanuel Marre’s (“Zero Fucks Given”) historical drama “A Man of His Time,” starring Swann Arlaud, best known for his role in 2023’s Palme d’Or winner “Anatomy of a Fall.” Set in 1940, it’s inspired by the life of the filmmaker’s own great-grandfather, with Arlaud’s Henri arriving in Vichy, France, as Nazis began to install themselves. There, he ingratiates himself with the regime against the backdrop of French resistance. Per the distributor, “As he sets his plan into motion, he does whatever is required to remain useful, serving the machinery of the new order with increasing skill, but as the war continues he may be pursuing something more urgent: escape from his own ruin.” Winner of the Best Screenplay prize out of the Cannes competition, “A Man of His Time” will open in theaters next year.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Manuela MartelliBuzz: Kino Lorber’s first acquisition from Cannes is this Chilean film from the director of the Pinochet-era political thriller “Chile ’76.” This one though is set in 1992 after the end of the Pinochet regime and follows a young girl at a ski resort who befriends a German competitive skier, only for the German to disappear without a trace. Our critic compared the eerie mystery to “Picnic at Hanging Rock” and “The Spirit of the Beehive.” Kino Lorber picked up U.S. rights and is planning a theatrical release for early 2027.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Sandra WollnerBuzz: Rising outfit 1-2 Special’s mandate at this year’s Cannes? It seems like “get proven winners.” After previously picking up Critics’ Week winner “La Gradiva,” the label has next bought Un Certain Regard winner “Everytime” the third film from filmmaker Sandra Wollner. The features tracks a family as they take a trip to the Canary Islands after a horrible tragedy.

Buyer: Janus FilmsSection: CompetitionDirector: Valeska GrisebachBuzz: “Western” filmmaker Grisebach’s Cannes contender, starring Yana Radeva and Syuleyman Letifov, premiered in the Competition section at the festival, where it was ultimately awarded the Jury Prize. The dreamy drama also sparkles with other genre beats, and our critic hailed its inventive spin on the Western, also noting that “Grisebach has a flair for finding faces with striking, weatherbeaten features that might have grown out of the landscape itself. We are in an era where the cinema normalizes faces interrupted by Botox and fillers, amounting to propaganda against aging and even mortality itself; by contrast, the faces that fill Grisebach’s frames are a cool drink of mountain water.” Janus Films will announce theatrical release plans in the coming weeks.

Buyer: NetflixSection: CompetitionDirector: Marie KreutzerBuzz: “Corsage” director Marie Kreutzer’s latest feature “Gentle Monster,” one of two competition films led by French star Léa Seydoux, marked Netflix’s third Cannes acquisition after the animated “In Waves” and Spanish epic “The Black Ball.” (Deadline first reported the news; IndieWire independently confirmed it.) The streamer obviously sees awards prospects in all three films, with Seydoux as a possible Best Actress contender for her performance as an avant-garde pianist whose life is blown apart by the news that her husband may be a child sex offender. Of the two Léa Seydoux films, “Gentle Monster” stood out over Neon’s “The Unknown” in terms of review response.

Buyer: MubiSection: CompetitionDirector: Lukas DhontBuzz: Mubi, which came to Cannes with “Minotaur” and “Fatherland” already in competition, just made its first acquisition for North America since the start of the festival with Lukas Dhont’s “Coward.” The Belgian filmmaker was nominated for the Best International Feature Oscar in 2023 for “Close”; here, he directs the furtive romance between two soldiers on the Western front in World War I. The film stars Emmanuel Macchia in his debut film performance as Pierre and Valentin Campagne (“Colours of Time,” “Case 137”) as Francis. Mubi already had rights in UK, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain, Turkey, Latin America, Australia, and New Zealand. The Match Factory, which has been part of Mubi since 2022, handles international sales.

Buyer: NetflixSection: CompetitionDirector: Javier Calvo and Javier AmbrossiBuzz: Rising filmmakers (and exes!) Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi premiered “The Black Ball” late in the competition to strong reviews and enthusiastic audience response. As Variety reported, a multi-studio bidding war ensued, with Mubi, A24, and Netflix, who eventually won out, in the mix. Set in 1932, 1937, and 2017 and following the lives of three men, the film is a tribute to poet Federico García Lorca and his unfinished works.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Special ScreeningsDirector: Pegah AhangaraniBuzz: Winner of the L’Oeil d’Or, this debut feature documentary from Iranian filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani is a deeply personal and autobiographical portrait of her own family that stretches 40 years, dating back to 1979 and up through the war going on in Iran as we speak. SPC, after grabbing “Iron Boy” earlier this week, landed all rights for North and Latin America, Asia (except Japan), New Zealand, Turkey, Portugal, and worldwide airlines.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: Critics’ WeekDirector: Marine AtlanBuzz: Our critic was enamored with the directorial debut of Marine Atlan, writing that it takes the simple premise of high school teens on a class trip and resists all tropes to find a film that nears “the sublime” and manages to “explore the vast worlds of their individual interiority with insight, empathy, and grace.” Just today the film won the Grand Prize from Critics’ Week, and it’s already one of the top 5 rated films on Letterboxd among this year’s crop of Cannes titles. 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Louis ClichyBuzz: Yet another animated sale among the Official Selection, “Iron Boy” is a hand-painted animated feature with director Clichy, who cut his teeth as a 3D animator on “WALL-E” and “Up,” returning to ink line drawings inspired by Manga comics and his own early short films. “Iron Boy” is his first feature as a solo director. The film follows 11-year-old in rural France as he tries to live up to his rigid and distant father on the family farm. But when the young boy starts to lean over and collapse without warning, he must wear an iron corset to keep himself upright. Clichy co-wrote the film with Franck Salomé.

Buyer: NetflixSection: Critics WeekDirector: Phuong Mai NguyenBuzz: The opening night film for the Critics Week sidebar, Netflix acquired the worldwide rights (excluding France) for this animated film that features the voice talent of Will Sharpe and Stephanie Hsu. The film is based on a graphic novel by AJ Dungo and follows a shy teenager in Los Angeles who falls madly in love with a surfer girl, only for their love and future to be tested when she faces a sudden illness, leaning on their new passion for surfing and the ocean to get them through adversity. Fanny Burdino and Samuel Doux. Read our review here.

Buyer: A24Section: Un Certain RegardDirector: Jordan FirstmanBuzz: Arguably the smash hit of the Cannes Film Festival, comedian/actor Jordan Firstman writes, directs, and stars in this New York comedy as a washed-up party promoter who wakes up one day to find the child he never knew he had on his doorstep. The cast includes Cara Delevigne, Diego Calva, and newcomer Reggie Absolom, with producers including Oscar-winning “Anora” producer Alex Coco. and Galen Core, alongside Topic Studios’ Ryan Heller and Michael Bloom. A24 acquired the film’s rights in a competitive situation, with most major distributors bidding at Cannes. Read our review here.

Buyer: Clockwork (Warner Bros.)Section: Cannes ClassicsDirector: Ken RussellBuzz: This uncut restoration of Ken Russell’s super controversial — and largely unavailable — gem “The Devils” is being positioned by Warner Bros.’ new indie label Clockwork as the experience Russell always envisioned but never got to show properly. It’s the first repertory release from the new WB label, and frankly the first release period after announcing that Sean Baker’s next film “Ti Amo” was its inaugural acquisition. After it premieres in Cannes Classics, Clockwork is planning a one-week special engagement of screenings in theaters beginning October 16. Read more about the re-release here.

Buyer: NeonSection: CompetitionDirector: James GrayBuzz: “Paper Tiger” is the sixth film James Gray has brought to Cannes, but it’s the first time Neon has partnered with him, and given that it’s one of just two American films in the competition slate this year and one of the starriest, it seems like a match made in heaven. Gray’s crime thriller stars Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson, and Miles Teller in a story about two brothers striving to achieve the American Dream only to get caught up with the Russian Mafia.

Buyer: Janus FilmsSection: Cannes PremieresDirector: Kiyoshi KurosawaBuzz: The latest film from the director of “Cloud” is a samurai film set in 16th century Japan that follows a Lord who rebelled against a tyrannical ruler and found himself beseiged within his own castle by a traitor and a prisoner being held in his own dungeon. Though based on real individuals, the film is an original story by Honobu Yonezawa.

Section: CompetitionDistributor: MUBIDirector: Andrey ZvyagintsevBuzz: The first film from the Russian director behind “Leviathan” and “Loveless” in almost a decade is a political fable and crime thriller about a businessman caught up in personal, political, and professional scandals.

Title: “All of a Sudden” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Ryusuke HamaguchiBuzz: After winning at Venice with “Drive My Car” and at Berlin with “Evil Does Not Exist,” the Japanese auteur is looking for the European festival trifecta with Neon backing his Palme D’Or bid.

Title: “Bitter Christmas” Section: CompetitionDistributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Pedro AlmodóvarBuzz: Almodóvar’s latest film curiously already opened to strong reviews in his native Spain back in March. A lush, colorful, and messy melodrama about pain and mourning sounds like an Amodóvar film to us.

Title: “Clarissa” Section: Director’s FortnightDistributor: NeonDirector: Arie Esiri and Chuko EsiriBuzz: The Nigerian directors behind “This Is My Desire” from 2020 team with Ayo Edebiri, David Oyelowo and Sophie Okonedo for a reimagining of Virginia Woolf’s “Ms. Dalloway” as set in Lagos.

Title: “Fatherland” Section: CompetitionDistributor: MUBIDirector: Pawel PawlikowskiBuzz: Polish director Pawlikowski’s first film in eight years since the searing “Cold War” is a docudrama about German author Thomas Mann in post-War Germany after having stood against the Nazis. Sandra Huller also stars.

Title: “Fjord” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Cristian MungiuBuzz: Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in the latest film from Romanian auteur Mungiu, his first since 2022’s “R.M.N.,” which is about a Romanian immigrant family under scrutiny for investigation by the Norwegian government.

Title: “Her Private Hell” Section: Out of CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Nicolas Winding RefnBuzz: “Her Private Hell” is “Drive” provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn’s first feature since 2016, and the film is a futuristic, fantastical story about a woman searching for her father and a soldier trying to recover his daughter from hell. It stars Charles Melton and Sophie Thatcher and should be loaded with stylized sex, violence, and glamor. The film opens July 24 in theaters.

Title: “Hope” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Na Hong-JinBuzz: Like an arthouse “A Quiet Place,” this action-horror monster movie from a South Korean director also stars some major Korean talent like “Squid Game” star Hoyeon as well as Michael Fassbender and Alicia Vikander.

Title: “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” Section: Director’s FortnightDistributor: NeonDirector: David GreavesBuzz: The final film of director William Greaves completed by his son and released more than a decade after his death, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” focuses on the “Harlem Renaissance” of 1972 New York.

Title: “Sheep in a Box” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Hirokazu Kore-edaBuzz: The Japanese auteur turns his family drama attention to AI and looks at the emotional impact of introducing a humanoid robot as a couple’s son.

Title: “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” Section: Un Certain RegardDistributor: MUBIDirector: Jane SchoenbrunBuzz: Riding high off “I Saw the TV Glow,” Jane Schoenbrun’s follow-up is a queer horror comedy obsessed with ’90s slashers, final girls, sexuality, and so much more. The film stars “Hacks” star Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson.

Title: “The Unknown” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Arthur HarariBuzz: A body swap drama from the writer of “Anatomy of a Fall,” Léa Seydoux stars in this film about a man who follows a mysterious woman at a party and wakes up in her body the next morning.

Title: “Victorian Psycho” Section: Un Certain RegardDistributor: Bleecker StreetDirector: Zachary WigonBuzz: Acquired at last year’s Cannes market, this haunting Gothic horror from the director of “Sanctuary” stars Maika Monroe in what is said to be an unexpected and eccentric turn.

#3528. Bill Skarsgård Addresses X-Men Casting Rumors And His Interest In A Major DC Comics Superhero Role

Marvel Studios is gearing up to unleash "Avengers: Doomsday" in 2026. Meanwhile, the studio is preparing to reintroduce us to the X-Men, with a reboot film overseen by "Thunderbolts*" director Jake Schreier, which has already cast some impressive talent ahead of its 2028 debut. One actor who won't be in the film, however is Bill Skarsgård, who was supposedly in contention for the role of Charles Xavier but has now downplayed his connection to the movie following the official casting of Christopher Abbott.

Back in July 2026, industry insider Jeff Sneider reported that Skarsgård and "Ozark" actor Tom Pelphrey (who also played Ward Meachum in Netflix's "Iron Fist" series) were up for the part. None of this was ever officially confirmed, however, and in August 2026, we learned that Marvel had cast "Kraven the Hunter" star Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, confirming that Skarsgård wouldn't be making his MCU debut with the X-Men movie. He does, however, quite like the idea of appearing as John Constantine in James Gunn's DC Universe.

During an appearance on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, the "It" star played down his involvement with the X-Men movie.

"I didn't read any scripts. It's Jake [Schreier], right?" he said. "I had a meeting with him, and I liked him. But no, it hasn't been close on a big [role]." But the actor did express an interest in another superhero role. "I thought Constantine was cool," he added. "I had an idea that Andy Muschietti and I could do Constantine. I just thought that it [would blend] truly visual horror and superhero. It's a cool thing."

Luckily for Skarsgård, it seems DC Studios is in the early stages of developing a new Constantine movie.

Roger Ebert might have hated Keanu Reeves' "Constantine" in 2005, but fans have long been waiting for a sequel. Now, however, it appears DC Studios will reinvent the character for a new generation.

Per Deadline, Francis Galluppi will write a new "Constantine" movie for the studio. The writer/director previously produced, wrote, and directed the 2023 crime thriller "The Last Stop in Yuma County," and is now working on the upcoming "Evil Dead Wrath," a prequel to the bloody good time that was 2026's "Evil Dead Burn." He's received praise from franchise creator Sam Raimi, who described Galluppi as "a storyteller who knows when to keep us waiting in simmering tension and when to hit us with explosive violence."

Created by writer Alan Moore and artists Steve Bissette and John Totleben, John Constantine first appeared in 1985's "The Saga of the Swamp Thing" #37. The British detective and exorcist is known for his incongruous mix of cynicism and deep commitment to helping those in need, and it seems Bill Skarsgård is eager to put his spin on the character.

While Galliuppi works on his script, there's no word from DC Studios on who might star in the film. But Skarsgård's idea of teaming up with his "It" director Andy Muschietti isn't a bad shout. The pair obviously have the horror bonafides, and Skarsgård seems perfect for the role of a conflicted anti-hero with a supernatural element. For now, we'll have to wait to see whether Galluppi's script works out and whether DC Studios also brings him on as director. But studio co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran would do well to at least consider Skarsgård's vision.

#3527. This Top-Rated 65-Inch LG OLED TV Is $200 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The 65-inch LG Evo C6 OLED TV has dropped to $1,399.99 from $1,599.99, a $200 price cut that brings it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers—and the savings aren't limited to this particular size either, with discounts extending across the C6 lineup, from the compact 42-inch model to the massive 83-inch version, although the 65-inch screen is particularly appealing if you want a larger OLED without spending more than $1,500. You also get a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music with the purchase and complimentary room-of-choice delivery (which would otherwise cost you an extra $19.99).

Beyond the discount, there's plenty to like about the C6 itself, with PCMag calling it an excellent midrange OLED that is slightly brighter than last year’s Evo C5 while still retaining its color accuracy and sleek design, giving you much of what makes LG’s flagship OLEDs appealing at a considerably lower price. The nearly bezel-free design also keeps the focus on the picture, while its 4K OLED panel delivers bright HDR highlights in Dolby Vision, HDR10, and HLG content. That should work well in most living rooms, although a particularly sunny space may still benefit from a brighter Mini-LED TV.

For streaming, LG’s webOS platform covers most major services, and AirPlay and Google Cast make it easy to share videos or photos directly from your phone. You can also use hands-free voice controls through LG's assistant, Google Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot to search for content or ask questions without reaching for the remote. Gamers will also appreciate the C6’s native 120Hz panel, which supports variable refresh rates up to 165Hz, along with AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync compatibility to help keep fast-moving games smooth and tear-free. It’s also highly responsive, with an input lag of just 4.6 milliseconds at 1080p120 and 12.8 milliseconds at 4K60.

The C6’s main drawback is its Wi-Fi 5 connection, which feels dated for a TV at this price, although it should still handle most 4K streaming without trouble. It also lacks an ATSC 3.0 tuner, meaning you won't get support for newer over-the-air broadcast standards.

#3526. Avengers: Doomsday's Final Writing Credits Confirmed, With Two Marvel Actors Reportedly Involved

With so many moving parts in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, it's perhaps inevitable that the movie scripts are always changing, too. That's especially true for the incoming team-up movie "Avengers: Doomsday," which features a dizzying array of superheroes alongside the return of Robert Downey Jr., not as Iron Man but as classic Marvel villain Doctor Doom. Directors Anthony and Joe Russo have confirmed the reports that the "Doomsday" script was still being written while they were filming, describing themselves as "improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors."

Even after filming is complete, it takes a while to determine which writers meet the criteria for a writing credit, per the Writers Guild of America's credit system. The WGA recently confirmed the two writers who will be given the main "written by" credit for "Avengers: Doomsday." One is Stephen McFeely, an MCU mainstay who co-wrote "Captain America: The First Avenger," "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Endgame," and several other titles. The other is Michael Waldron, who wrote the script for "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness" and created the well-received Disney+ series "Loki."

With a movie production as big as "Doomsday," however, there's almost always a hidden team of writers and script doctors who are brought in to help fine-tune and troubleshoot the script, or who worked on previous versions of it. And with an improvisational approach to production, actors will often add their own contributions via ad-libbing. Now, rumor has it that two actors in "Avengers: Doomsday" contributed enough to get an extra credit.

X/Twitter user Crystal4KQual, who has proven to be a reliable source for Marvel scoops, shared this tidbit: "I recently learned through their production companies, Ryan [Reynolds] and Hugh [Jackman] may get some form of screen writing credits on '[Avengers:] Doomsday,' too."

This wouldn't be the first writing credit for Reynolds, who co-wrote "Deadpool 2" and "Deadpool & Wolverine" alongside Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick. Actors aren't typically given writing credits just for ad-libbing some of their lines (or Reynolds would have a lot more credits to his name). However, in 2022, the Writers Guild of America introduced a new "additional literary material" credit for people who provided writing services for a movie but would otherwise be uncredited. The credit doesn't come with any residuals and doesn't equate to authorship (a writer can get an ALM credit even if none of their contributions end up on screen), but it does allow writers to put the experience on their resume.

"The Fantastic Four: First Steps," for example, had seven writers credited for additional literary material, including "Doomsday" screenwriter Michael Waldron. Indeed, given its complex development history, "Avengers: Doomsday" may end up with a similar number of ALM credits, including the "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" writing team of Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, who were reported to have worked on the script.

We'll find out if Reynolds and Jackman did manage to snag any writing credits when "Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3524. Keanu Reeves' Constantine 2 Could Be Dead After A Major DC Studios Development

John Constantine is about to enter James Gunn's DC Universe. Deadline reports that DC Studios has recruited filmmaker Francis Galluppi, writer/director of the upcoming "Evil Dead Wrath," to write a movie starring Constantine. But didn't Warner Bros. already have a Constantine movie in development?

Keanu Reeves played Constantine in the eponymous 2005 "Constantine" film. It's been criticized for its inaccuracies to the original "Hellblazer" comics (Reeves is often ranked as the worst onscreen John Constantine), but as a film unto itself, "Constantine" has found an audience who love it in spite of its infidelity.

Reeves himself has been pushing for a "Constantine" sequel, but "Constantine 2" has kept facing delays. With DC Studios moving forward with a new Constantine, it's unclear if Reeves' sequel will continue; Deadline's reporting does not mention the project one way or another. Compare how DC Studios has held off bringing in Batman to its new DC Universe, even when making a movie like "Clayface" that's set in Gotham City. That's clearly because Matt Reeves' "The Batman" franchise is existing in parallel with the DCU. While a DCU-set Batman movie, "The Brave and the Bold," was announced in 2023, there's been little movement on that project since then.

Two versions of Batman simultaneously existing already seemed like a risky move. Two competing John Constantine movies? Forget about it.

Co-created in 1985 by Alan Moore, Stephen R. Bissette, and John Totleben, John Constantine first debuted as a supporting character in "Swamp Thing." Just a few years later, he earned a spin-off comic, "Hellblazer," that ran for 25 years and 300 issues.

As for Constantine, he's a warlock, an occult detective, an exorcist, and a con man known for his acerbic cynicism and chain-smoking. (Noted "Hellblazer" arc "Dangerous Habits" by Garth Ennis and Will Simpson is all about John discovering he has lung cancer from his constant smoking and racing to save himself.) While initially presented as part of the main DC Universe, "Hellblazer," published by DC's Vertigo imprint, gradually drifted into its own separate world.

But then, DC Comics' 2011 reboot "The New 52" broke down those walls again. Suddenly, John was joining the Justice League Dark, a team for DC's supernatural superheroes. That integration carried over outside the comics. Welsh actor Matt Ryan played Constantine in a short-lived NBC series in 2014 — but that was only the beginning. Ryan guest-starred as John in Season 4 of "Arrow" and then became a regular on "Legends of Tomorrow." He also became the character's official voice actor in animation, beginning with a 2017 "Justice League Dark" animated movie.

This early, it's unclear who DC Studios could have in mind to play John Constantine, though actor Bill Skarsgård has put himself in contention. It's worth noting that DC Studios currently has a "Swamp Thing" movie, directed by James Mangold, in the works. This is pure speculation, but it wouldn't be out of place for John to show up in that.

#3522. AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

When we first wrote about the coming release of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the first fully AI-generated feature film being self-distributed into movie theaters in the U.S., it would’ve been easy to write the whole thing off as a stunt.

Coming from YouTuber Gossip Goblin, who has an impressive and loyal following, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” started earning comps from the press (and from the producers themselves) to the success Markiplier found when he self-released his film “Iron Lung” and made $50 million worldwide in the process. Would that success translate for an AI movie? A recent example from China suggests that may not be the case. Related Stories Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’ Sony Pictures Classics Buys Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s ‘Violette’

It’s clear though the team behind “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is treating this like a real project that needs to be seen in theaters and is worthy of serious critical consideration, and they’re doing that with real marketing dollars behind its theatrical push.

Today, Gossip Goblin announced that pop star Grimes is set to make a cameo in his film “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” as is YouTuber Mike Majlak, and their involvement is being revealed via a massive Times Square ad campaign that is also launching today, all ahead of the film’s release next month on December 4. Gossip Goblin is even launching a contest for people to use AI to create their own short films within the universe of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” that can net the winning creator $15,000.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” also sparked some headlines in the last few months with the news that the producers are plotting an Oscar campaign for Best Animated Feature. Turns out some FYC screenings have already started and a digital campaign begins at the end of November. All of the above suggests some real belief in the project, and with a collective 16 million views of the trailer thus far, they have reason to believe.

“We’ve been heartened already by the reaction,” producer Edward Saatchi of Fable Studios said in a statement. “One Oscar-Nominated animated film director compared ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ after seeing it to ‘2001,’ and we’ve had great feedback from Pixar folks (part of Fable’s team is ex-Pixar and we hugely respect their work).”

Zack London, the man behind the moniker Gossip Goblin, in speaking with IndieWire ahead of the announcement, said he’s “fully cognizant” of the controversy around putting a movie made with AI into theaters, and he acknowledges that all of this is “a big, unproven hypothesis.” But he says it would be “disingenuous to write it all off” as just an AI movie or not a real project.

Getting screens is easy, but the real battle is making people believe there are actually humans behind this movie, even if the images are all generated by AI. Roughly 30 to 35 people are credited in the making of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” and a behind-the-scenes documentary that is also in the works is aimed to humanize the process of making the movie. It includes interviews with the film’s composer and voice actors and shows its Foley guy doing real post-production work. Even the act of getting a real person like Grimes in the film — whose image is generated to resemble her but who does real voice acting — required an elaborate process of photo mashing atop existing character design to fit her into the movie, as well as contacting the model makers themselves to remove built-in censors for generating images of a public figure’s likeness.

On one hand, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” can be viewed as a scrappy indie made by a team of creatives, not just a sole prompter working alone, making a movie that wouldn’t exist otherwise. On the other hand, many would argue that the visuals on display would normally require a team of thousands to bring to life along with millions of dollars. Depending on where you fall on that spectrum may determine whether you also buy a ticket to see it.

But London and Saatchi have grander ambitions with “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” and AI filmmaking beyond just what it can do at the box office. Saatchi says that for as many great CG animated films have been released in the last 30 years since “Toy Story” first hit theaters, they’ve arguably all looked similar and been made with the same techniques. He views “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” as the next “Toy Story” moment in animation, with a movie that aims to look psychedelic and otherworldly, something that looks unique and looks like it could only be the product of AI generative models. Other films may use AI to create something cheaply that looks like a Pixar movie, but London wanted to make something that looked like nothing else.

“Pixar set the look for animated films in the ’90s — they didn’t use technology to more cheaply make a film that looked like ‘Beauty and the Beast,’ they created a radically new aesthetic with ‘Toy Story,'” Saatchi said. “That’s what ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ represents: a wild new aesthetic for animated films that will define much of animated, actor-voiced films in the coming decades. This is that ‘Toy Story’ moment for our generation — a radical departure for animated films — you only need to see Grimes’ brilliant performance in the film to understand how much things are about to change for animated movies. And we hope the Academy will recognize that a film that is seminal (the first AI film), wildly technically novel and most importantly good deserves a nomination.”

#3521. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.
