#3520. Godzilla Minus Zero Has Two Cameos Only Hardcore Franchise Fans Noticed

The following post contains brief spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is pure Godzilla spectacle. This is a bigger, badder king of the monsters that's not without its flaws, but nevertheless offers enough spectacle and kaiju action to make it a thrilling cinematic experience. Sure, we've had plenty of kaiju movies the past decade, but few manage to get anywhere near the scope or scale that Takashi Yamazaki offers in his follow-up to the Oscar-winning "Godzilla Minus One."

One of the things that makes this movie special is how it expands the world of the previous Godzilla. By bringing in King Ghidorah (whose design unfortunately leaked online before the film's release), the movie throws open the doors to all sorts of Toho kaiju. It's significant that it's Ghidorah who becomes Godzilla's first foe here, because the three-headed alien dragon that shoots gravity-affecting lightning is such a weird creature that it allows for pretty much anything to follow him. From here, you could easily do Mechagodzilla, or Mothra, or even Gigan.

That being said, "Godzilla Minus Zero" remains a surprisingly grounded and human movie even if it deals with extraterrestrial threats. This is a film with some of the most harrowing kaiju imagery in decades, as it shows how truly horrific the aftermath of a Godzilla attack would actually be. It's unlike any Godzilla movie we've had in this new era. This feels like classic Godzilla without trying to reinvent the wheel, and it feels more grounded than the bonkers and silly MonsterVerse.

Which is why it's funny that this movie features two cameos from two very different corners of the Godzilla franchise — cameos only hardcore fans will notice. Specifically, the film features cameos from directors Hideaki Anno and Jordan Vogt-Roberts.

Hideaki Anno is a legend of anime, having created the groundbreaking and hugely influential "Neon Genesis Evangelion." But Anno is above all else a massive nerd who's spent the past decade bringing every one of his childhood obsessions to life on the big screen, starting with "Shin Godzilla," and then with "Shin Ultraman" and "Shin Kamen Rider." Anno's "Shin Godzilla" was a revelation, a political satire about the failures of government to respond to a crisis that also happened to feature a terrifying Godzilla.

Anno has a blink-and-you-miss-it cameo in "Godzilla Minus Zero" when Koichi and Noriko leave Tokyo and are on a train south. The camera lingers for less than a second on a man reading a newspaper containing news of Ghidorah's attack. That man is the legend behind "Shin Godzilla."

Jordan Vogt-Roberts' cameo comes at the very end of the film when a group of American soldiers capture professor Murakami. What makes his cameo interesting is that Vogt-Roberts has not actually directed a Godzilla project. Instead, he's best known for directing "Kong: Skull Island," which is a very fun take on a kaiju movie and is part of the MonsterVerse, but doesn't actually feature the King of the Monsters himself.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, director "Godzilla Minus Zero" director Takashi Yamazaki explained how Vogt-Roberts ended up in the final film.

"Jordan makes quite frequent trips to Japan. During one of his trips, he reached out to us, and we set up a dinner," Yamazaki said. "That's when he said, 'Hey, I'd really love to be in the next Godzilla movie you're working on.' And I said, 'Well, if you're in Japan, perhaps there's a scene we could work you into.'"

#3519. James Cameron’s Avatar Franchise Gets a Massive New December Release

The latest installment in the sci-fi franchise is getting a new release with lots of behind-the-scenes material

James Cameron is giving Avatar: Fire and Ash another home-video release, and this one comes with enough behind-the-scenes material to keep Pandora fans busy for several hours. 20th Century Studios has announced a new Collector's Edition 4K Blu-ray, arriving this December, with more than six hours of previously unreleased bonus features.

The new edition builds on the sci-fi film's original 4K Blu-ray release from March, which already included roughly three hours of additional content. That means fans who pick up the Collector's Edition will have access to an extensive collection of material exploring the filmmaking process behind Cameron's latest trip to Pandora.

Among the biggest additions are Fire and Water: Making the Avatar Films, a two-part documentary exploring the production of the franchise, and a collection of deleted and extended scenes. The release also includes performance-capture demonstrations, scene breakdowns, and additional behind-the-scenes material examining how the filmmakers brought the film's elaborate digital environments and characters to life.

For fans interested in the technical side of Cameron's filmmaking, the performance-capture material could be a particular highlight. The Avatar franchise has consistently pushed the boundaries of visual effects and motion-capture technology, with Fire and Ash continuing that approach on an enormous scale.

The Collector's Edition also includes archival materials, production artwork, the screenplay, and a selection of awards-season panels featuring cast members and filmmakers. Combined with the previously released bonus features, the package offers a considerably deeper look at the production than the standard home-video edition.

Fire and Ash follows Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), Neytiri (Zoe Saldaña), and their family as they face another threat on Pandora, this time involving the aggressive Ash People and their leader, Varang (Oona Chaplin). Stephen Lang also returns as Colonel Miles Quaritch, whose increasingly complicated relationship with the Na'vi becomes another major part of the story.

In Polygon's review, we praised Cameron's commitment to the technical craft behind the franchise, particularly the performances and visual effects that give its digitally rendered characters a sense of physicality. The new Collector's Edition should provide a closer look at the enormous amount of work required to achieve that result.

Avatar: Fire and Ash Collector's Edition 4K Blu-ray arrives Dec. 8, just in time for the holiday season.

The American Cinematheque Awards Gala is officially back on with actor Robert Pattinson, star of several films from 2026, from “Primetime” and “The Drama,” to “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three,” as the 40th recipient. The milestone celebration will now take place on Tuesday, February 9, 2027, at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills.

#3516. Black Doves Season 3: Renewal Status & Everything We Know

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for Black Doves season 2.Netflix's spy thriller Black Doves only just ended its second season, but many viewers are likely already wondering if the story of Keira Knightley's Helen Webb will continue in season 3. There's already a lot of hype surrounding Black Doves season 3. That's partly due to the rave reviews for Black Doves season 2 and partly due to the very open-ended finale of Black Doves season 2.

Black Doves has been a critical and popular darling since it began, and there's still plenty of room to explore Helen's story, so season 3 should be a no-brainer. Despite its popularity and success, the fate of Black Doves season 3 is still undecided. There are, however, a few hopeful indications that Netflix is going to make the right decision and renew Black Doves for another outing.

At the time of writing, Netflix has not yet officially confirmed Black Doves season 3. That's not a very discouraging development, as streaming services typically take weeks or months to issue a series renewal. It is, however, a bit unusual for Black Doves specifically. Black Doves season 2 was confirmed even before the first season premiered back in December 2024. It seems season 3 didn't get the same early vote of confidence, and it's possible that Netflix wants to look at critical reception and viewership numbers before deciding whether to renew or cancel the series.

Keira Knightley's Helen Webb / Daisy Bradshaw takes on various personas and undercover aliases in Netflix's thrilling espionage series Black Doves.

It is worth noting that Netflix's official ending explainer for Black Doves season 2 does explore what's next for the Black Doves following this season's reveals (via Tudum). While that's nowhere near an official renewal, it is a promising sign that Netflix is willing to renew the show for a third season and is already trying to drum up intrigue for some new plot lines. For now, however, the fate of Black Doves season 3 is unconfirmed.

Unfortunately, even if Black Doves season 3 is confirmed soon, this delay may have some implications for when it could be released on Netflix. Black Doves season 2, despite being renewed before season 1 even began, took nearly two full years to premiere. Since production on season 3 hasn't even begun yet, it may take even longer than season 2 did. So much is still up in the air, but Black Doves season 3 may not arrive on Netflix until 2028 or potentially later, if it happens at all.

Though the show hasn't been officially renewed yet, Black Doves showrunner Joe Barton has already hinted that he has plans for a third season. In an interview with Esquire, Barton said that he wants to have Tom Hanks and Elliot Page guest star in Black Doves season 3. While it's not exactly a confirmation that the script has been written, Barton's comments indicate that he at least has some idea of the story Black Doves season 3 could take.

Additionally, Barton also hinted at Helen's future during his interview with Netflix (via Tudum). In that interview, Barton mentions that Helen will likely go through an "evolution" as a character, and that her only path forward is to get even more involved in the Black Doves organization. Clearly, Barton has ideas about how to continue the story of Black Doves, even though Netflix hasn't given the official order yet.

One of the strongest pieces of evidence suggesting that Black Doves could be renewed for a third season is the ending of the second season. The finale of Black Doves season 2 left the door wide open for another season to pick up where it left off. It is by no means a definitive ending to Helen's story or the tale of the Black Doves as an organization; on the contrary, it actually seems Black Doves season 2 is an expansion of the show.

The clearest way Black Doves season 2 has expanded the series is through Kestrel, the new anarchist covert organization that stands opposed to the Black Doves. Though Katia, aka Vita, died at the end of season 2, Patrick was able to escape alive. He even delivered a calling card to Helen, which Reed smartly deduced was a warning that Kestrel had not been destroyed and could still pose a major threat. Reed also explained that Patrick had been seen boarding a plane to Tokyo, presumably to resume Kestrel's operations in the wake of Vita's death.

Kestrel presents a perfect story for Black Doves season 3 to explore. The next season could follow Helen and Reed tracking down Kestrel and trying to thwart their future actions across the globe. Kestrel also presents an opportunity to get government intelligence organizations, like the CIA and MI6, involved, as the U.S. and U.K. likely want revenge for Kestrel's attack on the peace summit. In short, Black Doves has set itself up very nicely to continue its story in season 3, even if that third season hasn't yet been confirmed.

Many of Joon-ho's films explore elements of science fiction within them and for so many, their love of the director started with Snowpiercer.

#3513. ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

Among the bleakest films ever made, Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” (1977) famously ends not with the suicide of its title character, but with a haunting coda in which a chicken pecks at a miniature piano inside a surreal roadside tourist trap’s coin-operated display. It’s a visual metaphor for the inescapable banality of life on Earth, and for the dehumanizing work people are forced to do to disguise the many failures of the American Dream. It’s also the last thing that Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis saw before he killed himself. “Look into the eyes of a chicken,” Herzog has said, “and you will see real stupidity. It is a kind of bottomless stupidity, a fiending stupidity. They are the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world.” Related Stories Robert Pattinson to Receive 2026 American Cinematheque Award AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

That sentiment has long endured as modern cinema’s definitive stance on chickens (despite Aardman’s best efforts), but now, after witnessing the 50 years of entropy that followed “Stroszek,” Hungarian filmmaker György Pálfi is crying fowl. Chickens are not the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world, he contends. We are. How can you tell? Easy: Just look at us through the eyes of a chicken.

A cute, cockeyed yarn that unspools like a feathered cross between “EO” and “Flow,” Pálfi’s “Hen” tells the story of a jet-black Leghorn chicken who escapes a Greek factory farm after she’s plucked from the rest of her flock because of the color of her plumage. A worker decides to take the bird home so that his wife can serve it for dinner, but our sly heroine — played by a brave hen named Feri, in addition to her seven indistinguishable stunt doubles — makes a daring escape when her captor stops his truck to refuel. But she’s snapped up again by the teeth of a dog named Titan, who carries the chicken back to the ramshackle seaside restaurant where his owner (Yannis Kokiasmenos) has much bigger problems than what to serve for dinner.

If the precise contours of those problems are a bit difficult to deduce, that’s probably because — as we’ve already established — this movie is told through the eyes of a chicken. Sometimes literally, thanks to Pálfi’s judicious deployment of POV, which is useful for times when our ruffled protagonist is, say, trapped inside a cardboard box (there’s an excellent bit where the hen starts moving the cardboard box from the inside, a “Metal Gear Solid”-inspired visual gag that proves typical of the director’s wry humor). And what does a chicken know of Europe’s ongoing migrant crisis? Of a protest between angry citizens and riot police? Of human trafficking, and the complications thereof? To judge by the film’s regular assortment of amusingly blank reaction shots, I’d wager “very little.” The titular hen doesn’t even think to look both ways when she crosses the road after flying the coop, let alone have a good answer as to why she’s doing it.

For the most part, the hen is focused on clucking her neck, surviving the pecking order at the restaurant farm where she winds up, and potentially even laying a few eggs of her own someday (we see her hatch in the movie’s first scene, but they grow up so fast). Most of the human drama is relegated to the distant background, as Pálfi mines the humor from his movie’s conceit by using the restaurant as a lens onto the hen’s predicament rather than the other way around. The people are mere archetypes, but some of the animals we meet appear so layered and inscrutable that you’d happily watch a three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about them. (The terse and fiery courtship between the star hen and her most aggressive suitor is soundtracked by a classic Greek love song, a flourish that stands out in a film where desperate migrants are being left for dead just off-camera.)

Then again, couldn’t every film about — and starring — real live animals be considered a documentary to some extent? Feri the chicken has been trained by the best of the business, but she remains blissfully unaware of the camera, and Pálfi takes pains not to anthropomorphize her any more than necessary. Plenty of heightened enjoyment comes elsewhere, much of it laundered through Giorgos Karvelas’ saturated cinematography, Szabolcs Szoke’s hyper-dynamic score, and the furtive way Pálfi bends the film’s crafts into something that almost resembles a chicken’s idea of a Western.

Here, the hen is a hen is a hen, and while “Hen” is prone to long and repetitive stretches in which she basically just hens around as a result of that approach, the animal’s natural obliviousness is too crucial a contrast to our own willful antipathy for Pálfi to risk muddying the difference between the two. At the risk of making the movie’s side-eyed social commentary sound more didactic than it is in practice (save for one very pointed moment towards the end that explicitly affirms Herzog’s claim), “Hen” uses a chicken’s lack of moral responsibility to highlight the mandate we have to heed our own, no matter how effectively we’ve evolved to ignore it.

No matter how good we get at farming other species, and killing our own. Pálfi does very little to goose or otherwise manipulate our emotional attachment to his chicken star, but there’s still something to be said for how easily we become more invested in this witless hen’s fate than in that of the doomed people with whom she crosses paths. By the time it reaches its end, this strange but sober film starts to point back to the beginning, cutting from a single egg being squeezed out of a hen’s vent (Google says “vent”) to a vast sea of them bobbling around inside the factory’s machines. One is easy to follow, and to care about. Thousands are a statistic. We’re smart enough to farm other animals, but people — like chickens — won’t hesitate to eat each other the minute they get hungry.

Dekanalog will release “Hen” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3511. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3510. Nintendo Hints the Switch 2 Will Keep Getting Classic Remakes

Nintendo's Nate Bihldorff says that new games and remakes are of 'equal importance'

This time last year, Nintendo’s 2026 plans were a bit of a mystery. We knew that games like Pokémon Pokopia and Mario Tennis Fever would round out the Switch 2’s first year, but we still had few clues about what would be 2026’s big game for the platform. Now, we know that Nintendo was hiding a big secret during that time. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time would be the Switch 2’s tentpole 2026 game, giving players (and Nintendo’ holiday sales) a blockbuster remake. Nate Bihldorff, Nintendo’s SVP of product development and publishing, knew that would be a very big deal.

“I often have the best time anticipating which games are going to send the fandom into as big of a fervor as possible, and certainly the first time we heard about Ocarina of Time, we expected that to be the case,” Bihldorff told Polygon at the game’s launch event at Nintendo’s flagship New York store.

During our conversation about Ocarina of Time, Bihldorff explained how the critically acclaimed Zelda game fits into the Switch 2’s growing software lineup. The Switch 2’s first year of games was especially eclectic, giving players left-field swings like Kirby Air Riders and Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. While the lineup was strong, some Nintendo players wondered when the publisher would roll out its biggest guns. But Nintendo was confident about holding on to a system-selling announcement for a little while, because it had plenty of faith in the Switch 2’s initial software lineup.

“We always have confidence in our developers coming out with great games,” Bihldorff said. “There’s one constant that has been consistent through my entire career at Nintendo, and that’s that you can pretty much set your watch by the idea that we’re going to be coming out with stuff. And the beauty of having so many different IPs that appeal to different people is that you can have a cycle of different games that come out. It doesn’t matter how excited I am about Donkey Kong Bananza at launch; there’s always going to be more games that are coming down the pipeline. This felt no different than that.”

While Ocarina of Time was likely to be a slam dunk, it’s a creatively risky project on paper. Players have strong feelings about the original game, which has long been hailed as the greatest video game of all time. According to Bihldorff, the developers were aware of the stakes, but they were more excited than nervous about working on the remake.

“They knew the challenge that was before them when they decided to take on this project, but you can also read the enthusiasm in all of their comments about how excited they got, once they actually got in the mix, to bring this to a new generation of people,” Bihldorff said. “I think that outweighs any concern about ‘I hope we don’t screw this up!’ No, they have passion about this. Let’s get this out. The final product really speaks for itself.”

Part of that excitement comes from the hardware the game was built on. In an interview with Polygon earlier in the day, Zelda producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi stressed that the Switch 2 granted developers the opportunity to realize Ocarina of Time in a way that mid-’90s gaming technology simply wouldn’t allow.

“Now with the new hardware, Nintendo Switch 2, we're able to leverage all of the capabilities and try to do things that we weren't able to do with Ocarina of Time,” Fujibayashi told Polygon. “So I think this gave us an opportunity to really explore thoroughly what that kind of gameplay and game design is."

Ocarina of Time would have been an eye-catching move for Nintendo in its own right, but it’s even more interesting in context of the Switch 2’s 2026. It’s the second major remake of the year for the company, following June’s Star Fox. (Though not a literal remake, 2025’s Kirby Air Riders was also, in many ways, a revisiting of the GameCube’s Kirby Air Ride.) Was it a coincidence of timing, or a signal of a strategic shift for Nintendo as it looks to bring back its most beloved games? Bihldorff emphasized that while original games are still as important as ever for Nintendo, remakes are a big part of Nintendo’s software plans right now.

“I do think that new games and remakes both have a place in the Nintendo stable, of equal importance to be honest,” Bihldorff said. “There are fans of every single IP that we have out there. Of course, having new games in those series is wonderful, and I look forward to them as much as anyone else does, but there’s also a deep satisfaction in revisiting games that were very, very special, like Ocarina of Time… But it’s also important to think about how many people had never played the original, and for them, the remake of Ocarina of Time is going to be an absolutely brand-new, 2026 experience, and one that I just cannot wait for them to get their hands on.”

Bihldorff’s comments paint a picture of Nintendo's strategy in the second year of the Switch 2. The publisher is living in an interesting creative space, where it’s balancing niche games in smaller IP with high-profile remakes that feel like safer bets. That tightrope act seems to be working, especially considering that left-field releases like Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream are turning out to be financial winners for Switch 2. If any move — whether it be reviving a critically panned GameCube game or giving Ocarina of Time a radical facelift — seems surprisingly risky, you can chalk it up to the kind of bravado you’re bound to earn when those risks keep paying off.

#3509. Freida McFadden's 'The Housemaid' Stage Adaptation Announced

Freida McFadden has had no shortage of success, but 2026 has been especially fruitful for her.

The mystery author released a staggering four new books, all New York Times Bestsellers (The Witch, on October 6, The Divorce, on May 26, The Dinner Party on April 4, and Dear Debbie, on January 27). The Housemaid—the first film adaptation of McFadden's work—made over $400 million at the box office upon its December 2025 release, then became an even bigger streaming hit.

At least six more adaptations of her novels are now in development, including a sequel to The Housemaid, film versions of The Teacher, The Tenant, The Surrogate Mother, and The Divorce, and a series adaptation of Dear Debbie. The last year has been so big for McFadden that she even revealed the true identity behind her pen name after 12 years of keeping it a secret.

Now, however, the queen of mystery thrillers is venturing into even newer territory: one of her bestselling novels is coming to London as a play.

The Housemaid, a stage adaptation of McFadden’s 2022 novel, will premiere as a touring production in 2027, starting at Richmond Theatre in London.

Lionsgate, the studio behind the Housemaid films, will also produce this stage version. Playwright Bekah Brunstetter will write the script, while prolific West End director Matthew Dunster will direct. Both have experience developing major page-to-screen adaptations into stage productions: Brunstetter was Tony-nominated for her musical adaptation of Nicholas Sparks’ The Notebook, while Dunster recently directed The Hunger Games: On Stage.

While a straight play may not be the most expected avenue for adapting McFadden’s hit novels, mystery authors have a rich history with English theater. Agatha Christie wrote more than 15 plays during her life, including several adaptations of her own novels. One of her plays, The Mousetrap, has run consistently on the West End since 1952, making it the longest-running play in the world.

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote 12 plays, including an adaptation of his Sherlock Holmes novels, and all premiered in England, while Dorothy L. Sayers wrote nine.

Set on Long Island, The Housemaid follows Millie Calloway, a young woman with a dark past who accepts a job as a live-in maid for a wealthy family, only to discover they have much darker secrets of their own.

The film adaptation stars Sydney Sweeney as Millie, with Amanda Seyfried and Brandon Sklenar as Nina and Andrew Winchester, the couple who employ her. A cast for the stage adaptation has yet to be announced, though it will follow the same general storyline.

The Housemaid will run for eight days at Richmond Theatre, starting September 11, 2027, and closing September 18—but tickets will be on sale as early as Friday, November 6. Future tour dates and locations are yet to be announced.

#3508. ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups

There are dozens of scenes that capture “North of North’s” digestible, defiant kindness, but my favorite arrives near the start of the second season’s second episode. Siaja (Anna Lambe) wakes up, grabs a glass of water, and promptly spits it out. The local water supply is contaminated (“They must’ve cranked those chemicals again,” her mom says), so Siaja heads to the nearest store to load up on jugs of clean water. Outside, there’s an elderly woman perched on her snowmobile, smoking a cigarette, who loudly hassles Siaja for a little charity.

“Must be nice,” the woman shouts, getting Siaja’s attention. “[You] buying filtered water. It’s too expensive [for me]. [I] gotta drink government pool water. Back in the day, we had nice ice straight from the river. Pure, nice, and healthy.” Related Stories ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

On that last word, “healthy,” the woman takes a drag from her cigarette, and while she’s doubled over coughing, Siaja takes her forceful hint and puts one of her water jugs in the woman’s cart. “Here, you take this,” Siaja says. The woman, speaking in Inuktitut, does not say “thank you”; she asks if she can keep the jug. Then she hacks a loogie into the snow as Siaja drives off, punctuating just how little the gesture means to her.

Now, it’s clear this woman knows exactly what she’s doing. She didn’t end up outside the town’s only source for clean water by accident, and Siaja knows it. But she also knows the woman is telling the truth: She’s too old to get ice for herself, and she’s too poor to afford purified water. Siaja also knows this woman is her elder, and elders should be taken care of. So after acquiescing in the moment, Siaja expands on the idea soon after: She grabs Alistair (Jay Ryan), her big, burly dad, and they go get blocks of ice from the river to deliver around town — for free.

Of course, it doesn’t go exactly as planned (the rivers aren’t all “pure” and “healthy” anymore), but Siaja’s chance encounter with the woman serves as the impetus for the entire episode: Siaja uses it to prove to her boss that she can be more than an assistant at the community center. She bonds with her dad, who she’s still getting to know. She sets a good example for her daughter, Bun (Keira Belle Cooper), and she still finds time to flirt with her crush, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), in between deliveries.

Siaja is doing exactly what she set out to do from the start of the season: “level up” her life.

Reading it back now, the story sounds corny. But despite all that positive energy driving so many warm-hearted gestures, “North by North” never becomes saccharine. Siaja’s triumphs don’t feel like cheap schmaltz. They hit that tricky TV sweet spot, where characters’ helpful actions and benevolent intentions feel genuine even when, on paper, they seem too nice to be tolerable.

It helps, of course, that Siaja fucks up early and often. Nothing makes a win land like taking many embarrassing losses to get there, as she did in Season 1 after summoning the courage to leave her husband, get a job, and start fresh — with an adorable daughter in tow. In Season 2, her plan to charm tourists doesn’t go over as whimsically as she imagined. Her plan to get her own place doesn’t include dropping in the rankings on an endless waiting list for affordable housing. Her plan to ditch her small-minded ex-husband (who doesn’t appear in Season 2) doesn’t include sitting for rounds of speed-dating or waiting out a relationship that may never end.

Siaja’s self-actualization isn’t as easy as ditching the zero to get with the hero, even when she’s her own hero from the jump — it takes time to learn the ins and outs of public service, to connect with people, and to make sense of your own emotions. “North of North” respects each process while savoring her struggle through them. (Lambe’s comic timing remains pitch-perfect, and her ability to navigate tonal swings is just as sharp.)

Investing in Siaja’s incremental progress does wonders to keep “North of North” from feeling like forgettable fluff — especially when the back-half of Season 2 gets heavy wrestling with familial, cultural, and communal responsibilities — but none of it work without the attention to detail surrounding Siaja, too. When the first season premiered in January 2025, “North by North” earned plenty of well-deserved praise for its authenticity. The fictional town of Ice Cove represents real communities in Nunavet, the northernmost part of Canada within the Arctic Circle, and the series employed a heavily Indigenous cast and crew to help bring it to life.

And what life there is: Season 2 is rich with cultural specifics, from a Greenlandic mask-dancing celebration to public safety concerns. (Beyond the bad water, don’t forget to place your beer orders early! A birthday without a brewski could be your last!) Every episode whisks you away to a very cold, very kind small town, which is oh-so-welcoming on chilly winter evenings when you just want to bask in the season’s cozy glow.

Respecting and highlighting Inuk customs is step one. Step two expands the idea by grounding “North by North” in perspectives beyond their beloved lead screwup. That way, her work ethic and generosity stay sweet and meaningful (when overexposure could easily turn them sour) and the show’s overall tone avoids becoming rote. Siaja’s mom, Neevee (Maika Harper), is the sardonic balance her daughter demands, and how they flesh out her backstory to explain her sharp disposition offers some of the season’s strongest scenes. Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), Siaja’s boss, is an oblivious white lady desperate to be cherished as a leader, and her pushy ambitions help clarify Siaja’s unselfish aid to others (while generating laughs).

And then there’s the townsfolk, who may not always be as colorful as the woman demanding free water, but who share her fair yet formidable spirit. If Siaja’s community service was met with cheers and applause, it would be unbelievable. That’s not how citizens treat their local officials. But their measured disposition isn’t just authentic, it’s essential. Similarly, if the citizens were the butt of every joke (like in “Parks and Recreation”), Siaja’s dedication could feel misplaced. If they were mean, like too many real-life city council visitors, her above-and-beyond gestures could seem foolish. Instead, Siaja’s community is just there, living their own lives, waiting for her to get her shit together and do what’s right by them.

“North of North” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3507. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3506. How to find Richard the dog in Ocarina of Time

How to identify Richard and complete the quest

Finding Richard is a side quest in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. You might have seen Richard, the adorable dog, during your first visit to Hyrule Castle Town: a white energetic dog that you couldn’t pet because its owner would accuse you of trying to steal her dog. If you visit the town again later, you will learn that Richard has disappeared.

Luckily, you can help the distressed owner to find her precious dog. Below, we explain how to find Richard in the Ocarina of Time remake.

To find Richard, you must visit Hyrule Castle Town during the night and identify it among the running dogs. To know which one is Ricard, you must look for a white dog that will twirl and emit a high-pitched bark when you interact with it. All the other dogs have a deeper bark and briefly stand on their hind legs instead of spinning like Richard does. Since you can only look for Richard at night, consider unlocking the Sun's Song to change the time.

While it is possible to find Richard through trial and error, you don't need to. First look for the white dogs, then interact with them to see how they react. Since there aren't many white dogs, checking each one does not take much time. When I found Richard, he was on the street on the left side of the map, but I can't guarantee that it would always be in the same place for every player.

Once you have interacted with and identified Richard, he will follow you. Head to the street that leads to the entrance of the city to find its owner, then talk to her. After a detailed analysis, she will confirm that that dog is, indeed, Richard, and she will reward you with a Piece of Heart.

If you want to start this quest but Richard hasn't disappeared yet, be sure to deliver Zelda's letter to the guard in Kakariko Village after completing the "Princess of Hyrule Castle" quest. Progressing through the campaign until this point will trigger a change in Hyrule Castle Town and unlock the Richard quest.

#3504. Mike Flanagan's Next Stephen King Adaptation Marks A Career First

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

Mike Flanagan's chain of horror successes has cemented his status as one of the best filmmakers of the past few decades, with his ability to adapt Stephen King's work changing the game for both. Stephen King and Mike Flanagan's collaborations have been some of the greatest recent movies and TV shows in the horror genre, with the success of the Carrie TV adaptation laying the groundwork for much more ambitious projects. One of these is set to be a career first for Flanagan, not only due to its immense scale, but because of its genre change.

Stephen King's works have often been difficult to adapt, but this is where Mike Flanagan has shone, with a talent for screening the "unadaptable." With the filmmaker owning the rights to The Dark Tower, he has made no secret of the fact that he wants to make a TV version of the novel series after the movie adaptation failed disastrously, famously telling Empire Magazine that "we can’t let that [movie] be the final word. We really can’t." Still, the novel series is a complex mix of genres that is almost certain to give the horror filmmaker a creative challenge.

While Carrie is connected to Stephen King's wider mythology, with its confirmed second season set to explore his universe in greater detail, most of Mike Flanagan's best TV shows and movies have been on a relatively small scale. This has led many to wonder if The Dark Tower's epic scale will be too ambitious. Forming the center of the entire Stephen King universe, the story spans seven main novels and a novella, and takes place within a multiverse in which time is not always linear, allowing for some meta twists.

Flanagan appears to be growing in confidence, with his upcoming Warhammer 40,000 series being a drastic departure from shows like The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass, which are self-contained masterpieces but do not touch the level of complexity and lore that The Dark Tower will need. Still, another factor is likely to challenge him more than the novel series' scale, and that is its genre. The Dark Tower crosses Stephen King with Tolkien and a classic Western, with characters like The Gunslinger embarking on epic quests in mysterious lands full of strange creatures.

The Dark Tower lore crosses over into Stephen King's other works, with characters appearing in The Stand, Salem's Lot, and several other books.

Flanagan's shows are generally atmospheric and aesthetic, but they have a much more grounded tone than The Dark Tower, as King's fantasy writing can verge on the absurd. Despite delivering perfect TV shows involving demons and hauntings, The Dark Tower's wizards, talking animals and increasingly bizarre characters are an entirely different theme for Flanagan to tackle. Still, after delivering the news that Stephen King fans were waiting for, explaining that the books will be adapted in order, this removes one main challenge with adapting The Dark Tower, but whether Flanagan can convey its fantasy tone remains to be seen.

Of all the terrible book to movie adaptations, The Dark Tower is one of the most infamous. Despite its beloved source material and the presence of both Idris Elba and Matthew McConaughey, The Dark Tower has just a 16% positive score on Rotten Tomatoes, with both critics and audiences agreeing that it went wrong in virtually every way possible. Rather than starting on a small scale and expanding the story, the movie attempted to fit the entire novel series into just 95 minutes, resulting in a shallow and confusing disaster.

King's book series begins with the words "The man in black fled across the desert, and the gunslinger followed," instantly establishing a classic Western tone, while other genres like fantasy and horror emerge as the story continues. The movie failed to capture this genre blend, instead turning the epic tale into a PG-13 action movie with a revenge plot. However, with Flanagan confirming that he intends to build the story slowly, he will have time to capture its unique tone, and it will not be the first time that he has crossed genres.

Flanagan might be best known for horror, but his projects feature elements of other genres. Carrie captures an authentic high school atmosphere, selling the psychological drama before the iconic prom scene. His King adaptation, The Life of Chuck, leans into whimsy and fantasy, and Doctor Sleep introduces a dark fantasy tone that already proves he can blend genres. These might be minor when compared to the extensive lore of The Dark Tower, but Flanagan is ready for this career first, and with even its author calling him "the King whisperer," he is the perfect director to do the story justice.

#3503. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973.  Related Stories ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies.

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre.

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker.

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters.

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down.

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket.

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy.

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him.

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter.

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3502. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3501. All Great Fairy's Fountain locations in Ocarina of Time

Great Fairy's Fountains are home to, well, Great Fairies in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. The Great Fairies are your gateway to magic and abilities. They'll give you spells that let you create fire, teleport in and out of dungeons, and grant yourself temporary invulnerability.

However, the Great Fairies are hidden away across Hyrule, and they're pretty hard to find. That's not all though, as in the remake, you have to offer the fairies rupees before they'll provide you with any gifts.

Here's where to find every Great Fairy Fountain in the Ocarina of Time remake, as well as what abilities you'll receive and how many rupees you have to offer to each Great Fairy.

There are six Great Fairy's Fountains in Ocarina of Time, and each Great Fairy will provide you with a unique reward if you can provide them with enough rupees.

The Great Fairies can be found in the following locations:

For their exact locations, check out the sections below.

The first Great Fairy's Fountain can be found at the top of Death Mountain Trail, but you'll first need to unlock the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you have the Bomb Bag, take the path that takes you toward Death Mountain Crater, which is the easternmost path on Death Mountain Trail. Blow up the rocks blocking your way up, and make your way to the stone arch at the top. Go to the end of the tunnel, and the volcano will erupt, launching molten rocks onto the path in front of you. Avoid the rocks and run up the hill as fast as you can. Take out the three Skullwalltulas on the wall, and climb to the top.

On your left, you'll find Kaepora Gaebora and a breakable rock wall behind him. Blow up the wall and play Zelda's Lullaby on the Triforce inside. The Great Fairy will speak to you, and tell you that she'll grant you a new power if you put 25 rupees into the fountain.

Pay her 25 rupees, and you'll unlock magic power and Din's Fire. Magic power is a resource used to cast spells, like Din's Fire. Din's Fire costs two magic power, and when you cast it, fire will spread outwards, dealing fire damage to anything nearby.

The second Great Fairy's Fountain is located on the way to Hyrule Castle, but it's only reachable by young Link. Additionally, like the previous Great Fairy's Fountain, you need the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you climb up the vines and go past the first gate, you'll see a rock wall on the right side of the path. Break it with a bomb and you'll find a tunnel that leads to the Great Fairy.

This time, you need to offer her 50 rupees, but she'll give you Gift of Improved Spin. Now, you can hold down the attack button to charge up a spin attack with magic power. The attack itself won't cost any magic power, but it'll deal additional damage.

The third Great Fairy's Fountain is located at the Zora Fountain. To enter, you'll need the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you get King Zora to move, head behind him and you'll enter Zora Fountain. Go to the southeast corner of the map, and blow up the rock wall in the corner. Enter the cave, and you'll find the next Great Fairy.

Offer the Great Fairy 100 rupees, and you'll learn Farore's Wind, a spell that allows you to create a warp point in a dungeon for two magic power.

The fourth Great Fairy's Fountain is found in Death Mountain Crater, but first, you need to complete the Fire Temple and unlock the Megaton Hammer. Lastly, make sure you're in the future, and you have the Goron Tunic equipped.

From the Fire Temple warp point, head across the bridge to the east and cross the gap. Follow the path to the south, and you'll see a black rock embedded in the wall. Break it with the Megaton Hammer, and you'll discover the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Give her 200 rupees, and she'll give you the Gift of Doubled Magic, which will double your magic power bar.

The fifth Great Fairy's Fountain is located in Evil Desert Colossus, which is essentially the entrance to the Spirit Temple. You'll reach this area after traveling through the Mirage Desert.

Break the rock wall on the north side of the zone, and you'll find the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Put 300 rupees into the fountain, and you'll receive Nayru's Love, which will make you temporarily invulnerable for four magic power.

The sixth and final Great Fairy's Fountain is just outside of Ganondorf's Castle, but first, you need the Golden Gauntlets from the Shadow room inside the castle.

Before you cross the bridge into Ganondorf's Castle, you'll find a huge black and gold rock to the east. Pick it up and throw it away to find the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Offer the Great Fairy 500 rupees, and you'll receive the Gift of Halved Damage. This will literally halve the amount of damage you receive from any damage source.

#3500. Dungeons & Dragons’ New Species Is Officially Broken

A new playable species added to Dungeons and Dragons with the release of the World of Warcraft expansion is officially broken, and if you like taking to the skies with aasimar and aarakocra characters, you’re going to love this one. The release of D&D: World of Warcraft has added tons of character options, monsters, and much more from Blizzard’s iconic MMORPG to the TTRPG. Players can now control their favorite characters from Azeroth in a tabletop setting, and this expansion is quite complete, featuring things like classes, professions, and more.

By using the new subclasses in D&D: World of Warcraft, players can even play Death Knights, Demon Hunters, and Evokers at their tables. There are also new subclasses for classic classes, like the Oath of the Holy subclass for Paladins. In addition to all of that, players can choose new or reworked species. You can, for instance, play a Blood Elf, which is a lineage for the Elf in the 2024 Player’s Handbook, or pick an entirely new species, such as the Vulpera. In total, the expansion offers 16 species options, but one of them is delightfully broken.

Following the classes in D&D: World of Warcraft, there are species options, and the very first of them is already a perfect choice. The Dracthyr arrive in Dungeons and Dragons, and despite their visual similarities to the Dragonborn, they are very different, especially when it comes to rules. Dracthyr have Darkvision with a range of 60 feet, which feels standard, but there are many species that don’t have access to Darkvision. Dracthyr can also use their wings and tails as weapons with their Natural Weaponry trait, letting them make an Unarmed Strike to shove a creature as a Bonus Action.

However, Dracthyr have extra traits that make them even more special. Gliding Wings lets them subtract 100 feet from the distance fallen when calculating the fall’s damage, and they can move up to 2 feet horizontally for every 1 foot they descend. Mechanically speaking, you can fall up to 100 feet without ever taking damage, and up to 200 feet reducing the damage you take. It’s not as good as the damage-nullifying Glide trait from the Hadozee species in Dungeons and Dragons. However, Dracthyr also gain a ton of horizontal mobility, letting you reach far-away locations.

The Dracthyr from World of Warcraft, within the TTRPG setting, also have the Visage trait. This ability lets them use a Magic action to shape-shift into a humanoid form, called a visage, or back to their natural Dragon form. On top of how cool it is to technically design two different characters, a visage can come in handy in locations where a Dracthyr would feel out of place, or when trying to escape authorities. Last but not least, Dracthyr have the Draconic Flight trait, unlocked at level 5.

As a Bonus Action, you can leap into the air and gain a Fly Speed equal to your Speed for 10 minutes. This can only be used once per Long Rest. Flight is extremely powerful in the game, and while it isn’t as good as an aarakocra’s game-breaking level 1 flight, it is better than the aasimar’s flight. With it, you can fly around slinging spells or firing arrows in combat, or reach otherwise impossible locations. With the proper build to take advantage of these traits, Dracthyr are the most broken species in Dungeons and Dragons’ World of Warcraft expansion.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Thankfully, it's not unofficially broken.

#3499. ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

Yellow Veil Pictures has boarded North American distribution rights for Callum Devlin‘s “The Weed Eaters,” a New Zealand cannibal horror film that notched a best feature win at SXSW Sydney in 2025. The indie banner is planning a winter release.

The deal for “The Weed Eaters” comes after the independent feature first debuted in the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store, a video-on-demand streaming platform launched by the film-focused social media platform in 2025.

“Yellow Veil are consistently putting out the richest cinematic meals on offer, so it’s a real honour for ‘The Weed Eaters’ to be a part of their roster,” director Devlin wrote in a statement included in the deal’s announcement. “We always knew there was a global audience for this movie. I mean, this film is pretty gross. But the people that are into it are super into it, and we’re more than happy to make movies for the stoner freaks of the world.” Related Stories Inside Letterboxd’s Unlikely Distribution Pipeline: How ‘It Ends’ and Other Gems Found Their Way to a Deal Letterboxd Sale Talks Are Heating Up

“‘The Weed Eaters’ exemplifies what we have come to expect from New Zealand indie films. It’s filled with heart and humor, but this one’s not afraid to get weird and gross along the way,” reads a statement from Yellow Veil.

Exact details on the release plan for “The Weed Eaters” went undisclosed, though Yellow Veil is primarily a digital distribution company with ventures into limited theatrical play.

“The Weed Eaters” follows four friends that have their holiday getaway upended when they stumble upon a strain of marijuana that makes tokers crave the taste of human flesh. The film comes from Sports Team, Horse Bite, and Causeway Films, the Australian banner that was also behind titles like “The Babadook,” “Leviticus,” and “Bring Her Back.”

Prior to “The Weed Eaters,” several other titles featured on the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store have gone on to land wider distribution, with one of the best-known examples being Neon’s acquisition of the cerebral horror film “It Ends.”

“We would never presume whether these filmmakers want to have a traditional distribution,” Letterboxd’s head of Video Store content Courtney Mayhew told IndieWire in August. “Even if it’s just five really strong ambassadors for these independent gems who will sing their praises and push for it and tell their friends about it … that’s something that has value.”

#3498. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.
