From construction moratoriums on data centers to lawsuits, Musk is facing new challenges

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars trying to help Republicans win the 2026 midterm elections. Instead, Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, Texas elected a Democratic governor for the first time in more than three decades, and voters across the country backed new restrictions on AI data centers.

For Musk, those election results might have consequences beyond Washington since the billionaire has invested heavily in the infrastructure needed to power AI. Musk has massive data centers that support his Grok chatbot and agent Grok Bot and has built a significant part of his business empire in Texas. The incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, making her election particularly relevant to Musk's AI infrastructure expansion in Texas.

Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️November 4, 2026

According to campaign finance reporting from The New York Times, Musk contributed approximately $474 million to political groups and candidates during the 2026 election cycle.

The money included roughly $216 million for his America PAC and $168 million for the Senate Leadership Fund, which backed Republican Senate candidates.

Musk appeared to acknowledge the losses early Wednesday morning, joking on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time."

Jokes aside, Hinojosa's win is significant since Musk has relocated major business operations to Texas, and SpaceX has plans to expand its computing infrastructure at its Starbase complex in Boca Chica.

According to Reuters, chip research firm SemiAnalysis has identified more than 9 gigawatts of planned or developing computing capacity associated with Musk's AI ambitions, including projects in Texas.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

But companies planning new facilities may face longer approval processes, closer scrutiny of their electricity consumption and changes to the financial incentives that made Texas attractive in the first place.

Musk's political losses coincided with a broader change in public attitudes toward data centers. According to The Verge's November 4 election analysis, 45 local ballot measures addressed data center development nationwide. By Wednesday morning, results from 33 favored restrictions on construction.

Those restrictions varied considerably. Some communities supported temporary construction moratoriums, while others voted to prohibit facilities above certain electricity-demand thresholds.

In El Dorado, Kansas, voters approved a 10-year ban on data centers with peak electrical demand exceeding 10 megawatts. In Wells, Maine, voters favored a temporary moratorium on large facilities.

The concerns driving these votes have become familiar to residents living near proposed data centers: electricity prices, water consumption, noise, pollution and the question of who should pay for expensive infrastructure upgrades.

An NBC News Election Day poll also found that 76% of respondents opposed having a data center in their community.

The political shift aside, Musk's AI infrastructure was already facing challenges. Near Memphis, Tennessee, his company's Colossus data centers rely on enormous amounts of computing power to train and operate AI models.

The operation has also generated complaints from surrounding communities about the natural gas turbines used to provide electricity.

On October 30, a federal judge rejected a motion to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the NAACP over turbines operating in Southaven, Mississippi.

The lawsuit alleges that the turbines require air permits and expose nearby residents to harmful pollution.

These disputes are separate from Tuesday's election results, but they illustrate the regulatory and community opposition that can complicate even projects already under development.

Musk's companies have already committed substantial resources to computing infrastructure, and demand for AI processing capacity continues to drive expansion across the industry.

But now Texas could introduce new restrictions on development and local communities now have more political support for proposed facilities. For consumers, we might see more protections against higher electricity bills, increased water consumption and pollution near data centers. But, none of those changes will happen overnight.

America's data center boom isn't ending, but the companies building the infrastructure behind AI may have a harder time expanding.

#3493. Classic Halo Trilogy Gets Brand-New Release on Nov. 10

Fans can revisit the origins of Master Chief and the early battles that helped define the Halo universe

It's been a busy year for Halo fans, with plenty of new releases and surprises keeping the franchise alive. Halo: Campaign Evolved, a remake of the original game, is bringing Master Chief's first adventure to a new generation, while a tabletop adaptation is also in development. Even Halo Infinite isn't quite ready to call it quits, continuing to receive unexpected updates this year despite its major content support coming to an end.

Now, fans looking for even more Halo content have another release to look forward to this holiday season. A new book collection bringing together three classic novels from the franchise is on the way, giving longtime fans and newcomers a chance to revisit some of Master Chief's most important adventures.

Titled Halo: The Master Chief Omnibus, the hardcover collection arrives on Nov. 10, from Gallery Books. It brings together three bestselling novels by authors Eric Nylund and William C. Dietz, alongside a new foreword and additional material.

The new omnibus collects three novels that helped establish the Halo universe's expanded lore: The Fall of Reach and First Strike by Eric Nylund, and The Flood by William C. Dietz.

Originally published as stand-alone books, the novels explore different stages of humanity's war against the Covenant, the alien religious empire threatening humanity's survival. They also provide additional context for Master Chief, the Spartan super-soldier better known as John-117, and the events surrounding the original Halo trilogy.

The collection offers a broad look at the early days of the Halo storyline, starting with the origins of the Spartan program and eventually moving into the conflict that puts humanity's survival at stake.

The Fall of Reach explores the creation and training of the Spartan-II program, including John-117's transformation into the Master Chief. It also chronicles the Covenant's devastating attack on the human military stronghold of Reach, an important event in the franchise's history.

The Flood retells the events of the original Halo: Combat Evolved, expanding on the Master Chief's fight against the Covenant on the mysterious Halo ringworld. The story also introduces the terrifying Flood, a parasitic lifeform that poses an even greater threat to the galaxy.

Finally, First Strike bridges the events of Halo: Combat Evolved and Halo 2. Following the destruction of the first Halo ring, Master Chief and other survivors attempt to return to Earth while uncovering more about the Covenant's plans.

Together, the three novels provide a deeper understanding of the characters, conflicts, and major events that shaped the original Halo games. Halo: The Master Chief Omnibus releases in hardcover on Nov. 10.

#3492. ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites. Related Stories ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

#3491. HBO Max's 49-Episode Action Series With Alan Ritchson Is One Of Its Best

Alan Ritchson stars in an HBO Max series with four seasons that is one of the streaming service's most action-packed shows and features fan-favorite characters. Ritchson has cemented himself as one of the biggest actors in Hollywood thanks to his role as Jack Reacher in the Prime Video action thriller series Reacher. The actor has gone from that project to several action releases.

One of those was Netflix's War Machine, which became one of the most-watched Netflix movies of all time earlier this year, showcasing how the actor's connection with the audience is not only related to Prime Video and Reacher. Before Ritchson became as big of a name as he is today, the actor was already starring in high-profile projects and action-oriented shows and movies.

HBO Max's library of TV shows is filled with releases for fans of the action genre. They do not necessarily have to be straightforward action thrillers like Reacher, but shows with plenty of intense fighting scenes, such as House of the Dragon, Peacemaker, and so on. This is where Ritchson comes in, starring in one of the best TV shows on HBO Max in the action department.

Before he played Jack Reacher, Ritchson became a fan-favorite for playing two characters in live-action DC TV shows. The first of those was a Justice League member, as Ritchson gave life to Aquaman in Smallville opposite Tom Welling's Clark Kent/Superman. After that, the Reacher star moved to another DC character, playing Hank Hall, aka Hawk, in Titans, and the show deserves more attention.

Titans was originally released on the DC Universe app before it moved over to HBO Max, where all four seasons of the superhero series are currently available to stream. With Reacher season 5 only expected to be released in 2027, with no firm release date in sight, anyone looking for an action series where Ritchson gets to brutally beat bad guys can find that in spades on Titans. From the start, the live-action DC series set out to shock viewers and separate itself from other DC adaptations, being dark, gritty, TV-MA, and featuring brutal fight sequences. Even Robin was dishing out rage.

Titans is the adult version of the Teen Titans, and for the many viewers who grew up with the animated series starring that team, characters like Dick Grayson/Robin, Starfire, Raven, Beast Boy, and more will feel familiar, though the series does take all of them in bold and surprising new directions. Batman himself is present in the show, with an older Bruce Wayne being played by Game of Thrones' Jorah Mormont actor Iain Glen.

As for Ritchson, he plays the emotionally complex Hawk, a hero who deals with the pain from all the injuries he accumulated throughout his career as a street-level hero with no powers. Titans allows Ritchson to not only put his towering physique to the test, but also flex his acting muscles with many dramatic moments, emotional conversations, and even a few truly hilarious beats. Titans holds a stellar 89% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes for its four seasons and 49 episodes.

While Titans is worth watching for Ritchson, the show's perfectly cast DC heroes and the bond they create, exciting costumes, powerful villains, and more, I have to note that the superhero series could have reached a much higher shelf than it did. Given the sheer talent in front of the screen, with actors like Ritchson, Glen, Titus Welliver (Lex Luthor), Brenton Thwaites (Robin/Nightwing), and many more, as well as how the show focused on the most popular DC team besides the Justice League, Titans could have turned out to be one of the universally beloved live-action superhero adaptations.

However, with plenty of confusing decisions, such as nonsensical character deaths, botched finales, and more led to the show becoming divisive. Despite its high Rotten Tomatoes score, which is boosted by the show's final two seasons, where Titans really hit its stride, the DC series holds a lower 67% audience score. Still, action-wise, Titans is easily one of the best TV shows on HBO Max, and Reacher fans will get to see plenty of Alan Ritchson breaking villains' bones and leaving them a bloody mess as Hawk.

#3490. This Samsung 32-Inch OLED Gaming Monitor Is $300 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3488. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3487. ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in limited theaters Friday, November 6, with a wide release to come in February 2027.]

I don’t believe in an afterlife, but that’s OK because the people I love most are never going to die. Not to me. At least, not in the way they used to before our species began to migrate online, to store our memories in the cloud, and to digitally encode the raw data of our existence onto everything we touch.

My father was born in 1939, the same year that Iowa State College scientists John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built the prototype for the first binary-based computer; in the months after he died 75 years later, I often felt the reflex to reach down and call him from the iPhone that fit inside my pocket. To ask if he’d seen the Rangers game, or to tell him that I’d gotten engaged. I knew that he was gone, of course, but the piece of consumer technology I’d used to connect with him when he was alive had created a separate neural pathway between my brain and his being — a crude one-way network that didn’t begin to break down until much later in my grieving process.  Related Stories I Remember ‘Rocky’: My Front Row Seat to the Marketing of a Million-to-One Blockbuster MUBI Has Cleared the Path for Sandra Hüller to Land Multiple Oscar Nominations This Season

A decade later, those pathways have grown exponentially more complicated and convincing. The emergence of AI has led to a variety of ghoulish attempts at deathlessness and resurrection (from bots that feed on your grandma’s Facebook data to the ChatGPT Theodore Roosevelt who Trump was “honored to be with today” at the former’s Presidential Library), but such products and publicity stunts miss the fact that everyone is already being (temporarily) immortalized on a server farm somewhere, the traces of our existence shed into the digital ether like a Pollock-like splotch of invisible ink.

Charlie Kirk’s face is Twitter’s most ubiquitous meme. My long-deceased college friend you’ve never heard of sends me hacked emails full of links to “old pictures they found of us together.” The cancer-stricken hedgehog I fostered for a few months in 2016 still cycles onto my home screen at random sometimes, and he’s now been buried behind a house in suburban New Jersey for longer than he was ever alive. People have always looked for errant glimmers of the dead in the world around them, but now the past runs parallel to — imprints upon, and circles around — the present to a degree that can severely confuse the relationship between the two.

Sandra Wollner doesn’t believe in an afterlife either, but she’s certainly attuned to the mysteries of this one. Picking up where the equally spectral likes of “Personal Shopper” and “Aftersun” left up, the Austrian writer/director’s mystical and magnificently beguiling “Everytime” takes a rather ambivalent stance towards what happens when people die these days, or at least — per its curious title — towards how we mourn them from inside the flat circle of a temporal overlap where yesterday and tomorrow are folded into the pockets of an ever-expanding now.

There are no clear answers to be found in this astonishing third feature, which shares a number of thematic similarities with Wollner’s “The Trouble with Being Born,” but retains one crucial difference (that film, about a man who has an implied sexual relationship with a child-sized android coded with the memories of his missing 10-year-old daughter, unsurprisingly had trouble securing American distribution). Indeed, the grounded portraiture of the movie’s first 70 minutes eventually gives way to a final act so cosmic and surreal that it becomes all but impossible to pinpoint the precise location of Wollner’s characters in space-time; to say for certain whether “Everytime” has glitched into another dimension, or if it has invited another dimension to glitch into our own. Initially timeless in its nuanced and deeply recognizable depiction of loss, and then even more so as it gets devoured by the meta-modern flourishes that have fringed its story from the start, this is perhaps the most forward-thinking film I’ve ever seen about the changing face of grief.

The premise couldn’t be simpler, though Wollner’s incredible prologue — a careful arrangement of low-event long takes that emphasize how people move through spaces in time — trains our eyes to privilege texture over incident. While there’s little to distinguish single mother Ella (“Everyone Else” star Brigit Minichmayr) and her children from any of the other families strolling through the soft orange haze of a summer afternoon in Berlin, our senses pick up on the uneasy tension between the watchfulness of Gregory Oke’s 35mm camera work and the vivid intensity of the film’s sound design (it’s worth noting that Oke also shot “Aftersun”). The voices are close, but the bodies far away. Teenage Jessie (Carla Hüttermann) turns her head to look at an unseen pop as her family walks home through their local metro station, but we don’t think much of it at the moment. It’s probably nothing. And yet, I suppose it could be anything.

At the very least, that sharp noise is enough to suggest that the film’s environments may not be as benign as they seem, and a silent but soon unbearable tension starts to mount as the day wears on. As Jessie’s boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) comes over to hang out while her kid sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling) annoys the shit out of her by banging on a keyboard; as Ella cooks dinner; as Jessie plays “Minecraft” late into the night on an island bathed in the light of a sinking square sun.

Later, in the waning hours before Jessie’s family is due to leave for a holiday in Tenerife (where she once vacationed as a toddler), Jessie and Lux will sneak out to a dance club, take a few pills, and watch the next day begin from their perch atop the roof of an apartment building. He will note that he’s recently noticed a strange number of seagulls in Berlin, and then fall asleep. She will stand up to film one of them flying past on her iPhone, and then — in one of the most arresting screen images in recent memory, a vertiginous collision of everything and nothing all at once — she will fall off the edge of the building to her death. The city doesn’t notice. The camera scans the treetops. The euphoric synth-pop of David Schweighart’s score kicks in as we suddenly begin to soar through the skies of Jessie’s “Minecraft” world, eventually plunging down through the dirt and into the unrendered levels of code below.

From there, “Everytime” settles into a crushingly quotidian register. Months have passed, and everyone is doing what they can to move on with their lives. Ella takes work calls while visiting her daughter’s grave, while the stoic young Melli texts life updates and other messages to her dead sister’s phone (she’s big on emojis). But things are not as settled as they seem, and Lux’s return from a semester abroad forces Ella and Melli into a more direct confrontation with Jessie’s memory — with the unresolved feelings she left behind. The girls keep running into Lux (and to his nice new girlfriend) around town, and soon begin spending time with him on purpose. They are bound together not only by their shared grief, but also by the unspoken guilt and blame that Lux and Ella can only hope to expiate through each other.

While Jessie is seldom mentioned by name, the bizarre mutual reliance between a middle-aged woman and her dead teenage daughter’s former boyfriend makes her the subject of every scene (much to the annoyance of people who would prefer to compartmentalize the pain of her loss). Jessie is the reason why Ella and Melli attend Lux’s birthday party; Jessie is the reason why Lux joins Ella for a tense lunch at her ex-husband’s house, and why he begins sleeping over at her apartment.

But these domestic frictions are — largely, but not merely — a means to an end so far as Wollner is concerned, as her film leverages them to focus on a series of increasingly abstract phenomena. Jessie is certainly the reason why each of the locations we saw her walk through before her death feels haunted when “Everytime” revisits them, but could she also be the reason why the shadow that falls across her bedroom at night appears to resemble a polygonal cube? Why a seemingly pilotless drone shows up to beckon Ella into a pitch-black parking garage? Why the dead girl’s computer glows with an unnatural brightness whenever the lights turn off?

Wollner’s characters never ask such questions aloud, but she poses them to all three of her leads in a way that compels them to look for signs in the digital detritus that Jessie left behind. Lux is drawn back to the old pictures and voice notes on his phone, while Mille stares at the WhatsApp chat with her sister as if waiting for a response. These signs complement, but never overwhelm, Wollner’s attention to the analog poetry of the natural world — to the shimmer along the surface of a lake, or the sound of the wind rustling through the trees in the woods where Jessie and Lux got high on her last night.

It’s easy to imagine a version of this film that more explicitly addressed how digital technology is transforming how we mourn the dead, but Wollner would rather plumb the mysteries of the present than speculate about the answers of the future; the portals between worlds have already been ripped open, and will only begin to lose their power as they get labeled and branded.

Eventually, Ella makes the spontaneous decision to bring Mille and Lux to Tenerife for the trip they never got to take. That’s where things get weird, and the math of the universe starts to contradict itself. It would be a terrible disservice to reveal anything specific about what happens next (and so I won’t), but the extraordinary magic trick that “Everytime” pulls off in its final stretch is rooted less in incident than in execution.

Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together, and how the look on Minichmayr’s slacken face — her restrained but masterful performance a wonder of tightly bottled pain and lingering disbelief — reconciles those opposite energies with the instinctive naturalness of a mother’s love. It also belongs to the almost unquestioning acceptance that Keiling endows within Melli, the young actor’s posture embodying how this movie teeters on the precipice between a child-like vision of the world (soft and malleable) and the more hardened sense of reality that arrives with adulthood.

Wollner may not trace the character’s arc in the legible terms of a typical coming-of-age story, but Melli experiences a remarkable transformation over the course of the film, her petulant first line (“You always leave your stuff lying around!”) assuming an unforeseeable new context by the time we arrive at her closing narration.

As a medium born from — and once dependent upon smoothing over — the friction between stillness and movement, stasis and change, cinema has always been uniquely adept at conveying the radical effect that technology can exert on how we perceive time and space in the world around us. The switch from celluloid to computer chips saw the movies transform from an illusory art form to a representative one, at the great and continued risk of forfeiting its original power. Engaging in a thrilling and increasingly contested negotiation between 35mm film stock and crude DV video formats, “Everytime” pulls at that tug-of-war from both ends until the uncertain space at the center grows large enough to sail through, and still enough to hang like a painting in the sky.

I am now a father myself, the parent of two young kids whose faces sometimes remind me of my own dad in the same tactile way that people have been survived by their children since before the invention of the wheel. We keep a framed 4×6 photograph of him with a cigar in his mouth on the Blu-ray shelf in our living room, and I sometimes catch my kids talking about it as if the picture itself were their grandfather, rather than just a capture of his likeness. Ask my six-year-old to draw a self-portrait and he’ll sketch you the image of his Roblox avatar. If I ever were to lose him, I wonder how long it would take my nervous system to process that he was gone.

Like many 21st century parents, my wife and I take photos and videos of our kids throughout the day without thinking, and — after wrestling them to bed at night in an exasperating forever war of attrition — we invariably scroll through our phones and take stock of their cuteness in peace. Stills, videos, stickers, and more, these two-dimensional images, I sometimes feel with an uncertain pang of dismay, are our real children. The versions of them we commit to memory. The after images we see in our dreams. They are the kids we mourn as our son and daughter eagerly outgrow their current models every time you look away for too long, and the ones we would cling to in the unthinkable event that either of them disappeared from this mortal coil before we did.

And so, Wollner’s staggering new film suggests with a tender but uneasy twinkle in its eye, we’ve gradually steeped ourselves in a world that guarantees they never will. How strange and unnatural is that? Compared to the alternative, I fear it may not feel that strange or unnatural at all.

“Everytime” is screening at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release it in theaters in the United States.

Geoffrey Hinton gives his latest thoughts on the evolving tech

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Geoffrey Hinton’s name has been making the rounds a lot more often nowadays due to his commentary on the very technology his research helped develop.

During an interview with the Financial Times, he predicted who will benefit financially the most from the continued evolution of AI. “It's going to create massive unemployment and a huge rise in profits,” he pointed out. “It will make a few people much richer and most people poorer. That's not AI's fault, that is the capitalist system.”

And during an appearance on The Diary Of A CEO podcast, Hinton gave his thoughts on the topic of AI being misused and the associated risks that come with it. “There's risks that come from people misusing AI, and that's most of the risks and all of the short-term risks,” he noted. “And then there's risks that come from AI getting super smart and understanding it doesn't need us.”

Now he’s back in the news for (once again) giving a stern warning about AI. Here’s what he had to say during his latest interview.

During a conversation with The Guardian, Hinton made it clear that he doesn’t see himself as an AI doomer and that he genuinely believes that AI has the potential to lead to great things happening in the future. But he balanced out that optimistic outlook with a more sobering one when he stated that “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it.”

Hinton also gave a very blunt answer when the discussion moved over to the major leaders backing the companies that keep releasing even more advanced versions of their signature models. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a s**t,” he said. “They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.” As Hinton’s conversation with The Guardian continued, he presented the idea of a federal agency that keeps a close eye on AI and makes sure the companies that develop it release it in the safest state possible.

“We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released,” he declared. “We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

One of Hinton’s other more recent comments about AI that proved to be alarming for many was said during a CNN segment. Simply put, he warned everyone that the threat of humanity’s destruction via AI is a real possibility if we don’t get it under control. “If we don’t figure out how to make it safe, there’s a real possibility it could destroy us,” he declared. “We’ve never made things that are smarter than ourselves. We don’t know what it’s like to deal with them.” He went on to say that it would simply be “foolish to keep developing these things until we understand how we can live with them.”

Hinton’s sentiments about AI fall in line with most of the American voters who made their voices heard against the technology. According to Data Centers on the Ballot, 37 measures aimed at restricting data center development have won over a single measure that’s attached to allowing the continued expansion of those same centers.

And while the Trump administration’s push for AI and renaming it “Super Intelligence” has made the rounds, Americans are largely pushing back against those initiatives (as evidenced by this site’s current 90.5% rate of people who oppose data centers). Even with Hinton’s negative sentiments about AI while speaking with The Guardian, he remained optimistic about humanity and the ability to intervene to keep it under control.

“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he proclaimed. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”

#3484. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3483. Marvel's New Punisher Replacement Officially Unveiled

There's a lethal vigilante stalking New York's streets in Marvel Comics, killing off gangsters in his family's name... and it's not the Punisher. Marvel just replaced Frank Castle as its de facto lethal vigilante, bringing back a character fans haven't seen in forty years.

This week saw the launch of a new volume of Spider-Woman, setting up an explosive new status quo with Jessica Drew acting as the newest host of Carnage. While the serial killer symbiote is at its weakest, its lust for violence is slowly but surely seeping into Spider-Woman's mind.

The new comic sees Jess working as a professional investigator for the Daily Bugle, investigating crimes and reporting back to star reporter Ben Urich. As the issue opens, Spider-Woman is onto a grisly new lead...

In Spider-Woman #1 - from Dan Watters, Andrea Broccardo, Mattia Iacono and Joe Sabino - Jessica Drew discovers that an old villain, long assumed dead, is actually alive and well. Debuting in 1973, Harlan Krueger is the Hangman - a vicious vigilante who started his career slaughtering the criminals of Los Angeles with a scythe and noose.

Krueger has a twisted sense of morality, executing anyone he considers to be making the world a worse place, from criminals to movie directors whose films he believes are a corrupting influence on young people. The Hangman seemingly died in 1982's Bizarre Adventures #31, but Spider-Woman retcons this as Krueger faking his death and becoming a killer for hire, while still targeting his favorite prey.

After years staying off the radar of everyone from the Avengers to SHIELD, the Hangman has returned. As Spider-Woman investigates, she learns that Krueger's daughter Christine was almost killed in the crossfire of a gang war, inspiring him to return to his no-holds-barred attack on New York's underworld.

The Hangman starts out hanging various underworld enforcers before carrying out a gory massacre in a hospital, targeting the minions of gang leader Tombstone. Alison Sante - Krueger's former partner and Christine's mother - begs Spider-Woman to put a stop to his rampage, believing that once he considers his work done, he'll kidnap Christine and disappear.

While Punisher has a lot of negative qualities, Frank Castle is an expert tactical operator with a firm moral line. In contrast, the Hangman is erratic and incautious, with a disturbing sexist streak that leads him to believe he's 'rescuing' women by kidnapping them from 'dangerous' situations.

However, with a major confrontation between Punisher and the Avengers on the horizon, fans are getting suspicious whether the Hangman's return may be intended to take his place.

Marvel recently teased that the second arc of the newly launched Avengers Volume 10 would be 'The Red Line,' involving some kind of face-off with the Punisher. It's possible that the new street-level Avengers team will take it on themselves to bring Frank Castle to justice. If so, then Spider-Woman could be positioning the Hangman as his replacement.

Even if that's not the case, it's fascinating to see a Marvel hero go up against a villain so similar to the Punisher without the usual sympathy shown towards Frank Castle, especially one whose motive to 'protect his family' is so similar.

The latest volume of Spider-Woman has gotten off to an incredibly strong start, establishing a fascinating new status quo for Jessica Drew and confronting her with a villain who is the Punisher dialed up to 11.

Spider-Woman #1 is available now from Marvel Comics.

#3482. The 10 Most Perfect Movie Plot Twists of the 1980s, Ranked

A New York native, Joe graduated from an avant-garde theater school upstate, where he was obsessed with sketch comedy. There, he and his lunatic friends founded The Sketchies — which still lives on at Skidmore College today. Living in New York City, a screenwriter friend of his then taught him how to write for film. This awakened a new passion in Joe. Since then his scripts have garnered over 200 festival selections, nominations, and wins all over the globe (including the BlueCat Best Feature award). Several of his screenplays have been made into feature films — some of them not that bad! Overall, he loves to create unique, hilarious, touching, and bizarre stories.

Let’s twist again, like we did (in the) last…scene of these 80s movies. Everyone loves a good twist ending, where expectations are completely reversed, and the cinematic rug is pulled out from under the audience’s feet. With mind-bending, twisty films released each year, perhaps no decade encapsulated the perfect twist ending more than the totally radical 80s.

Needless to say, this list is chocked full of spoilers, so if any of these movies initially appear intriguing and the end reveal is not already common knowledge in your particular orbit, it’s perhaps best to discover them all on your own. Alas, here are the best twist endings that the 80s had to offer, in all their tumultuous, gobsmacking glory.

War/military movies aren’t typically known for their huge twist endings; fans of this sub-genre are really just there to watch generals strategizing and soldiers shooting at one another. Spy movies are naturally more prone to contain some mystery; they’ve got “spy” right in the name. Director Roger Donaldson’s hit political thriller No Way Out is actually packed with tons of interesting twists and turns, but ultimately concludes with a really massive one that was truly unexpected.

Tom Farrell (Kevin Costner) is a naval officer who’s having an affair with Susan Atwell (Sean Young), a temptress who is also involved with Tom’s superior, Secretary of Defense David Brice (Gene Hackman). During a jealousy-filled fight, Brice kills Susan, and pins the crime on a seemingly fictitious Russian spy named “Yuri.” The rest of the film, Tom and others in the U.S. military try to uncover the real identity of Yuri. After a thrilling climax, it finally comes out that Tom actually is Yuri, the very Russian operative he’s been allegedly hunting the whole time. This twist is pretty unexpected if only for the fact that Costner doesn't look Russian in the slightest bit.

While Fight Club famously did the whole “He was him” thing in the late 90s, there was another 80s flick that basically did this first — which saw the protagonist trying to pin down an elusive rock-star type who eventually turned out to be himself. This is director/co-writer Alan Parker’s Angel Heart, and, wow, did this reveal take audiences off-guard.

The story takes place in 1955, in New York City. A good-looking private eye, Harry Angel (Mickey Rourke), gets hired by an eccentric (weird) rich guy, Louis Cyphre (Robert De Niro), to locate a missing singer named Johnny Favorite, who owes Louis some cryptic debt. Harry goes on a bizarre journey from Manhattan’s sultry jazz scene to the voodoo swamps of New Orleans, and every time he interviews someone, they end up six feet under. So, the big reveal is that Harry is Johnny; well, Johnny got caught up in some voodoo mumbo jumbo and switched bodies with (the now amnesiac) Harry, a WW2 solider. In any event, Louis is the devil, and with Faustian flare he indirectly urged Harry to commit the murders and so now he’s got his soul on lock. It’s the fun type of twist where the main character and the audience are simultaneously thrown for a loop.

Not every twist has to come in the third act. Writer-director Steve De Jarnatt proves this with his clever subversion of genres in Miracle Mile. The movie starts out as a light-hearted romp, bursting with romcom possibilities. By the end, not only has the entire type of movie switched, the protagonist’s view of what is really happening has his head spinning (right along with the audience’s collective noggin).

The ostensibly fun tale begins with the freewheeling musician Harry Washello (Anthony Edwards) meeting and falling for a diner waitress, Julie Peters (Mare Winningham). Harry tries to catch Julia on her shift, but hears a payphone annoyingly ringing outside the diner. Instead of just letting the darn thing ring, he elects to answer the call. The person on the other line is a solider who is in a nuclear facility. He dialed the wrong number, wouldn’t ya know it, and Harry hears some pretty distressing info indeed: nuclear missiles have been deployed, and the City of Angels is about to be toast in less than an hour. So, the frantic Harry tries to find Julia so they can flee L.A. before they're trapped there and atomized. The audience is intermittently led to believe that this may all be a big prank that the paranoid Harry has fallen for…until the bombs are seen exploding in the distance. It’s an anxiety-inducing film from the minute the phone is picked up, but the ultimate reveal is even more mind-(and metropolis)-blowing.

When one thinks of the films of Steve Guttenberg, they typically conjure a string of innocuous, somewhat heartwarming dramedies, like Three Men and a Baby and Cocoon. And then, there’s the entire Police Academy franchise… So, to stick him in a steamy noir thriller is kind of a twist in its own right.

Directed by Curtis Hanson, The Bedroom Window is about an architect, Terry Lambert (Guttenberg) who is a bit of a naughty fellow. He’s having an affair with his boss's wife, the seductive Sylvia Wentworth (Isabelle Huppert), — who gives femme fatale vibes from the outset. While at Terry’s place, Sylvia witnesses a woman, Denise (Elizabeth McGovern), get assaulted, right through Terry’s window (*paging Alfred Hitchcock). Terry is a gentleman, and tells the cops he’s actually the one who saw the attack, to not drag Sylvia’s good name into this mess (and save his own professional reputation in the process, of course). This backfires, naturally, and Terry is soon suspected of this crime and subsequent ones. Eventually, the real perpetrator is apprehended, Collin Wentworth (Paul Shenar), but during his trial, Terry’s lies are exposed and Collin is acquitted — and then tracks down and murders Sylvia. The irony is quite thick in this one.

Double-twist! Aka, the twist within a twist. That’s how the film that launched a million sequels, Friday the 13th, concluded — with not just one major reveal but another, suddenly supernatural one tacked on as well (that director Sean S. Cunningham apparently OK’d toward the end of filming — inspired by the movie Carrie).

Crystal Lake was once a peaceful body of water, where little campers came to frolic for the summer. Except, one fateful day, one of the camp counselors wasn’t paying enough attention to one small guy, Jason Voorhees. He drowned, and the rest is horror history. 22 years later, a new crop of counselors find themselves being stalked and systematically slashed into the afterlife. The major question is: who is the murderer? That is revealed in the final portion of the film: it’s a woman, Mrs. Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), the mother of the poor drowned boy. Now, once she gets a few more kills in, and there is just one counselor left, Alice (Adrienne King), that’s when the real humdinger happens. As Alice floats on a row boat, blood-splattered and mentally toast, and the police arrive…a seemingly undead kid pops out of the water and grabs her. It’s Jason! This unexpected event turned the straight slasher into a supernatural horror in mere seconds.

A nuclear explosion typically means “game over.” Well, not in this zany zombified sequel. An off-shoot of the George A. Romero Dead franchise, this film, with director Dan O’Bannon at the helm, really ups the ante in terms of scope. The Return of the Living Dead may be a bit campy (talking zombies can have that effect), but it’s got one heck of a finale.

The undead tale begins with two dudes, Frank (James Karen) and Freddy (Thom Mathews), working in a warehouse. They accidentally open a canister of military gas that spreads through the atmosphere. Naturally, this toxic mist causes the local dead to rise, and go on a quest for delicious brains. So, as things descend into pure chaos, and the town looks to be completely overtaken by the gallivanting ghouls, the warehouse boss, Burt (Clu Gulager), phones the military. The head honchos decide to nuke the whole town and be done with this mess…which only ends up spreading the gas over a much wider region of the country… Ergo, atomic zombies galore.

Every once in a while, a person likes to break bad. When you have a thriving psychiatric practice, but an otherwise mild social life, it just may be time to spice things up. That’s the basic premise of famed playwright David Mamet’s cinematic directorial debut, House of Games. Yet, this movie isn’t just about engaging in some promiscuous fun; it’s a lesson in being too cocky and believing you are more clever than everyone around you.

Naturally, earlier decades produced a bunch of cringe-worthy, problematic films — when viewed through a modern lens. Writer-director Robert Hiltzik’s Sleepaway Camp is no exception, but its final reveal was so shocking at the time, it still has to be acknowledged as one of the decade’s most eye-popping, jaw-dropping twists.

The story is about a summer camp where a plucky plethora of murders takes place (shocker). At this sleep away sojourn in the woods, there is one particular girl, Angela (Felissa Rose), who is constantly mocked and bullied by her peers. Anyway, more kids die, and it’s eventually disclosed (in feral, raw fashion) that Angela is the killer. Not much of a bombshell there…except for the astonishing fact that Angela is really a boy named “Peter,” who, when his sister died, was raised by his caregiver aunt, Martha (Desiree Gould), as a wee lass. The way that this is expressed to the audience is with a shot of Angela, where she gives a snarling, lunatic smile…while “she” is stark naked. Yup. Sometimes, you have to let it all hang out.

Sometimes the best twists are revealed right in the film’s title. Director Sidney Lumet’s Deathtrap really spells it all out in the very name of the movie. With some really compelling performances throughout, this twisty flick is actually not what it seems at all, with motivations and allegiances switching right up until the film’s conclusion.

The plot is centered on a successful Broadway playwright, Sidney Bruhl (Michael Caine), who has hit a bit of a career snag. When he ostensibly learns that his former protégé, Clifford Anderson (Christopher Reeve), has written a new work that is sure to be the next big sensation, Sidney appears to become so consumed with envy that he devises a plan to murder Clifford — and claim Clifford's script as his own, thus returning Sidney to his former glory. But…it turns out that Sidney doesn’t really want Clifford dead…he wants him in his bed. In reality, they are lovers, and the whole “murder plot” was designed to give Sidney’s feeble wife, Myra (Dyan Cannon), a life-ending heart attack. Paying a bit of an "homage" to Les Diabolique, only now with a gay spin, this film is shocking in its ingenuity in redefining the kill-one’s-spouse plot.

For good or bad, this pick shouldn’t come as a surprise to basically anyone who calls themselves a fan of film. Co-writer George Lucas and director Irvin Kershner not only supplied one of the best sequels of all time with The Empire Strikes Back, but they also delivered one of the most shocking twists in all cinema, ever, in any decade, in any galaxy.

One doesn’t need to be a Star Wars nerd to know the plot of this movie inside and out, but here’s the gist anyway. The evil Empire discovers the Rebel Alliance, and the key players are compelled to flee. Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) ventures to the planet Dagobah to receive instruction from the wise little creature Yoda (voiced by Frank Oz) in the wily ways of the Jedi. Meanwhile, Han Solo (Harrison Ford), Princess Leia (Carrie Fisher), the fur-ball Chewbacca, and the bot C-3PO hide out in Cloud City in Bespin. Eventually, the Empire tracks them down, and Luke (now all Jedi-ready) has a lightsaber face-off with Darth Vader (David Prowse), the dark leader of the Empire. As the gravitas-imbued James Earl Jones (the voice of Darth Vader) delivers one of the most epic lines ever uttered onscreen, Luke’s head is spun. His greatest foe has been the very person who supplied him with his DNA (well, half anyway). It’s the type of realization that’s kind of hard to come back from (just watch any paternity-themed episode of The Maury Povich Show). Hamill handles this revelation really nicely, with just the right amount of shock and awe — but, at the end of the day, Luke’s a Jedi, and will not bow down to evil authority, no matter who is wielding it, or how many hands he has left. In one of the 80s’ best films, this twist is a true force to be reckoned with.

#3481. Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear

“Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” retells a millennia-old Hindu epic on a splashy scale. The Hindi-language studio film — part one of a planned duology — has been released outside India by Sony Pictures, which hopes to make it a cross-cultural hit by courting audiences who don’t normally spend every weekend watching the latest Bollywood fare. Among the strategies for this rollout have been a lavish Comic-Con panel, as well as an English dub of the movie, which was the version shown to press prior to the review embargo. However, language isn’t the only difference; this version is almost half an hour shorter than the Hindi original and excises some make-or-break material. Related Stories ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

The Hindi version did eventually screen for press (about a day before the film’s release), but by then, early reviews quickly noted the awkward method of its transposition. Dubbing into different languages is hardly new, but AI-assisted lip syncing to match the actors’ mouth movements gives the English performances a stilted quality. Granted, the in-house program developed for this purpose (named “Brahma AI” after the Hindu creator-god, who features in one of the movie’s many prologues) seems a tad more ethical than most generative AI. The process involves real human beings recording the English lines — in some cases, the original actors themselves — as well as real mouth performances (creepy as that sounds) captured to map onto the original faces. Essentially, its data sets seem to be entirely internal, so the stealing aspect of the wider AI problem isn’t a concern here. However, the effect is distracting by way of exaggerated lip movements, and the English dialogue itself is clunky and emotionally restricting.

This becomes all too clear when watching the Hindi version for comparison, which I managed to on opening day at New York’s Mecca for Indian movies: the labyrinthine, 25-screen AMC in Times Square. The original cut doesn’t make the movie magically great — it still has the same haphazard approach to building action, and the same uncanny CGI — but it does call into question the methods by which Sony has attempted to localize (and globalize) the film for wider viewership. Most obviously: performances are more emotionally convincing in their original form, and the reverb on the original dialogue is much more befitting of a large-scale epic, while the mixing for the English lines conjures images of a claustrophobic studio booth. However, the more baffling comparison is between the different cuts, and how each one affects the story.

The English cut runs 166 minutes, which is about half an hour shorter than the original. With that much of a lag, you’d expect the discrepancies to be obvious early on, but surprisingly, the two films are mostly identical for about the first two hours. They cover largely the same ground, between the origins of the demon king Ravana (Yash), the condensed upbringing of the heroic prince Rama (Ranbir Kapoor), and his eventual exile to the forest alongside his graceful wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) and his devoted brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey). The differences are largely in how scenes play out, especially montages backed by songs.

The film has few traditional dance numbers, but in sequences where wider details from the poem are squeezed into the running time, the English version snips them here and there, removing only minor subplots at first. For instance, when Rama and Sita meet and talk for the first time, Rama’s three brothers can also be seen flirting with various women around the palace, as the prince mentions only wanting to marry Sita if his siblings can be married on the same day. This is absent in the English version, as are shots of the additional three weddings during Rama and Sita’s ceremony. It’s not the most vital thing to include from a plot standpoint, though it arguably gestures toward the nature of the story at large, as one in which Rama tries to stick to his promises, as fate contorts itself in his favor.

Still, this and some other deletions aren’t necessarily missed for much of the running time, like a few extra action beats in existing scenes, and additional shots of Rama and Sita living in their kingdom, Ayodhya, and getting to know its people, in another musical montage. However, they give the story a bit of breathing room, which is never a bad thing. In any case, the most destructive removal is far more noticeable. It arrives about two hours into the Hindi running time, by way of a single dramatic scene (or a trio of scenes in quick succession, depending on how you count them) that makes for the film’s emotional centerpiece, and practically resolves major issues with the English version’s latter half.

Both films conclude with the giant, humanoid bird king Jatayu trying to rescue Sita from a flying chariot when she’s kidnapped by Ravana, in a scene that, while visually dazzling, feels a tad random as the climax to its own movie (rather than a midpoint or inciting incident; the epic has been split quite inelegantly). This in turn leads to a mournful speech from Rama about rejecting his destiny and writing his own path as he plans to march on Ravana’s kingdom of Lanka. In the English cut, this feels like a distinction without a difference, since Rama’s training by various priests and sages has, in fact, been in anticipation of a conflict with Ravana. However, many of these dangling threads feel more emotionally whole in the Hindi version, thanks to the aforementioned scenes, known traditionally as the Bharat Milap, or the meeting with Bharat, Rama’s brother, who was placed on the throne in his stead.

In a subplot wholly absent from the English cut, a royal procession reaches Rama’s humble hut, where Bharat — who knew nothing of the palace conspiracy to replace Rama as king — informs him of their father’s death. In the English version, it’s never clear when, if ever, Rama learns about this major development (which even comes up in the film’s concluding scene), leaving viewers to intuit that it probably happened off screen. However, this isn’t even the only problem the Bharat Milap solves.

After Rama scatters his father’s ashes, the two brothers have an emotional conversation with Lakshmana by their side. Bharat tries to convince Rama to return to Ayodhya and take the throne, but Rama believes this ascetic path has been laid out for him as part of his fate and sacred duty, so he decides to remain in the forest. All the while, Lakshmana harbors a grudge against Bharat, and is angered by Rama’s decision to remain in exile, though he goes along with it as part of his own duty and moral code.

For one thing, this makes Lakshmana make a whole lot more sense as a character in subsequent scenes, in which he occasionally flies off the handle. Without these vital exchanges informing his state of mind, his volatility seems arbitrary (though sadly, neither version manages to make his comedic quips really land). For another, these missing scenes give Rama an actual character arc, and imbue the film with a vital throughline of how various characters approach the idea of divine destiny.

When Sita is kidnapped, and Rama comforts the dying Jatayu — who, by the way, features briefly in these missing scenes as well, making his climactic arrival less sudden — there’s a sense of direct causality to these events. Rama isn’t just a witness to his wife’s abduction and Jatayu’s slaying, but he feels the guilt of having made the decision to remain alone and vulnerable in the first place. When he talks of rejecting destiny and writing his own story, these cease to be the mere platitudes of the English version. They become a direct callback to his own decision-making, in which he chose to follow the lifelong path laid out before him, out of a sense of divine obligation.

This, in turn, affects another scene (albeit a smaller one) in which Ravana and his siblings bicker over whether to kidnap Sita in the first place. The notion of destiny comes up once more, in the idea that Ravana going down this violent path is something the gods might actually want to entrap him in a battle with Rama. Since the movie is a mere first half, its primary hero and villain never interact, and they don’t even feel thematically bound in the English version. In the original cut, these notions of destiny, as laid out by Rama’s chat with Bharat, set the protagonist and antagonist on an unavoidable collision course.

The decision to cut the running time makes roundabout sense, given that one of the few things most Western viewers know about Hindi movies is their historically enormous lengths. However, when Hollywood films like the “Avatar” sequels and “Avengers: Endgame” (and even Indian hits like the Telugu-language “RRR”) draw crowds with three-plus-hour running times, this phantom barrier clearly isn’t insurmountable. Shaving things down to a still-robust 2 hours and 46 minutes isn’t likely to be the deciding factor for many viewers; people tend to round up or down at that length.

While this feels akin to a Harvey Weinstein-esque interference, this particular decision was, according to Sony, made with the input of the team behind “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” But whatever the impetus for these competing cuts — both of which are now in theaters — the decision to cleave out such a vital emotional and thematic crux, the meeting between the brothers, is utterly confounding. It’s the story’s heart and soul, and erasing it is downright destructive to how the movie plays. So, if you’re deciding between the two versions, the choice should be pretty clear.
