#3480. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3479. Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained: Who Becomes King Of The Monsters & How It Sets Up A Sequel

The following contains spoilers for Godzilla Minus ZeroGodzilla Minus Zero builds off the history of the franchise and sets up a thematically rich direction for any prospective sequels. Building off the events of Godzilla Minus One, the period-piece setting allows the filmmakers to directly reflect the societal fallout from the end of World War II through a battle between Godzilla and the alien entity dubbed Ghidorah.

The Kaiju battle is the bulk of the film's latter half, with the humans doing their best to tip the battle in Godzilla's favor and even giving the monstrous creature an edge it takes advantage of to assert itself as King of the Monsters. However, that doesn't mean the danger posed by Godzilla has been resolved.

Paying off the sequel's thematic arc of exploring the cycle of violence that causes warfare and bloodshed, Godzilla Minus Zero's climax leaves the door open for a larger plot that follows governments and militaries as they try to turn creatures like Godzilla into weapons. It's a compelling ending that never loses sight of what makes the film so thematically rich.

Godzilla Minus Zero closes out with the titular Kaiju as the undisputed king of the monsters, but with a very different type of target on his back, courtesy of the United States military. Initially, the battle between Godzilla and Ghidorah is meant to weaken the victor enough so that the American and Japanese forces could sweep in and take them down once and for all.

However, the American soldiers back off, implicitly revealing that the military wants to weaponize Murakami's Resonance Wave generator. This is a pointed thematic direction for the film, given Murakami's underlying subplot about wanting to do the same thing but as a means of getting revenge on the United States for the nuclear bombs that hit Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The film ends with Godzilla making its way back to the ocean, firmly establishing itself as an engine of destruction on a global scale. The idea that governments and militaries would immediately try to weaponize them presents this world with a new version of the Cold War that could heat up very quickly. It's a grim evolution of the destructive potential that wartime America exhibited when it bombed Japan.

While Murakami destroys his invention and Noriko flees before she can be taken into custody, this lays the groundwork for future efforts to use Godzilla (or other creatures like him) as the bedrock for a new generation of weapons of mass destruction. It's a clever way to evolve the setting and set up other creatures to be brought into this continuity, and it pays off the movie's themes about the cycle of violence

Shikishima speaks for the film's themes throughout the movie, but never more pointedly when he refuses to let Noriko be made into a weapon. Still reeling from a survivor's guilt that only grows across the course of the film, Shikishima underscores the movie's perspective on how the creation of new weapons, even in pursuit of good intentions, can only lead to more death.

Noriko's status as the only survivor of the G-Cell infection from Godzilla Minus One means she's the one person capable of using the Resonance Wave generator to connect with (and effectively summon) Godzilla. Although Noda promises to let her be used as a tool for destruction, both Murakami and the US government think differently.

While Murakami changes his mind and even helps them escape, the US military will likely keep looking for the pair so that they can use Noriko as a means of causing massive destruction with Godzilla. This is why they go on the run, initially even planning to leave Akiko at the orphanage out of fear for her life with them on the move.

Instead, Akiko's dogged refusal to let them leave leads to them all heading off into an uncertain future as a family. It's the big payoff of the film's emotional center, highlighting the bonds that endure in the face of death and destruction. It's also a good way to set up a more active adventure next time around, as a prospective sequel could follow the family on the move.

One of the biggest thematic throughlines of the film is the shadow of the atomic bomb. Murakami's family was killed in Hiroshima, leaving him reeling from a grief and fury that almost leads him to stage a calamitous rebuttal with Godzilla. It's the pursuit of an absolute power at the moral cost of countless lives that were and could have been.

It all makes Godzilla and the efforts to weaponize him an apt metaphor for the efforts to build upon the destructive power of the atomic bomb. Whether driven by national ambition or spiteful rage, the desire to have the biggest weapon just raises the risk that more innocent people will be caught in the crosshairs. There's a reason the film underscores the value of every person and is horrified at every death.

It's a key element of the DNA of the franchise, going all the way back to 1954's Godzilla. Famously, Godzilla was designed as a thematic reflection of the destructive power and mortal cost of the nuclear bomb. This makes its direct parallelism to Hiroshima, particularly as a movie openly reeling from America's actions, feel like the movie's most powerful political point.

As Nado pleads with Murakami before the final mission, it's on them to end the cycle of violence. While he could get revenge by bringing Godzilla to New York City, he would only be killing countless more and prompting more revenge. There's no way to escape the grief they suffer from but it's still on them to recognize the pattern and break it.

Godzilla Minus Zero builds on the survivor's guilt that pervaded the first film and takes it even further by highlighting the responsibility that the survivors take on in the world left behind. Much of the movie is focused on people reeling from trauma, either their experiences during the war or in the aftermath of Godzilla's last attack.

The heroes of the film are people like Shikishima, Noriko, and Nado, who recognize the price these kinds of events incur and refuse to let it be used again. They are traumatized, but focused on helping others and keeping that same pain from befalling others. That trauma can also spur on grimmer thoughts, like with Murakami, but it's possible to move beyond them. In fact, humanity must do so if it wants to thrive.

Godzilla Minus Zero doesn't hold back with its criticism of militarization in the nuclear age, the constant escalating and evolving danger represented by the ever-adaptable Godzilla and Ghidorah. The ending of Godzilla Minus Zero, with the survivors in Japan refusing to let the rest of the world suffer the same things they experienced, takes on a greater meaning as a result.

#3478. Why ASMR Invaded the Soundscape of ‘La Bola Negra’

There are a lot of things that can be done in a month, theoretically — but it takes a special kind of close-knit team to take the sound design of a film from picture lock to a premiere at Cannes in a month. Supervising sound designers Alejandro López and Anna Harrington had exactly that challenge with “La Bola Negra,” not only directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s most ambitious film to date, but one of the most epic films to come out of Spain in recent memory.

The pair, who’ve worked on Los Javis projects going back to “Veneno,” had a very condensed span to design multiple timelines and storylines that the directors wanted to each have a slightly different sonic feeling. Related Stories Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade

For the story of Carlos (Milo Quifes), set in 1932 in Grenada, López and Harrington had license to be a little bit more expressive in the sound design to heighten the emotions of the closeted young man accused of being a homosexual during his attempt to join his father’s members-only casino. This tracks with the fact it is, eventually, revealed to be the lost Federico García Lorca play, “La Bola Negra.”

For the 1937 story of Sebastian (Guitarricadelafuente), however, sound was an important, invisible storytelling partner, guiding its protagonist down the path towards rescuing that lost play by falling in love with Lorca’s (Alberto Cortés) former lover Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau) before he’s shot by fascists in the aftermath of the Battle of Santander during the Spanish Civil War. “The importance there was on the off-screen sound to help tell the story,” López told IndieWire. “To have an oppressive atmosphere beyond the frame.”

The gunshots, shouts, vehicles, movement, and marching that López and Harrington craft offscreen all create a kind of strident tide that threatens to wash Sebastian, Rafael, and/or both of them away at key moments in their story. Harrington did a lot of work with the cast of the 1937 section to precisely sculpt ADR, as much to concoct a sense of tragic, and especially Lorquian, chaos as to maintain key pieces of dialogue.

The contemporary 2017 storyline of Sebastian’s grandson Alberto (Carlos González) rediscovering the play his grandfather saved, meanwhile, was meant to be as irritatingly digital and constantly jittering as Alberto’s anxiety is. “Alberto is always surrounded by noise,” Harrington told IndieWire. “Like, he cannot think straight because he’s surrounded by so much noise all of the time.”

But while each storyline has its own specific texture, the sound design team also crafted moments of breathtaking contrasts. There’s invisible but undeniable power when all that noise falls away, where the harsh and heightened soundscapes resolve into softer and more beautiful sonic worlds.

Key among these is a sequence when Sebastian rushes back to the hospital where he’s based and where Rafael is held prisoner, believing that his unrequited (or so he thinks) love may have already been executed while he’d been given a night off. He rushes into the pale dawn light, relieved to find Rafael beaten, but still alive and asleep in a hospital bed. There’s a hush to the moment that brings relief, but not because it’s wholly silent — it’s because of the way that López and Harrington sculpt the sound.

“That moment has really close sound when Sebastian sort of traces [Rafael’s body] and almost touches him. The idea of the shot was for it to be like ASMR. No music at all. Really close, human sounds — the breathing of them both — [were designed] to make that moment immersive. And then I used a low rumble underneath that creates a really strange sensation. It’s like some kind of telluric sound that comes from the Earth. It’s Lorquian.”

“In Lorca’s universe, there are a lot of references to sound,” López added. “We used a lot of resonances with the wind, the ocean, the sound of the waves in the hospital resonating, the winds from the Sierra Nevada, when the old woman appears in the snow. It’s a leitmotif.”

Sonic leitmotifs, sounds that contain emotional and musical resonances, are important to how “La Bola Negra” moves between timelines, but they’re also how the sound design team added texture to the footage of each of the different timelines. The digital 4K world of Alberto tempted the designers to add sound to absolutely everything in the frame, and make it all as sharp and precise as the image. The 35mm footage, by contrast, could be a little more expressive, the textures a little unbounded by what we see. “It’s like the picture is asking for a certain kind of sound,” Harrington said.

It speaks to the strength of the story of “La Bola Negra,” then, that the sound has its own trajectory alongside the image and the characters. And all in about a month.

“Everybody worked like 200% helping each other. [Composer] Raül Refree was calling us. We were calling [Editor] Alberto Gutiérrez, like, ‘Are you cutting this?’ There was a lot of exchanging ideas and helping each other because we had no time at all,” Harrington said. “Everybody wants to do their best, because we knew from the start we were doing something that touches people.”

“La Bola Negra” is now playing in theaters.

#3477. We Officially Ranked Every Alien Movie

The Alien franchise is one of the most totemic in sci-fi and horror cinema. A lot of that legacy comes from the first two installments, which are universally considered great and have inspired a lot of spirited debate over which is superior. Beyond those films, the additional seven that feature xenomorphs have experienced varying degrees of appreciation over the years. Outside the variations in tone, that appreciation usually comes down to the difference between intent and execution.

There have been Alien movies that attempt ambitious expansions of the franchise by going well off course and there have been technically well-made movies that stay safely on the established rails. Individual appreciation of those films can really come down to the singular preferences of each fan. All that debate and personal differences can be put to bed now that we’ve officially ranked every Alien movie.

A movie that even the most die hard fans of either franchise would have trouble defending, Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem fails in almost every respect. It’s a bad Alien movie, it’s a bad Predator movie, and it’s bad at being a movie. The film’s notoriously poor lighting and editing make many scenes near incomprehensible, not that being able to see or understand what’s going on would make the movie much better.

Picking up directly after Alien vs. Predator, the movie at least makes good on its predecessor's promise of the Predalien hybrid monster, which crash lands back on Earth and begins wreaking havoc on a small town in Colorado. Space truckers, scientists, and Colonial Marines are replaced here with stock characters more suited to a slasher, which is really what this movie is, just dressed up in the hollowed out corpses of both beloved franchises. The only element worth applauding in the movie is the effects work, which should come as no surprise as directors Greg and Colin Strause have a background in visual effects. Even then, the creature effects, by Amalgamated Dynamics, are hidden in almost complete darkness. The abject failure of this film is what led both franchises to split back apart to try and find their own identities again.

Alien: Resurrection is not a good movie, by any measure, but it is a weird movie, and that counts for something. It was ill-advised to bring the character of Ripley back after her demise in Alien 3, even if she is a completely different clone character here. Sigourney Weaver, at the very least, gets to explore some strange territory with this iteration, and director Jean-Pierre Jeunet is more than happy to make things bizarre and sexual. The visuals are striking, the practical effects, again by Amalgamated Dynamics, are impressive and Alien: Resurrection is straight up one of the oddest blockbusters ever made.

In the film, Ripley has somehow been cloned in the even more distant future, along with a xenomorph embryo inside her. After some mad space scientists do their thing, the aliens escape and all hell breaks loose. Ripley has to team up with a motley crew of space pirates who were a clear progenitor for writer Joss Whedon’s later work on Firefly. The Whedon banter is discordant with Jeunet’s directorial style and the performances, which adds to the overall strange tone of this grotesque movie. Alien: Resurrection was the final nail in the space coffin for the franchise’s original continuity, but it’s got a weird charm for those in the right mood for it.

There is nothing artistic or narratively interesting about Alien vs. Predator. It’s a movie made purely for financial reasons and fan service. It doesn’t attempt to elevate the genre in any way and is more than happy to just be a B movie. There’s nothing wrong with that and there are a few moments in the movie that are enjoyable on a brainless blockbuster level. Unfortunately, those moments are spread thin across an overwritten story with underwritten characters and a PG-13 rating that doesn’t provide enough of the carnage that fans would expect from the first meeting of these two sci-fi monster titans.

Paul W.S. Anderson makes sense on paper for a film like this. He’s a steady hand at making slick genre movies that turn a tidy profit, but AVP shares more in common with his braindead Resident Evil movies than his more visceral Event Horizon. It follows a group of interchangeable experts and mercenaries who venture into an underground pyramid in Antarctica that was used by the Predators for ceremonial hunts using alien prey. The plot threads itself into knots and leaves holes big enough to fit an oblong xenomorph head through, but it occasionally can get exciting when the movie stops to let its monsters mash each other into pulp. As fan service cash grabs go, AVP could be a lot worse, but it could have been so much better too.

Ridley Scott is the only director to have made more than one film in the Alien franchise. It’s fitting, since he started everything with the original classic, but each subsequent film has been a diminished return. The nadir is Alien: Covenant, a tonally confused mess caught between being the movie Scott wanted to make and the movie he thought Alien fans wanted. It tries to serve too many masters and ends up satisfying none. All that said, it is still an Alien movie directed by Ridley Scott, so it has some incredible visuals and violence, and Michael Fassbender giving a dual performance worthy of a much better movie.

After the lukewarm response to Prometheus, this sequel was reconfigured to lean more heavily into the horror elements of the earlier Alien films while still attempting to keep the philosophical themes of its predecessor. The biggest casualty of that change was Noomi Rapace’s character Elizabeth Shaw, who is killed off-screen, while Fassbender’s android David is upgraded to an evil villain. Fassbender also plays the more user-friendly Walter, who’s part of the wholly new cast of colonists who land on the alien planet that was once home to the Engineers and proceed to make a series of increasingly stupid decisions. Every moment of Covenant that does something new or interesting is immediately followed by something inane. The entire third act is a hollow retread of the first film and a painful reminder of how far Scott and the franchise have drifted astray.

Speaking of retreads, Alien: Romulus was designed to be a back-to-basics reinvigoration of the franchise, though it does still have connective tissue to Scott’s divisive prequels. Fede Álvarez was brought in to inject fresh acid blood, and while the director does craft some suitably suspenseful sequences, the film as a whole plays like the greatest hits of the franchise rather than its own unique experience. It’s also awkwardly inserted into the continuity between Alien and Aliens, and far too often relies on fan service instead of trying to create its own iconic moments. It’s still a solid reminder of why the Alien franchise is so beloved, but it doesn’t do anything to truly justify its existence.

The human, and android, characters here are a group of colonists trying to get out from under the corporate thumb of Weyland-Yutani, the villainous conglomerate that has featured heavily in every film. They escape their mining planet and connect with a seemingly abandoned space station that turns out to have been a research vessel studying the original film’s xenomorph that was found floating in space and then revived. From there, Alien: Romulus becomes a remix of fan favorite moments throughout the franchise, some executed better than others. The worst offender is the character of Rook, an android identical to Ash from the first film created using CGI to resurrect deceased actor Ian Holm. He’s a soulless recreation that’s technically impressive, much like a lot of the film itself.

Here’s where the true dividing line of intent versus execution comes down for the Alien franchise. For all its faults, Alien: Romulus is an undeniable accomplishment in recreating the mood and atmosphere of the early Alien movies. Prometheus, on the other hand, tries to distinguish itself from the franchise as its own sci-fi story exploring the background of the Engineers instead of rinsing and repeating. It’s an admirable idea, and one that was compelling enough to bring back Ridley Scott, but its execution is far from flawless. It’s hard to rank based on intent, but the ambition of Prometheus ultimately makes it more interesting, even if it does come crashing down by the end.

The fundamental flaw in Prometheus is that it seeks to explain things that were more interesting when they were left unexplained. The Engineer that appeared in Alien, known then as the Space Jockey, suggested an entire backstory to the origin of the xenomorph that was far more fascinating than what Prometheus ultimately offers. Following a scientific expedition to a far off planet that explains the origins of humanity and their creators, the movie is dealing with heavy themes of existential and cosmic horror, but every further plot development lessens the impact. The characters also make irrational decisions for no reason other than to serve the plot, and the tenuous prequel connections to Alien are more confusing than anything else. Much like co-writer Damon Lindelof’s Lost, Prometheus had so much promise but failed to deliver.

Much like Prometheus, what makes Alien 3 so interesting isn’t so much the movie that was made, but the movie that could have been made. The tortured production history of the third film in the franchise is too long to recount here, but the fact that David Fincher, in his directorial debut, was able to deliver a semi-coherent movie is nothing short of a cinematic miracle. Fincher has long since disowned the movie due to his disagreements with 20th Century Fox, but it has gained a strong cult following since its original release, partially thanks to the so-called Assembly Cut that attempted to edit the film closer to Fincher’s original vision.

Both versions of the movie are still disjointed and suffer from serious pacing issues and inconsistent characters. They also both begin with the beloved characters of Newt and Hicks from Aliens being killed off, a decision many franchise fans still take major issue with. Setting that all aside, the film, which finds Ripley contending with another xenomorph, this one born from an animal on a prison planet, is a nihilistic and nasty sci-fi horror movie that’s atmospheric as hell. Through all its flaws, Alien 3 still has moments that are individually effective, and that sometimes showcase Fincher’s directorial skills that would become more pronounced in his later films where he had more creative control. Alien 3 is far from perfect, but its imperfections are better than some of the best moments of the later films in the franchise.

Trying to rank Alien and Aliens is an impossible task. Both films are vastly different from one another yet remain thematically connected, but it’s their differences that make them individually great. What James Cameron accomplished with Aliens is a masterclass in sequel making. It expands on the core plot elements established in the first film without betraying them while also shifting the genre elements closer to what Cameron excels at as a filmmaker. Aliens is bigger, if not necessarily better, than Alien, but that increased size is tied directly to the plot of the film and isn’t an act of arbitrary inflation. Aliens is a different starbeast than Alien, and how it ranks against it is more dependent on personal preference than it is on the individual achievement of either film.

Sigourney Weaver famously received an Academy Award nomination for her performance in Aliens, and it’s really in this sequel where the character became a genre icon. Where she was a practical and intelligent protagonist in the first film, she was very much a part of the larger ensemble and defined mostly by Weaver’s performance than character traits. In Aliens, the character is given more dimension through both the trauma she sustained in the first film, and a greater motivation as maternal protector over Carrie Henn’s Newt, the sole survivor of the colony built on the alien planet LV-426 where Riley returns with a group of colorful and overconfident Colonial Marines. Using post-Vietnam disillusionment as a basis, Cameron establishes a militarized plot to drop Ripley into, and crafts a massively entertaining action-sci-fi-horror hybrid blockbuster around her.

The original Alien is still the best. The franchise may have evolved and expanded far beyond its humble beginnings, but there’s a purity in the first film that should be admired. From Dan O’Bannon and Ronald Shusett's original script that pulled influence from classic sci-fi pulps and B movies and synthesized them into a lean horror movie. From the influence of producers David Giler and Walter Hill, who introduced a working class versus corporate interests conflict to the plot. From the iconic production and creature designs of artists like Ron Cobb and H.R. Giger. From the ensemble cast that eschewed typical horror archetypes. From Ridley Scott’s focused direction and a million other elements that went into the film’s production, a sci-fi horror masterpiece burst forth and it hasn’t been improved upon since.

What began as Starbeast, a simple sci-fi concept destined to be a cheap Roger Corman production about astronauts who discover an alien lifeform on a strange planet and unwittingly bring one on board their ship, became one of the most influential sci-fi films of all time. It launched huge careers, was endlessly imitated and ripped off, including by Corman, and became permanently implanted in pop culture. Thousands of things had to go right, and wrong, for Alien to become the film it is. Thank the stars it did, because it’s hard to imagine what sci-fi, or horror, would like without, and how different both genres might be without the continued work of so many of those involved. It started the franchise that we all love and continue to debate to this day, and it’s still the best part of it, officially.

Despite its size, the Miniroll can get surprisingly loud—which PCMag confirms in its review—and at moderate volume, it has enough sound for a kitchen or backyard without sounding thin. #3474. These Feature-Packed JBL Headphones Are $110 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, you’re getting a feature-rich pair of wireless headphones with active noise cancellation, high-resolution audio support, and battery life that can last through several days of commuting or work sessions. They’re designed for people who like to wear headphones for hours at a time, too, with adjustable metal sliders and earcups that pivot to fit comfortably around your head. The earcups also fold flat to make them easier to pack, although the included soft pouch offers less protection in a bag than a hard case would.

Sound-wise, its 40mm drivers deliver a wide frequency response of 10Hz to 40kHz, while Bluetooth 6.0 support, LDAC, and LE Audio give you options for high-quality wireless listening with compatible devices. The catch is that the default tuning pushes the bass a little too hard (according to this PCMag review), so you may want to spend some time adjusting the sound through JBL’s app—which includes a 10-band equalizer, preset profiles, personalized sound settings, and virtual spatial audio, letting you tailor the listening experience to your preferences.

You also get Bluetooth multipoint for connecting two devices at once, plus a proximity sensor that pauses playback when you remove the headphones. Physical controls handle power, pairing, and volume, while a touch-sensitive surface lets you manage playback and call up your phone’s voice assistant. As for its battery life, JBL claims up to 80 hours of playback with active noise cancellation turned off, or up to 50 hours with ANC enabled. That should be plenty for long-haul flights, extended workdays, or several commutes between charges, although the noise cancellation itself isn’t quite as effective as what you’ll find on some higher-end competitors. The headphones also lack water and sweat resistance, so they’re not the best choice for workouts or rainy commutes.

#3473. Apple TV’s Best New Sci-Fi Show Is Officially Not Returning In 2027

Few other streamers even come close to Apple TV’s science fiction catalog, so it’s quite the feat when a new sci-fi show on the platform marks itself out as a work of unique brilliance. That’s exactly what happened last November, when a mind-bending masterpiece like nothing we’d seen before arrived on our screens for the first time.

This series is surely the best new arrival on Apple TV in any genre since Severance’s first season in 2022. From the moment it dropped, it’s been hailed as one of the outstanding sci-fi shows of the 2020s. The show has already developed a devoted fanbase, who’ve been waiting with bated breath for updates about its second season.

Given that it debuted in 2025, viewers are naturally expecting Vince Gilligan’s Pluribus to return in 2027, following the two-year production cycle that’s been typical of prestige TV dramas across the past decade, particularly when following up their first season. Yet, the latest news from producers has effectively confirmed that this dystopian psychological thriller won’t be back next year.

When it premiered on Apple TV last November, Pluribus immediately broke an Apple TV record Severance had held for the previous three years, by achieving a perfect 100% Rotten Tomatoes score for its first two episodes. A new sci-fi rivalry was born in an instant. Now, the team behind Severance can celebrate their third season having a clear run at 2027.

Pluribus season 2 is currently being filmed, which gives fans even more time to unpick its first season, and come up with their own speculative theories about what’s going to happen next. The show’s premise is ostensibly simple, yet opens a Pandora's box of mysterious implications as terrifying as they are complex.

Longtime Vince Gilligan collaborator Rhea Seehorn plays protagonist Carol Sturka, who is seemingly immune to an alien virus that merges the consciousness of almost everyone on Earth into a single hive mind. Carol must uncover the truth about the virus, partly by connecting with the handful of other humans who’ve also seemingly avoided its effects.

Pluribus has finally revealed what the “Others” have been drinking from milk cartons, and the truth is more shocking than one could have imagined.

At the same time, she’s in a race against time, as the hive mind itself is looking for ways to ensnare her and the rest of the outsiders, absorbing them into its singular consciousness. This bizarre and deeply unsettling metaphor for herd mentality clearly draws on classic sci-fi shows like The Twilight Zone, The Prisoner, and The X-Files.

It’s little wonder, then, that it’s gone down a treat with fans of the genre and more casual viewers alike, with audiences spanning generations and cultures. Pluribus is one of the TV sci-fi events of the century so far, which is why we’re waiting with bated breath for confirmation about the release window of its second season.

A fresh update on the release timeline of Pluribus season 2 has essentially confirmed the fears of those who were worried about the lack of news before now. Sci-Fi Spiral writer Ava Harper officially revealed on X that shooting for the season began on November 1. What’s more, filming is due to wrap on June 14, 2027.

We should then expect at least a year of post-production work on the new episodes, in line with the post-production schedule for Pluribus season 1. Taking this work into account, the most optimistic estimates predict a summer 2028 release for season 2. That feels like a long time away, especially in light of Rhea Seehorn’s tantalizing tease about episode 1 of this new Pluribus season.

It should be worth the wait, of course, but Apple TV and Vince Gilligan are certainly testing the patience of their audience with this schedule. Pluribus season 3 will be out two years in the next decade at this rate, and could well be one of the sci-fi events of the 2030s.

Vince Gilligan's sci-fi series Pluribus stars Rhea Seahorn as Carol Sturka, one of the few remaining people on earth uninfected by a peculiar virus which has unified the rest of humanity into a collective hive mind.

#3472. ‘Silo’ and ‘Breaking Bad’ Stars Join Apple TV’s New Godzilla Series

With a purposeful grimace and a terrible sound, another MonsterVerse series is rising from the depths. The series, a spin-off of Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, will star the father-son duo of Kurt Russell and Wyatt Russell, and has recruited a bevy of intriguing guest stars. Now, it's recruited two titans of the silver and small screens: they're not exactly King Kong and Godzilla, but they're bound to make an impact when they drop into the new show.

The series, which is still untitled, will center around Lee Shaw, a founding member of the monster-tracking organization Monarch. As in Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, he'll be played by Wyatt Russell in the past and Kurt Russell in the present day. The series will center around Shaw being sent behind enemy lines in 1984 as the Cold War is threatening to heat up; he's on the trail of a Soviet plan to unleash a monstrous kaiju that could change the course of history. Joining the Russells in the series are Corey Stoll (Ant-Man), Ralph Ineson (The Witch), Millie Brady (Surface), Pilou Asbaek (Foundation), Nyasha Hatendi (Seven Dials), Connie Nielsen (Gladiator), and Stana Katic (Castle).

Now, the Legendary Entertainment series is adding two notable actors as guest stars: The Shawshank Redemption's Tim Robbins and Breaking Bad's Giancarlo Esposito. Robbins is no stranger to Apple TV, the MonsterVerse's streaming home, as he currently stars in their mind-bending science-fiction hit Silo; Esposito, meanwhile, can currently be seen in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York and Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother and heard in The Cat in the Hat. Character details for both characters are being kept hidden in the Hollow Earth for now. The series, which is showrun by Joby Harold (Obi-Wan Kenobi), does not yet have a release date.

The two biggest stars of the MonsterVerse are set to collide once more on March 26, 2027 in Godzilla x Kong: Supernova, which will pit them against a threat from outer space. Meanwhile, Monarch: Legacy of Monsters has not yet been renewed for a third season, but earlier this week we learned that it's in development, with the search now on for a new creative team for the series.

The Lee Shaw MonsterVerse series is in development; no release date has yet been announced. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3471. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

The Christmas countdown is officially underway, and if you’re anything like me, a few festive movies and shows are essential for getting into the holiday spirit. Thankfully, Netflix is making it easier to get started, with the streaming service adding a fresh batch of Christmas movies throughout November. Whether you’re ready for cozy festive romances, family-friendly adventures or something a little different to break up the usual holiday viewing, there’s plenty to watch.

With new originals joining some overlooked Christmas gems, this month’s lineup has a little something for different tastes. It’s also a good excuse to revisit your festive watchlist and discover a few new favorites before December rolls around. I’ve picked out five Christmas movies and shows I’d recommend checking out first, so you can get your holiday viewing off to a good start.

“The Best Christmas Pageant Ever” is a charming comedy-drama based on Barbara Robinson’s much-loved 1972 children’s novel. Directed by Dallas Jenkins, best known for creating the hit series “The Chosen,” the movie was a passion project more than 15 years in the making, with Jenkins describing the book as an important part of his childhood. Released in November 2024, it earned positive reviews from critics and audiences, with Judy Greer and Beatrice Schneider among the standout performers. It’s a lovely choice for a family movie night.

Six unruly siblings known as the Herdmans have a reputation for causing trouble wherever they go. When they turn up at the local church looking for free snacks, they end up volunteering for the annual Christmas pageant and landing all the leading roles. Grace Bradley (Judy Greer), who has taken over directing the production for the first time, is left scrambling to prepare the children for their big performance. With the Herdmans unfamiliar with the Christmas story and the rest of the town convinced the show will be a disaster, rehearsals quickly become unpredictable.

“No Sleep ’Til Christmas” is a cozy holiday rom-com that first premiered on Freeform as part of its annual “25 Days of Christmas” lineup. The movie puts a fun spin on the festive formula with a quirky premise centred on two strangers struggling with severe insomnia who discover they can only fall asleep when they’re together. Dave Annable and Odette Annable lead the cast, and their real-life marriage brings an easy chemistry to the central relationship. It’s a lighthearted pick if you’re after a feel-good Christmas movie with a slightly unusual twist.

Lizzie (Odette Annable) is a successful event planner struggling with insomnia just weeks before her wedding to fiancé Josh (Charles Michael Davis). One night, she has an unexpected encounter with Billy (Dave Annable), a bartender who is also having trouble sleeping. After discovering they can both drift off peacefully when lying next to each other, Lizzie suggests an unusual arrangement. She offers to help Billy fund his dream of opening a bar in exchange for keeping her company at night. However, their increasingly complicated arrangement starts to interfere with Lizzie’s wedding plans.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Netflix is kicking off its original holiday movie lineup with “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a family drama based on W. Bruce Cameron’s 2019 novel. The story follows a family navigating a difficult festive season, with plenty of emotional moments alongside the usual Christmas cheer. Cameron co-wrote the screenplay with director Cathryn Michon, continuing their creative partnership after working together on “A Dog’s Purpose” and “A Dog’s Journey.” This is perfect for anyone who enjoys heartfelt animal movies and festive family stories.

Widowed grandfather Sander Goss (Dennis Quaid) is struggling to get along with his teenage granddaughter Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson) two years after losing his wife. When a sudden medical emergency leaves Ello’s mother in an induced coma just before Christmas, the family is thrown into turmoil. With the household struggling to cope, their loyal basset hound, Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), takes matters into his own paws. Alongside an energetic Corgi puppy named Ruby, Winstead sets out to bring the family together and help them prepare for Juliana’s return.

If you’d rather binge-watch a cozy mystery over the festive season, “Mistletoe Murders” is a great choice, especially with the series already climbing Netflix’s top 10. It originally began as an Audible audio drama in 2021, starring Cobie Smulders, before making the jump to television for Hallmark+ and the Hallmark Channel. The story brings a festive twist to the cozy mystery formula, pairing a charming small-town setting and plenty of Christmas decorations with a series of murder investigations. There’s nothing wrong with your holiday viewing having a little crime and suspense.

Emily Lane (Sarah Drew) runs Under the Mistletoe, a Christmas-themed gift shop in the small town of Fletcher’s Grove. Although she appears to be an ordinary shop owner, Emily has a mysterious past and a set of unusual skills that make her particularly good at investigating crimes. When a local murder puts one of her new friends under suspicion, Emily takes matters into her own hands to uncover the truth. Along the way, she crosses paths with Detective Sam Wilner (Peter Mooney), whose own investigations bring them closer together while raising questions about Emily’s real identity.

Another major Netflix original arriving this month is “Guarding Stars,” a festive romantic comedy based on Katherine Center’s bestselling novel “The Bodyguard.” The story follows a highly trained female protection agent who is assigned to look after a famous Hollywood actor, turning the usual action-romance formula on its head. Leighton Meester, best known for “Gossip Girl,” and Jared Padalecki of “Supernatural” and “Gilmore Girls” lead the cast, giving fans of both stars another reason to tune in. If you enjoy fun holiday romances with a little action and plenty of familiar faces, this one is worth adding to your watchlist.

Hannah Brooks (Leighton Meester) is a no-nonsense professional bodyguard assigned to protect Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki), a famous action movie star, during the Christmas holidays. When Jack returns to his family’s Montana ranch, Hannah accompanies him to keep him safe from an unwanted threat. To avoid raising suspicions about her real job, she agrees to pose as his girlfriend while staying with his family. However, as they spend more time together, their pretend relationship becomes increasingly complicated.

"A Dog's Perfect Christmas" (Netflix film)

From the bestselling author of A Dog’s Purpose, a tale of a family in crisis where a teenager, her grandfather, and his trusty basset hound struggle to keep the household together at Christmas.

A struggling pastor moves his family to a troubled New York neighborhood, where they must save a neglected church from foreclosure before Christmas.

A no-nonsense bodyguard heads to a Montana ranch with the famous actor she's protecting. But posing as a couple for Christmas soon sparks a real romance.

#3469. iPadOS 27.2 adds convenient new multitasking option on iPad

iPadOS 27.2 launched last week with a variety of new features for iPad, including a convenient change for multitasking.

When iPhone Duo first got into users’ hands, several reviews mentioned how the new Split View system felt more intuitive than iPadOS multitasking ever has.

And in iPadOS 27.2, there’s a convenient new multitasking change that’s likely inspired by iPhone Duo.

Apple hasn’t brought over the entire iOS system to the iPad. But it has made one common multitasking feature easier to set up: Split View.

From the official iPadOS 27.2 release notes:

Side-by-side multitasking is easier to set up with the option to choose a second app whenever you tile apps to the left or right with the window controls or menu bar

Starting with iPadOS 26 last year, setting up two apps side-by-side could fairly cumbersome.

You needed to open the first app, resize it, then swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see your other apps, select one, and in many cases manually resize the second app too.

But in iPadOS 27.2, any time you use Apple’s window resizing controls to tile an app left or right, you’ll immediately see the Home Screen and be able to tile a second app with a single tap.

FTA: "Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side."

Ok, great, but…then no one lists these keyboard shortcuts. Sure would have been helpful to paste them in here when talking about new features.

It’s not identical to the iPhone Duo experience, but it’s a lot closer to it than the old system was.

Once you master the built-in keyboard shortcuts for app tiling, it becomes even quicker and easier to set up your apps side-by-side.

What do you think of this multitasking change in iPadOS 27.2? Do you think Apple should apply its iPhone Duo learnings to the iPad? Let us know in the comments.

#3468. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3467. New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more

Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

Would you be interested in a product like HomeView Ultra? Let us know in the comments.

#3466. The 6 Best Thrillers Released Between 2020 and Now

The thrill of a thriller is how the story makes you feel. A great thriller film relies on sustained tension, high stakes, and constant uncertainty that keeps you on the edge of your seat. A great thriller works by manipulating how and when the audience learns crucial information. Often featuring tight editing, sharp sound design, dim lighting, and deliberate pacing to suffocate the comfort zone and build toward a memorable climax, a thriller becomes legendary when it leaves a lasting impression.

The 21st century has provided some extraordinary entries within the genre, but this current decade seems to be turning into a profound golden age. Since 2020, the thriller has become brilliantly risky, mixing big-budget masterpieces with mind-blowing indie projects that have altered the landscape. With so many brilliant films over the last six years, the six on this list have emerged as the very best. From game-changing horror thrillers to psychological dramas that mess with your mind, these six films became instant classics the moment they were released. What’s your favorite thriller of the 2020s?

In the highly underrated Pig, directed by Michael Sarnoski, Rob Feld (Nicolas Cage) is a reclusive truffle hunter living in the Oregon wilderness whose beloved foraging pig is suddenly stolen. To rescue her, he must return to his past life in the Portland culinary scene and confront the grief he left behind. It is a quiet, meditative drama about loss, artistic expression, and connection, not a traditional revenge thriller. By subverting genre tropes, Pig became the antithesis of thrillers, honing in on themes of authenticity and the power of connection.

Initially set up to look like a gritty "John Wick with a pig," where a hermit tracks down his stolen pet, the film abandons blood and retribution in favor of deep conversations and emotional vulnerability. Cage delivers a grounded, mournful, and restrained performance, moving into a new chapter of his storied career. The dynamic between Rob and his young, status-obsessed truffle buyer Amir (Alex Wolff) acts as a mirror for both to face their traumas head-on. The film becomes a poetic examination of how people process loss, regret, and the difference between fake artifice and genuine passion. Pig is a mesmerizing and moving story of love and loss that redefined how a thriller can be presented. ​​​​​​​

Don’t sleep on foreign films! The 2020s have seen a rise of foreign films finding their way into the Hollywood mainstream. Such was the case for Anatomy of a Fall. Directed by Justine Triet, the psychological courtroom thriller follows Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller), a German writer accused of murdering her French husband, Samuel Maleski (Samuel Theis), after he falls to his death from their secluded alpine chalet. With their visually impaired son, Daniel Maleski (Milo Machado-Graner), as the sole witness, the trial transforms from a forensic investigation into an intense, public dissection of the couple's turbulent marriage and conflicting realities. Ultimately, Anatomy of a Fall explores the ambiguous boundaries of truth, language, and memory when a relationship is put on trial.

The film emerged as a legal and psychological thriller because it treats the "truth" as an elusive, multi-layered question rather than a simple puzzle to be solved. It turns a murder investigation into a surgical dissection of an ordinary, flawed, and decaying relationship. Through the ambiguity of truth, the narrative explores how personal history, bias, and fiction can be weaponized in a courtroom. The film put the sensational Hüller on the map thanks to her stoic, razor-sharp, and deeply vulnerable performance. Earning the Palme d'Or at Cannes, Anatomy of a Fall strips away genre clichés to offer a haunting look at how private grief is put on public trial.

You’ll never look at your food the same after watching The Menu. Directed by Mark Mylod and written by Seth Reiss and Will Tracy, the film follows a young couple, Tyler (Nicholas Hoult) and Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy), and a group of ultra-wealthy elites who travel to a remote island to dine at an exclusive restaurant. The evening takes a sinister turn as the enigmatic celebrity chef, Chef Slowik (Ralph Fiennes), reveals that each conceptual course is part of a calculated, deadly plan to punish his pretentious guests. The Menu serves as a sharp satire on class divide, foodie culture, and the exploitation of the service industry.

The Menu stands out as an acid-tongued examination of the pretentious, hyper-exclusive fine-dining industry, using it as a microcosm to skewer classism, economic inequality, and the vanity of the ultra-wealthy. Set almost entirely on a remote private island, the movie builds claustrophobic, uninterrupted tension where every course on the menu escalates the dread. With biting thrills and shocking twists, The Menu delivers a delicious dish in which the audience laughs wholly at absurd foodie culture one moment and feels genuinely disturbed the next. Fiennes commands the screen as the terrifying, cult-leader-like Chef Slowik, while Taylor-Joy masters the grounded outsider who becomes the beacon of promise. The Menu brilliantly keeps you off-guard until the very last dish is presented. ​​​​​​​

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

A masterclass in modernizing a classic text, The Invisible Man brings fear, terror, and profound social commentary. Written and directed by Leigh Whannell, The Invisible Man tells the story of Cecilia Kass (Elisabeth Moss) as she escapes her abusive, wealthy optics scientist boyfriend, Adrian Griffin (Oliver Jackson-Cohen). After Adrian seemingly commits suicide, Cecilia becomes convinced she is being stalked and terrorized by an unseen, invisible force. With no one else believing her claims, she must fight independently to uncover the deadly truth and save herself. The Invisible Man earns its honorable reputation by transforming a classic sci-fi monster tale into a tense, grounded study of domestic abuse and gaslighting.

Instead of focusing on the mad scientist, the narrative centers on the victim. It mirrors the psychological isolation of real-world coercive control and gaslighting, where no one believes that an abuser is still haunting you. Whannell frequently frames Cecilia off-center in wide shots, leaving empty hallways and seemingly vacant rooms on screen, forcing you to scan the background, generating constant paranoia and suspense. Moss delivers an intensely physical performance, reacting to empty space, silent dread, and invisible physical force with visceral realism. It’s one of her best performances to date. The film is a masterclass in thrills, putting Whannell on the visionary map. ​​​​​​​

2026 is the year of low-budget horror masterpieces. Leading the charge is the incomparable Obsession. Written and directed by Curry Barker, the story follows a socially awkward man named Bear Bailey (Michael Johnston) who uses a cursed novelty toy called the One Wish Willow to force his coworker crush, Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette), to fall in love with him. While his wish initially seems to come true, Nikki's affection quickly warps into an extreme, violent, and terrifyingly possessive fixation. As the supernatural compulsion takes over, Bear finds himself trapped in a dangerous nightmare of his own making that escalates into fatal consequences. Earning itself a spot as a towering cinematic phenomenon, Obsession brilliantly injects terror into a seemingly basic "be careful what you wish for" setup.

Shot on a microbudget, Obsession shocked the world by grossing over $500 million worldwide. The viral word-of-mouth campaign worked as audiences were taken by the brilliant premise and conversations it sparked. On the surface, the film plays with a classic Faustian premise that becomes a brutal critique of male entitlement. The true psychological horror doesn't come from a masked killer, but from Bear’s willingness to strip away Nikki's autonomy and stay with her terrifying, cursed doppelgänger just to preserve his own wish-fulfillment fantasy. The film’s instant legendary status was earned through the dynamic duo of Johnston and Navarette. Barker builds suspense through classic tricks and craftsmanship. The boxed-in frame physically traps the audience with the characters, amplifying the intense feelings of domestic captivity and dread. It’s a masterclass in making silence itself feel threatening, using subtle tonality shifts and unsettling audio rumbles to make viewers physically uncomfortable. Obsession continues the trend of new voices and faces reshaping the genre's landscape. ​​​​​​​

One of the most groundbreaking and masterful thrillers in decades, Weapons is sheer brilliance. Written and directed by Zach Cregger, the supernatural mystery-horror thriller centers on a small town thrown into chaos after seventeen third-grade children from the same classroom inexplicably vanish into the dark at exactly 2:17 AM. The story utilizes a non-linear, multi-perspective narrative to follow a pariah teacher, Justine Gandy (Julia Garner), a grieving father, Archer Graff (Josh Brolin), and other local figures as they unearth a sinister web of blood rituals, police corruption, and witchcraft. Beneath its terrifying mystery is a story centered on the eccentric Aunt Gladys (Amy Madigan). Weapons serves as a deeper, personal allegory exploring generational trauma, grief, and the destructive nature of addiction.

In a time when franchises and blockbusters dominated Hollywood, Weapons delivered something genuinely ambitious, unnerving, and profound. Cregger weaves an intricate web across six distinct chapters, building tension purely through withheld information. Shot by cinematographer Larkin Seiple, the film utilizes constant, creeping tracking shots and slow zooms that refuse to let the audience look away. The claustrophobic nature is matched by a haunting sound design, generating visceral dread even when the horrors occur entirely off-screen. The film effortlessly balances bleak, psychological terror with sharp, pitch-black humor. Its tonal agility lets it shift from pure terror to surreal absurdity without ever breaking its spell. The film earned high honors thanks to Madigan’s iconic performance. She ensured Aunt Gladys earned a spot in the horror villain hall of fame. Weapons is a thriller masterpiece that became the new gold standard.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
